sources.title: Paul Graham on startups: ambition, formidable founders, shipping speed and AI
sources.originalTitle: Paul Graham On Startups, Ambition, and Great Founders
sources.summary: In a short YC interview, Paul Graham argues that starting a startup is essentially unchanged despite AI. Founder quality (being "formidable", driven by fear of failure) and shipping speed still decide outcomes, and you can still start on little money by hitting milestones that unlock the next round.

principles.text: Formidable means getting what you want in any situation; it aligns investor and founder interests.
principles.quote: I think that it's someone who who gets what they want. That's that's the test, right? Do you get what you want?

principles.text: The next giant company comes from the right founders, not a particular idea; founders look the same as 20 years ago.
principles.quote: The answer to your question of where the next giant company comes from is it comes from the right founders, right? It's not some particular idea.

principles.text: Day to day, founders are driven by fear of failure, not by dreams of becoming billionaires.
principles.quote: You know what actually motivates founders dayto-day? The fear of failure.

principles.text: A startup is no credential or easy major; pursue it only if you can endure years of brutal hardness.
principles.quote: With startups, there's no easy major, right? It's like applying to Harvard and being forced to study theoretical physics, right?

principles.text: You can still start on little money: do what you can with what you have and hit a milestone that convinces investors to fund the next stage.
principles.quote: So, you just do what you can on the money you got. As long as you can get to some kind of milestone, then you can convince investors to give you more.

principles.text: AI hasn't changed startup fundamentals; shipping speed still varies and many startups don't ship fast enough.
principles.quote: Everyone always asks me like with all this AI, is anything still the same? And the answer is so far almost everything is exactly the same.

sources.title: Paul Graham: why founders should go to Silicon Valley, then come back
sources.originalTitle: Paul Graham, Founder of Y Combinator, Live from Stockholm
sources.summary: Graham argues ambitious founders should spend time in the world's startup center for its peer density, serendipitous meetings, speed, investor competition and pay-it-forward culture. He says the best way to help Stockholm thrive is to go to Silicon Valley (ideally via YC) and then return, bringing back better startups, money and culture.

principles.text: Go to the center of your field: you get the best peers, and the talent pool is both better and bigger there.
principles.quote: What exactly do you get when you move to the big center? Um the answer to that question is always the same, too. You get the best peers.

principles.text: Serendipitous meetings are enormously valuable, and big centers produce far more of them.
principles.quote: if you're working on something ambitious, there's nothing in the world that's better than serendipitous meetings with people who are working on the same stuff.

principles.text: Silicon Valley investor competition forces fast decisions, and the speed does not hurt returns.
principles.quote: Silicon Valley investors get better returns than European investors despite having to decide so quickly.

principles.text: Seeing top founders up close turns an impossible goal into a hard, definite one, which is ideal for ambitious people.
principles.quote: it no longer seems an impossible goal, just a hard one. And for an ambitious person, there is nothing better than a high but definite threshold.

principles.text: Silicon Valley's culture of helping people without keeping score lets favors scale, and it will make you more helpful too.
principles.quote: You just like do favors left and right and don't even keep track of whether you're ahead or behind.

principles.text: Go to the hub for a while, then return home: you improve your startup, bring money back and import startup culture.
principles.quote: You make your own startup better, so the average quality of startups here is increased. You're probably going to bring money back with you from Silicon Valley investors.

sources.title: Paul Graham on big startup ideas: start tiny, grow into the frightening thing
sources.summary: Graham's 2012 keynote lists seven huge startup ideas (search, email, universities, Hollywood, a new Apple, the old Moore's law, ongoing diagnosis) and argues the biggest ideas frighten founders away. The way in is to start with a small, concrete thing a few users want, not a direct frontal attack.

principles.text: The biggest startup ideas repel you because they threaten your identity; learn to tack into that wind.
principles.quote: the biggest startup idea is threaten your identity

principles.text: Attack a giant idea by finding the tiny seed that grows into it, like a search engine used only by top hackers.
principles.quote: the way to attack all these really gigantic ideas is to find the tiny thing that turns into the gigantic idea right

principles.text: Don't announce the big ambition; build a harmless-sounding small product and let people notice the replacement later.
principles.quote: do not make a direct frontal attack on the problem don't say for example that you're going to replace email

principles.text: Really big things empirically start small and grow; founders themselves rarely know how big they'll get.
principles.quote: empirically the way to do really big things seem to be to start with small things and um grow them bigger

principles.text: Prefer a blurry view of the future to a precise one: start with something that works, then move toward the opportunity.
principles.quote: empirically it's probably better to have a blurry one

principles.text: Powerful people in pain are an opportunity: they will adopt your product first and solve your chicken-and-egg problem.
principles.quote: whenever powerful people are in pain that is an opportunity to make lots of money

sources.title: Before the Startup: six counterintuitive rules Paul Graham would tell his own kids
sources.summary: Graham argues startups are counterintuitive, like skiing, so instincts mislead. Success comes from making something users want, not gaming the system or learning startup mechanics. Don't start one in college; instead learn powerful things and let ideas emerge unconsciously from side projects.

principles.text: What you need is expertise in your own users, not expertise in startups.
principles.quote: What you need to know to suceed in a startup is not expertise in startups, what you need is expertise in your own users.

principles.text: Growth hacks are bullshit; growth comes from making something users love and telling them.
principles.quote: the way to make your startup grow is to make something that users really love. Right, and then tell them about it. So that's what you have to do. That is growth hacks right there.

principles.text: Don't play house: going through the motions of a startup neglects making something people want.
principles.quote: while imitating all the outward forms of starting a startup, they have neglected the one thing that's actually essential which is to make something people want.

principles.text: Gaming the system stops working in startups because users are too blunt to fool.
principles.quote: There's only users. And all users care about is whether your software. Does what they want, right? They're like sharks.

principles.text: Best way to convince investors is to grow fast; tricks matter an order of magnitude less.
principles.quote: the best way to convince investors, is to start a startup that's actually doing well, meaning growing fast, and then simply tell investors so.

principles.text: Don't try to think of startup ideas; become the kind of person who has them unconsciously by learning things that matter.
principles.quote: 1, learn about things that matter. 2, work on problems that interest you. 3, with people you like and respect.

sources.title: Paul Graham: Why being good works as startup strategy (Startup School 08)
sources.summary: Graham argues that "make something people want" plus "don't worry about money early" describes something that looks like a nonprofit, and that successful startups often behave that way. Benevolence boosts morale, attracts help and talent, and works as a decision compass. Startups should launch fast and stay hard to kill.

principles.text: Make something people want; money is easier than making something great, so defer the business model.
principles.quote: Don't worry too much about money. Um, not because it's not important, but because it's so much easier than making something great.

principles.text: Very successful startups often behave like nonprofits, and nonprofit ideas often make good companies.
principles.quote: Very successful startups often behave like nonprofits. And when you think about nonprofit ideas, surprisingly often, they'd make good companies.

principles.text: When small you can't bully users, so you must charm them; being nice is how you grow.
principles.quote: When you're small, you can't bully your users, so you have to charm them.

principles.text: Use "do what's best for your users" as the compass for the thousands of decisions a startup faces.
principles.quote: Just do whatever is best for your users, right? You can hold on to that like a rope in a hurricane and it will save you if anything can.

principles.text: Launch quickly so users exist to take care of; serving them forces you to learn what they want.
principles.quote: as soon as you launch the Tamagotchi effect kicks in. Once you have users to take care of you're forced to figure out what they want and that information is actually very valuable.

principles.text: Commitment plus cheap operations makes a startup very hard to kill, which also impresses investors.
principles.quote: If you're really committed and your startup is cheap to run, you become very hard to kill.

sources.title: Paul Graham on startups: do things that don't scale, launch early, pick determined founders
sources.originalTitle: A Conversation with Paul Graham - Moderated by Geoff Ralston
sources.summary: In a Startup School conversation with Geoff Ralston, Paul Graham recounts how ViaWeb started and distills lessons on co-founders, manual early work, launching a quantum of utility fast, and why determination beats smarts. He also covers competitors, pricing, raising too much money, and user interviews.

principles.text: Do things that don't scale early: handmade, manual work for first customers teaches you the most.
principles.quote: what do things that don't scale means is do those things early on anyway because you know if you don't do them you'll never be big and you've got nothing to lose and also you learn a lot from it

principles.text: A constant growth rate compounds, so early on just keep manually getting the next customer.
principles.quote: as long as your growth rate is good it doesn't matter how small the number is because a grow a constant growth rate means exponential growth and that means the base number will soon take care of itself

principles.text: Launch as soon as one person would be glad you did; launching late is a risk too.
principles.quote: launch as soon as you have a quantum of utility which means as soon as you're there's one person in the world who is glad that you launched

principles.text: Determination matters far more than smarts for founders.
principles.quote: it's not that important to be smart um it's much much more important to be determined

principles.text: Competitors rarely kill startups; poor execution does. Just run your own race.
principles.quote: what makes companies fail most of the time is poor execution by the founders

principles.text: Founders' typical mistake is avoiding users and shipping too slowly; find someone with a problem and fix it.
principles.quote: you'd be way better off finding someone anyone who has a problem that they will pay you to fix and fixing it and then seeing if you can find more people like that

sources.title: Startup School 2013 office hours: Paul Graham and Sam Altman on launching, markets and founder fit
sources.originalTitle: Office Hours at Startup School 2013 with Paul Graham and Sam Altman
sources.summary: Live office hours where Paul Graham and Sam Altman question three early startups (a coding game, a progress-video site, a customs brokerage). Recurring themes: don't over-optimize early, test the thing that matters, copy industry defaults, avoid pitching huge markets, and prefer founders who can't stand big-company jobs.

principles.text: Don't over-optimize or wire in an outcome too early; let the product grow into what it becomes and stay empirical.
principles.quote: Don't be don't like like um overoptimize too early. Like let it grow into whatever it's going to grow into.

principles.text: Test the thing that actually matters during beta, such as whether content gets shared and watched, rather than assuming it.
principles.quote: It seems that would have been really important to test during the beta is will people share these on YouTube and do they get watched?

principles.text: Long tenure at a big company counts against a founder; the best founders can't stand it.
principles.quote: if we are looking at some someone's application and they worked for a long time for a large company that's that's actually bad to us because like the the best startup founders probably could not stand that

principles.text: In an unfamiliar industry, use that industry's norms as your default starting point.
principles.quote: whatever they do is probably the the default thing to start with.

principles.text: Huge market numbers hurt credibility with investors; very big markets are bad for startups, not good.
principles.quote: You know, really big markets are bad for startups, not good. Yeah. If you say a too big number, the investors just they just don't believe it, right?

principles.text: If the product is already engaging, stop holding back users for polish; launch and let them spread it.
principles.quote: Well, if it's engaging enough now, you've ironed off out ironed out enough kinks.

sources.title: Paul Graham on judging founders, boosting ambition, and YC interviews (Conversations with Tyler)
sources.originalTitle: Paul Graham on Ambition, Art, and Evaluating Talent | Conversations with Tyler
sources.summary: Graham explains how he evaluates early-stage founders (people over plans, determination via stories, real understanding), why YC interviews work in about 10 minutes, and how he pushes founders to think bigger. He also covers obsessing over missed companies and how fame arrived at YC unnoticed.

principles.text: The earlier the stage, the more you are judging the founders rather than the business plan.
principles.quote: the earlier you're judging startups the more you're just judging the founders

principles.text: Judge determination from stories of what people did when things went wrong, not from how tough they act.
principles.quote: the way you tell determination is not so much from talking to them as from asking them stories about things that have happened to them that's where you can see determination

principles.text: Test whether founders truly understand their idea versus having a newspaper-level grasp of it.
principles.quote: I can tell if people know what they're talking about when they come and talk about some idea especially some technical idea

principles.text: Help founders think bigger by asking how an idea could be larger; pushing costs the advisor no effort.
principles.quote: there is a skill to it to take an idea and say okay so here's an idea so how could this be bigger

principles.text: Working with someone for a few minutes reveals most of what you need; minds rarely flip after about seven minutes.
principles.quote: you see what it's like to work with people by working with them for 10 minutes and that's enough it turns out

principles.text: Obsess over failure cases and fix process flaws immediately, e.g. require two reviewers per application.
principles.quote: after that every application had to be seen by at least two people

sources.title: Paul Graham and Mike Moritz on early-stage investing: build, be candid, skip forecasts
sources.summary: At a revenue bootcamp fireside chat, Paul Graham explains how YC picks founders (people who build things for love, not proven résumés), why he ignores revenue forecasts, why founders should be candid with smart investors, and how to spot the next platform. Mike Moritz of Sequoia adds the VC view.

principles.text: Proven means evidence you love building: ask what they made outside school or work because they liked it.
principles.quote: the big question we ask is what have you made outside of school or work because you liked it? Because if you don't like it, you're not going to do well as a startup founder.

principles.text: Early on, ignore revenue forecasts; what matters is whether people will really want what you're building.
principles.quote: We have a don't ask, don't tell policy on revenue projections. We don't even ask.

principles.text: Show care rather than announce it; generic words like 'passion' set off the BS detector.
principles.quote: you shouldn't say the word passion. You should just seem like you care.

principles.text: With smart investors be candid, like telling a doctor your symptoms; they will spot a lie anyway.
principles.quote: the smarter the investor, the more you should just be candid.

principles.text: Best startup ideas are things the founders themselves want to use, or someone close to them wants.
principles.quote: It's ideal if they're building something they themselves want to use. The next best thing is something, you know, that someone very close to them, like their wife or sibling wants to use.

principles.text: Predict which platforms win by watching what hackers themselves use, because they build for what they own.
principles.quote: look for the platforms that hackers themselves use and those are the ones exciting things are going to happen to you

sources.title: Paul Graham: Why you should go to Silicon Valley, then come back
sources.originalTitle: Paul Graham speech at YC Startup School - Stockholm April 2026
sources.summary: At YC Startup School Stockholm, Graham argues ambitious founders should move to the center of their field, at least for a while. The big center gives better peers, serendipity, faster decisions, a calibrated sense of your own ability, and a culture of helping. Going and returning also strengthens your home hub.

principles.text: Go to the center of your field; you can return later, but you should at least go.
principles.quote: You can go there for a bit and then come back, but you should at least go.

principles.text: The main benefit of the big center is the best peers: more people and better people, concentrated in one place.
principles.quote: You get the best peers. And in fact, the talent pool expands in two dimensions. The people are better and there's also a lot more of them.

principles.text: Serendipitous meetings with people working on the same ambitious thing are enormously valuable, and big centers produce more of them.
principles.quote: if you're working on something ambitious, there's nothing in the world that's better than serendipitous meetings with people who are working on the same stuff.

principles.text: Silicon Valley investors decide fast because of competition, and it doesn't hurt their returns.
principles.quote: Silicon Valley investors get better returns than European investors despite having to decide so quickly.

principles.text: The biggest advantage of the center is what it does to you: seeing top founders up close makes ambition feel hard but achievable.
principles.quote: for an ambitious person, there is nothing better than a high but definite threshold.

principles.text: Silicon Valley's pay-it-forward culture: help people without keeping score, which lets favors scale.
principles.quote: You just like do favors left and right and don't even keep track of whether you're ahead or behind.

sources.title: Paul Graham on handing off YC, founder conflicts, focus, and finding your first 500 true fans
sources.originalTitle: Y Combinator's Paul Graham sits down with Jason at LAUNCH Festival 2014
sources.summary: A 2014 fireside chat where Graham explains why he handed YC to Sam Altman, how YC's early model was a summer-job accident, and what he has learned from 632 startups. Key themes: co-founder relationships, brute focus on the one bottleneck, starting with a small intense fire of users, and why determination beats raw intelligence.

principles.text: Pick the single most important thing and do only that; founders already know the answer but don't ask themselves.
principles.quote: the most important thing for startups to do is to focus ah right because there's so many things you could be doing one of them is the most important you should be doing that and not any of the others

principles.text: Start with a small, intense fire: find the few people who want your product a lot and make them extremely happy.
principles.quote: it's impossible to make something that a large number of people want a lot so you've got to find people who want what you're making a lot um and that's necessarily going to be a small number and that's okay

principles.text: Test product-market fit by whether users would be bummed if you stopped, not whether friends say it's good.
principles.quote: just so long as you make Sam feel that he would be bummed if you stopped working on this that's the test right not like your friends say oh yeah it's good I'll use it right

principles.text: Get a co-founder; founders must get along, and the best teams have each founder be king of their own domain.
principles.quote: that's the model that works that's how you have multiple people who are each extremely effective not step on one another's toes

principles.text: Determination and effectiveness beat raw brains; smart but ineffectual founders disappoint.
principles.quote: you can be surprisingly stupid if you're sufficiently determined right

principles.text: Starting a startup is the most efficient route to wealth but is necessarily painful; no pain suggests not trying hard enough.
principles.quote: if it's not a certain amount of painful you're probably not trying hard enough

sources.title: Paul Graham on startup ideas, founders, and making things people want (Moonshots clips)
sources.summary: Podcast hosts discuss Paul Graham using clips of him speaking. He argues good ideas come from side projects rather than brainstorming, that expertise in users beats startup mechanics, that founders matter more than ideas, and that doing things manually and iterating quickly with users beats polish.

principles.text: Don't brainstorm startup ideas; build a mind and life that produces them unconsciously, often as side projects.
principles.quote: the way to get startup ideas is not to try to think of startup ideas

principles.text: Succeeding requires deep expertise in your users, not expertise in how startups work.
principles.quote: What you need to know to succeed in a startup is not expertise in startups what you need is expertise in your own users

principles.text: Going through the motions of a startup (funding, office, hires) neglects the only essential thing: making something people want.
principles.quote: they have neglected the one thing that's actually essential which is to make something people want

principles.text: At the earliest stage, the founders matter far more than the idea.
principles.quote: the founder is more important than the idea a lot more important

principles.text: Do things manually for early customers; it is worth the unscalable work because you learn a lot.
principles.quote: it's so important to get early customers that if you have to do a ton of manual stuff that's okay you'll learn a lot from it

principles.text: Ship a rough first version fast and iterate through many rounds of user conversations.
principles.quote: as long as you get it out there very quickly it doesn't matter as if it's if it's not great because you start the conversation with users

sources.title: Paul Graham on picking founders, honesty with investors, and why forecasts don't matter
sources.originalTitle: Fireside Chat: Paul Graham, Mike Moritz, Guy Kawasaki
sources.summary: At a Revenue Boot Camp fireside chat with Mike Moritz and Guy Kawasaki, Paul Graham explains what YC looks for in early founders. He stresses people who build because they love it, candor with smart investors, and building something people want over spreadsheet forecasts.

principles.text: Back founders who build for fun, not duty. Ask what they made outside work or school.
principles.quote: the big question we ask is what have you made outside of school or work because you liked it because if you don't like it you're not going to do well as a startup founder

principles.text: Be candid with smart investors, like telling a doctor your symptoms. They will catch a lie.
principles.quote: the better the investor the more it should be like going to the doctor like don't lie about your symptoms tell them exactly what's going on

principles.text: The best financial forecast is building something people really want; the money follows.
principles.quote: I think the best financial forecast is a sense that you're developing something that people will really care and want and if they really care and want the money will follow

principles.text: Ideally build something you yourself want to use; next best is something someone close to you wants.
principles.quote: it's ideal if they're building something they themselves want to use the next best thing is something you know that someone very close to them like their wife or sibling wants to use

principles.text: Predict winning platforms by watching what hackers themselves use, since they build for those platforms.
principles.quote: look for the platforms that hackers themselves use and those are the ones exciting things are going to happen to you

principles.text: A startup isn't dead until the founders give up; early on they can morph it into anything.
principles.quote: as long as the founders haven't given up they can morph the company into anything

sources.title: Paul Graham on how YC grew by word of mouth, demo day "vertebrae" pitches, and AI's limits
sources.outlet: The Social Radars Podcast and Y Combinator
sources.summary: Paul Graham reminisces with Jessica Livingston and Carolyn Levy about how Y Combinator grew with no deliberate marketing: alumni told their friends. He also explains how he coached demo day pitches, expanded founders' ideas, and why founder needs remain the best source of startup ideas even with AI.

principles.text: Growth came from being genuinely helpful so users told their peers; word of mouth compounds exponentially.
principles.quote: I think it was simply that it helped them a lot and they would tell their friends and then their friends would do it, too. And then, you know, well, that's a recipe for exponential growth

principles.text: Publicity only matters if your actual target audience sees it; press the audience doesn't read barely helps.
principles.quote: the only kind of out there that you care about is whether potential applicants know about you.

principles.text: Build a pitch around about five memorable sentences, framed as a logical proof that expected value is high.
principles.quote: you really can only hope that they'll remember about five sentences worth of stuff in the very best case. And so, you should decide in advance what those sentences will be.

principles.text: Pitches should be logical proofs, not fast-talking marketing speak.
principles.quote: Demo day presentation shouldn't be like fast-talking marketing speak. They should be almost like logical proofs of why this company is good to invest in.

principles.text: Early in a startup, often the best help is making the idea much bigger.
principles.quote: I would do it like maybe 1/3 of the office hours I did. We would figure out how to make an idea much bigger.

principles.text: The best source of startup ideas is the founders' own needs, which AI lacks.
principles.quote: You know what the best source of startup ideas is? Your own needs.

sources.title: Do Things that Don't Scale: recruit users manually and delight them
sources.summary: Startups take off because founders push them, usually through unscalable work: recruiting users one at a time, over-delivering on experience, and starting in a narrow market. Big launches and partnerships rarely work. The unscalable effort also shapes company culture for the better.

principles.text: Startups rarely grow by themselves; founders must manually recruit the first users.
principles.quote: Actually startups take off because the founders make them take off.

principles.text: Measure progress by weekly growth rate; small absolute numbers compound into big ones.
principles.quote: The mistake they make is to underestimate the power of compound growth. We encourage every startup to measure their progress by weekly growth rate.

principles.text: Make the experience of being your user insanely great, even if the early product is buggy and incomplete.
principles.quote: It's not the product that should be insanely great, but the experience of being your user.

principles.text: Start with a deliberately narrow market to reach critical mass quickly, like a contained fire.
principles.quote: It's like keeping a fire contained at first to get it really hot before adding more logs.

principles.text: Do manually what you plan to automate later; you'll know exactly what to build.
principles.quote: When you only have a small number of users, you can sometimes get away with doing by hand things that you plan to automate later.

principles.text: Big launches and partnerships usually don't work; happy early users matter more than launch size.
principles.quote: How well you're doing a few months later will depend more on how happy you made those users than how many there were of them.

sources.title: Startup = Growth: why growth rate is the compass for every startup decision
sources.summary: Paul Graham argues a startup is a company designed to grow fast, and everything else (funding, acquisitions, technology) follows from growth. Founders should know their weekly growth rate, pick a target, and use it to make every decision, letting growth pressure evolve the idea.

principles.text: A startup is defined by growth, not by tech, funding or an exit; everything else follows from it.
principles.quote: A startup is a company designed to grow fast. Being newly founded does not in itself make a company a startup.

principles.text: Know your growth rate as a ratio, not an absolute count of new customers.
principles.quote: What matters is not the absolute number of new customers, but the ratio of new customers to existing ones.

principles.text: Benchmark weekly growth: 5-7% is good, 10% exceptional, 1% means you haven't figured it out yet.
principles.quote: A good growth rate during YC is 5-7% a week. If you can hit 10% a week you're doing exceptionally well.

principles.text: Pick a target growth rate and just hit it every week; use it to decide everything.
principles.quote: You can use that target growth rate to make all your decisions for you; anything that gets you the growth you need is ipso facto right.

principles.text: Use growth as evolutionary pressure: modify the idea until it grows, and follow it past your initial vision.
principles.quote: anything that grows consistently at 10% a week is almost certainly a better idea than you started with.

principles.text: Act rather than over-strategize; weekly targets force action, which is the high bit of success.
principles.quote: Nine times out of ten, sitting around strategizing is just a form of procrastination.

sources.title: How to Get Startup Ideas: live in the future, notice what's missing, build what's interesting
sources.summary: Paul Graham argues you shouldn't try to think up startup ideas. Become someone at the leading edge of a fast-changing field and notice problems, ideally ones you have yourself. Good ideas are narrow, deep "wells" that a small group wants badly. Ignore the schlep and unsexy filters, and worry about users rather than competitors.

principles.text: Don't brainstorm startup ideas; look for problems, preferably your own.
principles.quote: The way to get startup ideas is not to try to think of startup ideas. It's to look for problems, preferably problems you have yourself.

principles.text: Build a narrow, deep well: a small group wanting it badly beats a broad group mildly interested.
principles.quote: you can either build something a large number of people want a small amount, or something a small number of people want a large amount. Choose the latter.

principles.text: Test an idea by asking who wants it right now, even as a crappy v1 from unknown founders.
principles.quote: Who wants this so much that they'll use it even when it's a crappy version one made by a two-person startup they've never heard of? If you can't answer that, the idea is probably bad.

principles.text: Live in the future and build what's missing; notice ideas rather than think them up.
principles.quote: The verb you want to be using with respect to startup ideas is not "think up" but "notice."

principles.text: Turn off the schlep and unsexy filters; tedious problems hold valuable, uncrowded ideas.
principles.quote: If you let your mind wander a few blocks down the street to the messy, tedious ideas, you'll find valuable ones just sitting there waiting to be implemented.

principles.text: Focus on users, not competitors; a crowded market signals demand if you see what others overlook.
principles.quote: Err on the side of doing things where you'll face competitors. Inexperienced founders usually give competitors more credit than they deserve.

sources.title: Default Alive or Default Dead?: Know if you reach profitability before the money runs out
sources.summary: Paul Graham argues that any startup older than 8-9 months should know whether, at current expenses and growth, it reaches profitability on its remaining money. Not knowing leads to the fatal pinch. The main way to avoid being default dead is not to hire too fast, and to seek growth through product evolution and doing things that don't scale.

principles.text: Know whether you're default alive: do you reach profitability on current money at current growth and expenses?
principles.quote: Assuming their expenses remain constant and their revenue growth is what it has been over the last several months, do they make it to profitability on the money they have left?

principles.text: Start asking the default alive/dead question too early rather than too late.
principles.quote: it's probably not that dangerous to start worrying too early that you're default dead, whereas it's very dangerous to start worrying too late.

principles.text: Never treat fundraising as more than plan A; write down plan B and when you'll switch to it.
principles.quote: you can never safely treat fundraising as more than a plan A. You should always have a plan B as well: you should know (as in write down) precisely what you'll need to do to survive if you can't raise more money

principles.text: Investor interest is a function of growth; over 5x a year lets you start to count on it, but never fully.
principles.quote: As a rule their interest is a function of growth. If you have steep revenue growth, say over 5x a year, you can start to count on investors being interested even if you're not profitable.

principles.text: Don't hire too fast; it's the biggest killer of startups that raise money.
principles.quote: Hiring too fast is by far the biggest killer of startups that raise money.

principles.text: If growth is slow, fix the product rather than hiring; early on the product needs to evolve more than be built out.
principles.quote: At this early stage, the product needs to evolve more than to be "built out," and that's usually easier with fewer people.

sources.title: Maker's Schedule, Manager's Schedule: why meetings cost makers half a day
sources.summary: Paul Graham distinguishes the manager's schedule (one-hour slots) from the maker's schedule (half-day blocks at least). A single meeting can wreck a maker's afternoon and even the morning before it. He explains how Y Combinator copes with office hours clustered at the end of the day, and why speculative meetings are only cheap for managers.

principles.text: Makers need half-day blocks; hour slots are barely enough to get started on hard work.
principles.quote: You can't write or program well in units of an hour. That's barely enough time to get started.

principles.text: One meeting can wreck a maker's whole afternoon by splitting it into pieces too small for hard work.
principles.quote: A single meeting can blow a whole afternoon, by breaking it into two pieces each too small to do anything hard in.

principles.text: Anticipated interruptions lower morale and discourage ambitious projects, which sit near the limit of your capacity.
principles.quote: ambitious projects are by definition close to the limits of your capacity. A small decrease in morale is enough to kill them off.

principles.text: Cluster unavoidable meetings at the end of the day using office hours, so they compress the day but never interrupt it.
principles.quote: By using the classic device for simulating the manager's schedule within the maker's: office hours.

principles.text: Split the day into a maker half and a manager half, protecting deep work from interruption.
principles.quote: in effect I had two workdays each day, one on the manager's schedule and one on the maker's.

principles.text: Speculative meetings like grabbing coffee are free for managers but very costly for makers.
principles.quote: Speculative meetings are terribly costly if you're on the maker's schedule, though.

sources.title: Founder Mode: why scaling advice to "hire good people and let them work" fails founders
sources.summary: Graham argues there are two ways to run a company: founder mode and manager mode. Standard advice to hire good people and give them room is how to run a company you didn't found, and it damages founder-led companies. Founder mode breaks the rule that CEOs deal only with direct reports, and is still poorly understood.

principles.text: Conventional scaling advice is manager mode, written for professional managers, and it often damages founder-led companies.
principles.quote: what they were being told was how to run a company you hadn't founded — how to run a company if you're merely a professional manager. But this m.o. is so much less effective that to founders it feels broken.

principles.text: Scaling a startup does not have to mean switching to manager mode. Founders can do things managers can't.
principles.quote: There are things founders can do that managers can't, and not doing them feels wrong to founders, because it is.

principles.text: Treating org-chart subtrees as black boxes and avoiding details can let weak hires drive the company down.
principles.quote: hire good people and give them room to do their jobs. Sounds great when it's described that way, doesn't it? Except in practice, judging from the report of founder after founder, what this often turns out to mean is: hire professional fakers and let them drive the company into the ground.

principles.text: Founder mode breaks the rule that the CEO engages only through direct reports. Skip-level meetings become normal.
principles.quote: it's going to break the principle that the CEO should engage with the company only via his or her direct reports. "Skip-level" meetings will become the norm

principles.text: Founders can use unconventional mechanisms, like Jobs's retreat for the 100 most important people regardless of rank, to keep a big company feeling like a startup.
principles.quote: Steve Jobs used to run an annual retreat for what he considered the 100 most important people at Apple, and these were not the 100 people highest on the org chart.

principles.text: Delegation is still necessary at scale, and autonomy borders vary by company and over time as managers earn trust.
principles.quote: Obviously founders can't keep running a 2000 person company the way they ran it when it had 20. There's going to have to be some amount of delegation.

sources.title: Before the Startup: six counterintuitive lessons for would-be founders
sources.summary: Paul Graham explains why startups defy instinct and how to prepare. Expertise in your users and problem beats expertise in startup mechanics. Gaming the system stops working; only making something people want matters. Good ideas come from learning deeply and following interesting problems, not from brainstorming startup ideas.

principles.text: Startups are counterintuitive, so don't blindly trust your instincts about them.
principles.quote: But whatever the reason, starting a startup is a task where you can't always trust your instincts.

principles.text: Be an expert on your users and their problem, not on startup mechanics.
principles.quote: The way to succeed in a startup is not to be an expert on startups, but to be an expert on your users and the problem you're solving for them.

principles.text: Gaming the system stops working in a startup. Users only care whether the product does what they want.
principles.quote: So this is the third counterintuitive thing to remember about startups: starting a startup is where gaming the system stops working.

principles.text: Growth and fundraising both come down to making something people want.
principles.quote: And we have to tell them the best way to do that is simply to make something people want.

principles.text: A product users love beats fundraising tricks and a flat usage graph.
principles.quote: A founder who knows nothing about fundraising but has made something users love will have an easier time raising money than one who knows every trick in the book but has a flat usage graph.

principles.text: Don't try to think of startup ideas; become the kind of person who stumbles onto them.
principles.quote: that the way to get startup ideas is not to try to think of startup ideas.

sources.title: How to Raise Money: Paul Graham's rules for seed fundraising
sources.summary: Graham gives founders a simple rule set for phase 2 (seed) fundraising: stay out of fundraising until you decide to raise, talk to investors in parallel ranked by expected value, treat anything short of a firm offer as a no, and accept acceptable offers quickly. Fundraising is a means to an end; the real test is revenue, so get it over with and get back to making things and talking to users.

principles.text: Be in fundraising mode or not; it is so distracting that you should focus fully, finish fast, and get back to work.
principles.quote: Because fundraising is so distracting, a startup should either be in fundraising mode or not.

principles.text: Treat every investor as a no until they give a definite offer with no contingencies, and get commitments confirmed.
principles.quote: Treat investors as saying no till they unequivocally say yes, in the form of a definite offer with no contingencies.

principles.text: Talk to investors in parallel, prioritized by expected value (chance they say yes times how good it would be).
principles.quote: When you talk to investors your m.o. should be breadth-first search, weighted by expected value.

principles.text: Judge investors by actions, and always ask what happens next and what they need to decide.
principles.quote: Never leave a meeting with an investor without asking what happens next.

principles.text: Valuation is not what matters. Priorities are getting the money you need, then good investors, with valuation at best third.
principles.quote: The number one thing you want from phase 2 fundraising is to get the money you need, so you can get back to focusing on the real test, the success of your company.

principles.text: Accept acceptable offers greedily rather than waiting for something better; investors who only invest after others do are worth nothing early.
principles.quote: If someone makes you an acceptable offer, take it.

sources.title: Schlep Blindness: why the best startup ideas hide behind tedious, unpleasant work
sources.summary: Paul Graham argues that founders unconsciously avoid ideas involving painful schleps, so great ideas like Stripe sit unexploited in plain sight. Schleps are what business consists of, and scary, ambitious ideas face less competition. Ignorance, and asking what problem you wish someone else would solve for you, are the antidotes.

principles.text: Schleps are not avoidable; they are largely what business consists of. Jump in like a cold pool.
principles.quote: schleps are not merely inevitable, but pretty much what business consists of. A company is defined by the schleps it will undertake.

principles.text: Dislike of schleps is unconscious, so your mind filters out ideas involving painful work before you consider them.
principles.quote: Your unconscious won't even let you see ideas that involve painful schleps. That's schlep blindness.

principles.text: Ambitious, intimidating ideas are undervalued because fewer founders pursue them, so there is less competition.
principles.quote: If you pick an ambitious idea, you'll have less competition, because everyone else will have been frightened off by the challenges involved.

principles.text: Stripe is the prime example: thousands knew payments were painful, yet founders built recipe sites instead.
principles.quote: Because schlep blindness prevented people from even considering the idea of fixing payments.

principles.text: Ignorance of obstacles is the best antidote; founders grow with the problems, which explains young founders' edge.
principles.quote: the most valuable antidote to schlep blindness is probably ignorance.

principles.text: To spot schlep-heavy ideas, remove yourself: ask what problem you wish someone else would solve for you.
principles.quote: Instead of asking "what problem should I solve?" ask "what problem do I wish someone else would solve for me?"

sources.title: Ramen Profitable: why covering founders' living expenses buys time and leverage
sources.summary: Paul Graham defines ramen profitability as a startup making just enough to pay the founders' living expenses. It buys time and independence from investors, and it is not the destination. He lists four advantages (better terms, investor appeal, morale, no fundraising distraction) and warns about sliding into consulting.

principles.text: Ramen profitability means covering founders' living expenses; its value is buying time, not signaling success.
principles.quote: Ramen profitable means a startup makes just enough to pay the founders' living expenses.

principles.text: Once you're ramen profitable you stop being at the mercy of investors and get better terms.
principles.quote: The main significance of this type of profitability is that you're no longer at the mercy of investors.

principles.text: Even small profitability reassures investors: someone pays you, you're serious about users, and you keep costs low.
principles.quote: If you're already profitable, on however small a scale, it shows that (a) you can get at least someone to pay you, (b) you're serious about building things people want, and (c) you're disciplined enough to keep expenses low.

principles.text: Covering your own expenses lifts morale by making survival the default, and responsibility is what makes startups hard.
principles.quote: Now survival is the default, instead of dying.

principles.text: Fundraising wrecks productivity because it takes over the one urgent problem you think about constantly.
principles.quote: Raising money is terribly distracting. You're lucky if your productivity is a third of what it was before.

principles.text: Beware drifting into consulting: startups must make a product that scales, and ramen profitability is only a trick for not dying.
principles.quote: A startup's destination is to grow really big; ramen profitability is a trick for not dying en route.

sources.title: The Hardest Lessons for Startups to Learn: release early, ship constantly, fear the right things
sources.originalTitle: The Hardest Lessons for Startups to Learn
sources.summary: Paul Graham distills seven counterintuitive startup lessons he finds himself repeating to YC founders. The core themes: release a minimal v1 fast, keep shipping small improvements, obsess over users and conversion, fear other startups and self-inflicted wounds instead of big companies, stay determined but flexible, and never count on a deal until it closes.

principles.text: Release a minimal v1 fast, then improve it from user reactions. Startups die from being too slow, not too quick.
principles.quote: I've seen a lot of startups die because they were too slow to release stuff, and none because they were too quick.

principles.text: Keep pumping out small improvements every day or two. Constant improvement doubles as marketing and builds fanatical loyalty.
principles.quote: If you're the rare exception-- a company that actually listens-- you'll generate fanatical loyalty. You won't need to advertise, because your users will do it for you.

principles.text: Explain what you do in one or two sentences, put your best stuff on the front page, and show rather than tell.
principles.quote: A startup should be able to explain in one or two sentences exactly what it does.

principles.text: Measure conversion of casual visitors into users via growth rate. Decent growth wins in the end; if not, fix something.
principles.quote: If you have decent growth, you'll win in the end, no matter how obscure you are now. And if you don't, you need to fix something.

principles.text: Fear other startups and self-inflicted wounds (internal disputes, inertia, ignoring users), not big companies. Ignoring users is worst.
principles.quote: Way more startups hose themselves than get crushed by competitors. There are a lot of ways to do it, but the three main ones are internal disputes, inertia, and ignoring users.

principles.text: Assume deals won't happen and keep looking for alternatives. Your only leverage in a deal is genuinely not needing it.
principles.quote: The only way a startup can have any leverage in a deal is genuinely not to need it.

sources.title: What Startups Are Really Like: 19 founder surprises that all trace back to "a startup is not a job"
sources.summary: Paul Graham surveyed 100+ YC founders on what surprised them about starting a startup, which amounts to asking what he got wrong. The surprises (cofounder character, persistence, slow deals, minimal launches, talking to users, luck, clueless investors) were all things he already says, because people unconsciously model a startup on a job.

principles.text: Pick cofounders for character and commitment, not ability, then work hard to maintain the relationship.
principles.quote: What people wished they'd paid more attention to when choosing cofounders was character and commitment, not ability. This was particularly true with startups that failed. The lesson: don't pick cofounders who will flake.

principles.text: Persistence matters more than raw intelligence, and everything takes longer than you expect.
principles.quote: Several founders mentioned specifically how much more important persistence was than intelligence.

principles.text: Launch the simplest possible version. If trolls don't make fun of your first version, you waited too long.
principles.quote: If your first version is so impressive that trolls don't make fun of it, you waited too long to launch.

principles.text: Treat the initial version as a trick to get users talking to you; product development is a conversation with users.
principles.quote: Product development is a conversation with the user that doesn't really start till you launch.

principles.text: Treat your idea as a hypothesis, not a blueprint. Determination without flexibility can trap you in a local maximum.
principles.quote: We've always encouraged founders to see a startup idea as a hypothesis rather than a blueprint.

principles.text: Assume deals fall through and you won't get investor money; be optimistic only about what you control.
principles.quote: The mistake is to be optimistic about things you can't control. By all means be optimistic about your ability to make something great.

sources.title: Why to Not Not Start a Startup: dismantling the 16 reasons founders hesitate
sources.originalTitle: Why to Not Not Start a Startup
sources.summary: Paul Graham lists the reasons people hesitate to start startups and says which are real and which are bogus. Most are bogus: youth, inexperience, intelligence, business knowledge and no idea matter little. The real ones are no cofounder and a family to support. The essay also argues for making something people love first and worrying about revenue later.

principles.text: Don't worry about business knowledge at first. Build something people want, and money follows.
principles.quote: All you need to know in this phase is how to build things people want. If you succeed, you'll have to think about how to make money from it. But this is so easy you can pick it up on the fly.

principles.text: If users love you, you can always make money from that. If they don't, a clever business model won't save you.
principles.quote: if users love you, you can always make money from that somehow, and if they don't, the cleverest business model in the world won't save you.

principles.text: The most valuable truths are the ones most people don't believe. Push toward ideas you know are good that others reject.
principles.quote: The most valuable truths are the ones most people don't believe. They're like undervalued stocks. If you start with them, you'll have the whole field to yourself.

principles.text: Get a cofounder before anything else. A startup is too much for one person, and investors prefer teams.
principles.quote: Not having a cofounder is a real problem. A startup is too much for one person to bear.

principles.text: Determination is probably the single best predictor of founder success. Many founders underestimate how much of it they have.
principles.quote: You need a lot of determination to succeed as a startup founder. It's probably the single best predictor of success.

principles.text: Find startup ideas by supplying something missing in your own life, even if it seems narrow.
principles.quote: A need that's narrow but genuine is a better starting point than one that's broad but hypothetical.

sources.title: The Fatal Pinch: how startups die when runway runs short and what to do about it
sources.summary: Paul Graham names the "fatal pinch": a startup with about 6 months of runway, high burn and weak revenue growth that assumes it can raise more money. Founders overestimate investor interest, so he advises treating the odds of a raise as zero and then either cutting costs or making money in a different way, including consultingish work.

principles.text: Founders badly overestimate how easily they can raise a second round, and that delusion is what kills them.
principles.quote: There may be nothing founders are so prone to delude themselves about as how interested investors will be in giving them additional funding.

principles.text: Raise money as if it's your last. The less you need investment, the easier it is to get.
principles.quote: Y Combinator tells founders who raise money to act as if it's the last they'll ever get. Because the self-reinforcing nature of this situation works the other way too: the less you need further investment, the easier it is to get.

principles.text: If you're in the pinch, assume the probability of raising more money is zero and act on what's left.
principles.quote: The first step is to re-evaluate the probability of raising more money. I will now, by an amazing feat of clairvoyance, do this for you: the probability is zero.

principles.text: When cutting costs, let go of the people you already know you should fire. Lean toward cuts if overhiring caused the trouble.
principles.quote: Deciding to fire people is usually hard, but there's one case in which it shouldn't be: when there are people you already know you should fire but you're in denial about it. If so, now's the time.

principles.text: With a small team, put everyone on selling and build only what brings the most revenue soonest.
principles.quote: What good will more code do you when you're out of business? If you have to write code to close a certain deal, go ahead; that follows from everyone working on selling.

principles.text: Make money differently by asking customers what they'd pay a lot for, and keep the IP rather than billing by the hour.
principles.quote: So if you change your sales conversations just a little from "do you want to buy our product?" to "what do you need that you'd pay a lot for?" you may find it's suddenly a lot easier to extract money from customers.

sources.title: Mean People Fail: why benevolence beats meanness in startups
sources.summary: Paul Graham argues that mean founders tend to fail because meanness makes you stupid, repels the best hires, and clashes with the benevolent drive that sustains great companies. As the games that matter shift from zero-sum control of scarce resources to building new things, the historical advantage of meanness is reversing.

principles.text: Fighting makes you stupid: wins come from case-specific tricks, not big ideas, so your brain spins its wheels.
principles.quote: One is that being mean makes you stupid. That's why I hate fights. You never do your best work in a fight, because fights are not sufficiently general.

principles.text: Startups win by transcending competitors, not attacking them. Race ahead instead of stopping to fight.
principles.quote: Startups don't win by attacking. They win by transcending. There are exceptions of course, but usually the way to win is to race ahead, not to stop and fight.

principles.text: Mean founders can't attract the best people, who have other options; top talent is critical for startups.
principles.quote: They can hire people who will put up with them because they need a job. But the best people have other options.

principles.text: Founders driven by improving the world outlast those driven by money, who take the early acquisition offer.
principles.quote: The ones driven by money take the big acquisition offer that nearly every successful startup gets en route. The ones who keep going are driven by something else.

principles.text: Success is shifting from zero-sum control of scarce resources to non-zero-sum building of new things, so meanness loses its edge.
principles.quote: Increasingly you win not by fighting to get control of a scarce resource, but by having new ideas and building new things.

sources.title: The 18 Mistakes That Kill Startups: why startups fail to make something users want
sources.summary: Graham argues there is really one cause of startup death: not making something users want. He lists 18 controllable mistakes that feed into it, from single founders and derivative ideas to slow launches, bad fundraising and half-hearted effort. The deepest cause he names is not trying hard enough.

principles.text: Nearly all startup failure funnels through one mistake: not making something users want.
principles.quote: In a sense there's just one mistake that kills startups: not making something users want. If you make something users want, you'll probably be fine, whatever else you do or don't do.

principles.text: Look for problems, ideally ones you have yourself, rather than imitating existing companies.
principles.quote: Instead of starting from companies and working back to the problems they solved, look for problems and imagine the company that might solve them.

principles.text: Launch something quickly: it forces you to finish work and to learn from real users.
principles.quote: The other reason you need to launch is that it's only by bouncing your idea off users that you fully understand it.

principles.text: Launch a core that is useful on its own and can grow into the whole product.
principles.quote: identify a core that's both (a) useful on its own and (b) something that can be incrementally expanded into the whole project, and then get that done as soon as possible.

principles.text: Solve for value creation first and leave the business model for later; users come before profit.
principles.quote: It is irresponsible not to think about business models. It's just ten times more irresponsible not to think about the product.

principles.text: The biggest mistake is not trying hard enough; most startups fail because founders don't go all in.
principles.quote: Most startups fail because they don't make something people want, and the reason most don't is that they don't try hard enough.

sources.title: Startups in 13 Sentences: Paul Graham's core startup principles
sources.summary: Graham distills startup advice into 13 principles, from picking cofounders and launching fast to spending little and never giving up. If he had to keep one, it would be understanding your users, since it underlies launching early, evolving the idea, serving a few users deeply and good customer service.

principles.text: Launch fast: launching teaches you what you should have been building, and the launch is a pretext for engaging users.
principles.quote: you haven't really started working on it till you've launched. Launching teaches you what you should have been building.

principles.text: Make a few users love you rather than many ambivalent. Satisfy all needs of a subset first; it's easier to expand users than satisfaction.
principles.quote: Initially you have to choose between satisfying all the needs of a subset of potential users, or satisfying a subset of the needs of all potential users. Take the first.

principles.text: Understand your users above all. The hardest part is knowing what to make; making it is mere effort.
principles.quote: Once you know what to make, it's mere effort to make it, and most decent hackers are capable of that.

principles.text: Offer surprisingly good customer service early, even unscalable, because it teaches you about your users.
principles.quote: In the earliest stages of a startup, it pays to offer customer service on a level that wouldn't scale, because it's a way of learning about your users.

principles.text: You make what you measure: track the key number daily and you'll learn what moves it. Be careful what you measure.
principles.quote: Merely measuring something has an uncanny tendency to improve it.

principles.text: Spend little and get ramen profitable: cheapness equals rapid iteration, and covering founders' living costs changes your relationship with investors.
principles.quote: Most startups fail before they make something people want, and the most common form of failure is running out of money.

sources.title: How to Make Wealth: startups as measurement plus leverage for working fast
sources.summary: Paul Graham argues that wealth is what people want, not money, and that startups let small groups of ambitious people work as hard as possible on hard technical problems and get paid in proportion. The recipe is measurement (small teams) and leverage (new technology), with users as the test of whether you created wealth.

principles.text: Wealth is what people want, not money. Businesses make money by creating wealth, so start by doing something people want.
principles.quote: People think that what a business does is make money. But money is just the intermediate stage-- just a shorthand-- for whatever people want. What most businesses really do is make wealth. They do something people want.

sources.title: Frighteningly Ambitious Startup Ideas: why the biggest ideas repel you and how to start small
sources.summary: Graham argues the biggest startup ideas feel frightening, so most idea-hunters filter them out subconsciously. He sketches seven examples, then gives tactics: don't announce the giant goal, start with something deceptively small, and head "westward" like Columbus rather than plotting a precise future.

principles.text: The biggest startup ideas feel scary and threaten your identity, so your subconscious filters them out; approach them obliquely.
principles.quote: You'd expect big startup ideas to be attractive, but actually they tend to repel you. And that has a bunch of consequences. It means these ideas are invisible to most people who try to think of startup ideas, because their subconscious filters them out.

principles.text: Win a market by first owning a small, intensely loyal core of users, even if it constrains you later.
principles.quote: Don't worry if something you want to do will constrain you in the long term, because if you don't get that initial core of users, there won't be a long term.

principles.text: Build what you yourself want; if you are the target user, the route to the first users is straightforward.
principles.quote: Since anyone capable of starting this company is one of those 10,000 hackers, the route is at least straightforward: make the search engine you yourself want.

principles.text: Don't announce the giant ambition; describe it as something harmless to avoid inflated expectations and haters.
principles.quote: Don't say, for example, that you're going to replace email. If you do that you raise too many expectations. Your employees and investors will constantly be asking "are we there yet?" and you'll have an army of haters waiting to see you fail.

principles.text: Really big companies start from deceptively small things, and founders themselves should start small.
principles.quote: Empirically, the way to do really big things seems to be to start with deceptively small things.

principles.text: Head in a general direction like Columbus instead of building toward a precise vision of the future; a blurry view may be better.
principles.quote: The popular image of the visionary is someone with a clear view of the future, but empirically it may be better to have a blurry one.

sources.title: Relentlessly Resourceful: the two-word recipe for a good startup founder
sources.summary: Paul Graham distills what makes a good startup founder into two words: relentlessly resourceful. Relentlessness alone fails because startup difficulties are novel and of unknown hardness, so founders must keep trying new approaches. The quality can often be taught, and works as a self-test and a cofounder-selection test.

principles.text: A good founder is relentlessly resourceful: persistent, but constantly trying new approaches.
principles.quote: A couple days ago I finally got being a good startup founder down to two words: relentlessly resourceful.

principles.text: Pure relentlessness isn't enough because startup obstacles are novel and their difficulty is unknown in advance.
principles.quote: In any interesting domain, the difficulties will be novel. Which means you can't simply plow through them, because you don't know initially how hard they are

principles.text: The opposite of a good founder is hapless: passive, letting circumstances batter you instead of shaping them.
principles.quote: To be hapless is to be battered by circumstances — to let the world have its way with you, instead of having your way with the world.

principles.text: Resourcefulness can often be taught, especially to people who have always been under authority.
principles.quote: After four years of trying to teach it to people, I'd say that yes, surprisingly often it can. Not to everyone, but to many people.

principles.text: Use the phrase as a test for yourself and for potential cofounders.
principles.quote: If you want to know whether you're the right sort of person to start a startup, ask yourself whether you're relentlessly resourceful. And if you want to know whether to recruit someone as a cofounder, ask if they are.

principles.text: "Make something people want" is the destination; "be relentlessly resourceful" is how you get there.
principles.quote: "Make something people want" is the destination, but "Be relentlessly resourceful" is how you get there.

sources.title: How to Convince Investors: Convince yourself first, then tell the truth
sources.summary: Graham argues founders should stop relying on pitch skills and instead make a startup worth investing in, understand why, and explain it plainly. Investors want formidable founders and a plausible path to owning a big piece of a big market. Seeming formidable comes from truth and domain expertise, not swagger.

principles.text: Don't pitch with your back. Understand why your startup is worth investing in, then simply explain it well.
principles.quote: Most would be better off if they let their startup do the work — if they started by understanding why their startup is worth investing in, then simply explained this well to investors.

principles.text: Investors decide fast whether you're a winner, and that first impression colors how they read everything else about your startup.
principles.quote: If investors are impressed with you as founders, they say they want to invest because it's a rich market, and if not, they say they can't invest because of the slow sales cycle.

principles.text: Inexperienced founders seem most formidable by sticking to the truth, not by imitating swagger.
principles.quote: Investors are not always that good at judging technology, but they're good at judging confidence. If you try to act like something you're not, you'll just end up in an uncanny valley.

principles.text: Truly evaluate whether your startup is worth investing in; if it isn't, don't raise. You need domain expertise to judge this.
principles.quote: I mean truly evaluate whether your startup is worth investing in. If it isn't, don't try to raise money.

principles.text: Raise when you can convince investors, not when you need money or hit an artificial deadline.
principles.quote: The time to raise money is not when you need it, or when you reach some artificial deadline like a Demo Day. It's when you can convince investors, and not before.

principles.text: Investors think in markets, not ideas. You need a plausible path to owning a big piece of a big market, riding a 'why now' wave.
principles.quote: Founders think of startups as ideas, but investors think of them as markets.

sources.title: The Right Kind of Stubborn: persistence is attached to the goal, obstinacy to the method
sources.summary: Graham argues persistence and obstinacy are different behaviors, not labels applied after the fact. The persistent are attached to the goal and open to disagreement; the obstinate cling to their first ideas. Persistence is built from five qualities: energy, imagination, resilience, good judgement, and a focus on a goal.

principles.text: Be attached to the goal, not to your ideas about how to reach it.
principles.quote: The persistent are attached to the goal. The obstinate are attached to their ideas about how to reach it.

principles.text: Seek out disagreement: the persistent get more engaged when you point out problems.
principles.quote: They're never _more_ engaged than when you disagree with them. Whereas the obstinate don't want to hear you.

principles.text: Persistence needs imagination: to keep trying things, you must keep thinking of things to try.
principles.quote: Which means the persistent must also be imaginative. To keep trying things, you have to keep thinking of things to try.

principles.text: Resilience means setbacks can't change your morale, but they can change your mind.
principles.quote: Resilience means setbacks can't change your morale, not that they can't change your mind.

principles.text: Judge by expected value and give way on low-level details, while holding firm on the goal chosen higher up.
principles.quote: You'll give way on any point low down in the decision tree, if its expected value drops sufficiently, but energy and resilience keep pushing you toward whatever you chose higher up.

principles.text: Make the goal specific enough to guide action; start small and expand once moving.
principles.quote: Start by erring on the small side. If you're inexperienced you'll inevitably err on one side or the other, and if you err on the side of making the goal too broad, you won't get anywhere.

sources.title: Organic Startup Ideas: build what you wish someone would make for you
sources.summary: Paul Graham argues the best startup ideas grow organically from your own life rather than being decided from afar. Focus on fixing things that seem broken, don't worry about whether it's a company, and don't be put off if others call it a toy.

principles.text: Find ideas by asking what you wish someone would make for you.
principles.quote: The best way to come up with startup ideas is to ask yourself the question: what do you wish someone would make for you?

principles.text: Organic ideas, born from your own needs, beat made-up ideas for others; the most successful startups skew organic.
principles.quote: There is no sharp line between the two types of ideas, but the most successful startups seem to be closer to the Apple type than the Viaweb type.

principles.text: Young founders especially should avoid made-up ideas, since predicting what others want takes experience.
principles.quote: It takes experience to predict what other people will want. The worst ideas we see at Y Combinator are from young founders making things they think other people will want.

principles.text: Focus on the idea, not the startup: fix broken things without asking if it's company-sized.
principles.quote: I'd encourage you to focus more on the idea part and less on the startup part. Just fix things that seem broken, regardless of whether it seems like the problem is important enough to build a company on.

principles.text: Being dismissed as a toy is a good sign; it explains why others overlooked the idea.
principles.quote: Don't be discouraged if what you produce initially is something other people dismiss as a toy. In fact, that's a good sign.

principles.text: The most valuable opportunity is an unmet need that is just becoming fixable; use the latest tech to spot it first.
principles.quote: There's nothing more valuable than an unmet need that is just becoming fixable.

sources.title: What I've Learned from Users: why YC works and why founders misjudge their problems
sources.summary: Graham reflects on what YC learned from advising many startups: most share the same problems, founders misjudge which matter most, and they resist advice because startups are counterintuitive. Speed defines startups, focus enables speed, and YC's value is improving focus and providing colleagues.

principles.text: Best application advice: explain what you've learned from users. It tests attention, understanding and how much they need your product.
principles.quote: Explain what you've learned from users.

principles.text: Founders often miss their biggest problem. Ask whether you'd use the product yourself if you hadn't built it.
principles.quote: Or founders will come in worried that they still haven't cracked the problem of user acquisition, and the reason turns out to be that their product isn't good enough.

principles.text: Prioritize ruthlessly: founders know their problems but not their relative importance, so find the one that will kill the company.
principles.quote: Often founders know what their problems are, but not their relative importance.

principles.text: Advice sounds wrong because startups are counterintuitive, so founders don't believe it until experience teaches them.
principles.quote: when you tell someone something counterintuitive, what it sounds to them is wrong. So the reason founders don't listen to us is that they don't believe us.

principles.text: Work in short cycles: find the key problem, try a fix, measure within a week. Be decisive at micro scale, tentative at macro scale.
principles.quote: If you correct course at a high enough frequency, you can be simultaneously decisive at a micro scale and tentative at a macro scale.

principles.text: Speed defines startups and focus enables it. Better navigation makes you faster twice over.
principles.quote: Speed defines startups. Focus enables speed. YC improves focus.

sources.title: Why It's Safe for Founders to Be Nice: growth rate beats rapacity
sources.originalTitle: Why It's Safe for Founders to Be Nice
sources.summary: Paul Graham argues startup founders can afford to be nice because great products spread by word of mouth and compound, while rapacity doesn't. Being bad at extracting money only scales the growth curve by a constant factor, whereas improving growth rate changes its shape. The math: a founder extracting half as much is only 15 weeks behind, and a faster growth rate overtakes quickly.

principles.text: Being soft on monetization only scales your growth curve by a constant; it keeps the same shape.
principles.quote: a constant multiple of any curve is exactly the same shape. The numbers on the Y axis are smaller, but the curve is just as steep, and when anything grows at the rate of a successful startup, the Y axis will take care of itself.

principles.text: If you optimize one number, make it growth rate, not revenue extracted per user.
principles.quote: If you're going to optimize a number, the one to choose is your growth rate.

principles.text: A founder who extracts half as much from users is only a fixed 15 weeks behind one who extracts every penny.
principles.quote: In fact since 2 ≈ 1.05 ^ 15, the un-rapacious founder is always 15 weeks behind the rapacious one.

principles.text: Startups usually win by making something so great people recommend it, and rapacity probably hurts that.
principles.quote: Startups usually win by making something so great that people recommend it to their friends. And being rapacious not only doesn't help you do that, but probably hurts.

principles.text: Great things compound; rapacity doesn't. That is why founders can safely be nice.
principles.quote: The reason startup founders can safely be nice is that making great things is compounded, and rapacity isn't.

principles.text: Be as nice as you want, provided you work hard on growth rate to compensate.
principles.quote: Tell yourself you can be as nice as you want, so long as you work hard on your growth rate to compensate.

sources.title: What We Look for in Founders: determination, flexibility, imagination, naughtiness, friendship
sources.originalTitle: What We Look for in Founders
sources.summary: Paul Graham lists the five qualities Y Combinator looks for in founders. Determination matters most, balanced by flexibility. The other three are imagination, a naughty streak of beating the system, and a strong bond between cofounders. Each is illustrated with YC founders such as WePay, Greplin, Airbnb and Justin.tv.

principles.text: Past a basic intelligence threshold, determination matters most in founders, because you will hit many obstacles.
principles.quote: But as long as you're over a certain threshold of intelligence, what matters most is determination. You're going to hit a lot of obstacles.
