principles.text: Pair determination with flexibility: stay set on the goal but be ready to change the plan, like a running back.
principles.quote: The world of startups is so unpredictable that you need to be able to modify your dreams on the fly.

principles.text: The most useful kind of intelligence is imagination: coming up with surprising ideas, since good startup ideas initially seem bad.
principles.quote: In the startup world, most good ideas seem bad initially. If they were obviously good, someone would already be doing them.

principles.text: Look for founders who beat the system. Breaking rules that don't matter is a good sign.
principles.quote: They delight in breaking rules, but not rules that matter.

principles.text: Ask founders about a time they hacked something to their advantage. It became one of YC's most-watched application questions.
principles.quote: He said to ask about a time when they'd hacked something to their advantage—hacked in the sense of beating the system, not breaking into computers.

principles.text: Cofounder friendship is essential: startups strain the relationship, so founders must genuinely like each other and work well together.
principles.quote: Startups do to the relationship between the founders what a dog does to a sock: if it can be pulled apart, it will be.

sources.title: The Top Idea in Your Mind: why fundraising and disputes starve the work that matters
sources.originalTitle: The Top Idea in Your Mind
sources.summary: Paul Graham argues that people have one "top idea" their mind drifts to (e.g. in the shower), and it gets all the benefit of ambient thought. Letting money or disputes become that idea kills progress on everything else, so you must shape your situations to control it indirectly.

principles.text: Ambient thinking is necessary for hard problems, and only your top idea gets it.
principles.quote: I think most people have one top idea in their mind at any given time. That's the idea their thoughts will drift toward when they're allowed to drift freely.

principles.text: Raising money stalls startups because it becomes the top idea, not because of meeting time.
principles.quote: The problem is not the actual time it takes to meet with investors. The problem is that once you start raising money, raising money becomes the top idea in your mind.

principles.text: You can't steer your thoughts directly; control them by choosing which situations you get into.
principles.quote: Try to get yourself into situations where the most urgent problems are ones you want to think about.

principles.text: Avoid disputes: they feel engaging like real ideas but have no substance.
principles.quote: they have the same velcro-like shape as genuinely interesting ideas, but without the substance. So avoid disputes if you want to get real work done.

principles.text: Ignoring injuries avoids the second hurt of spending your time thinking about them.
principles.quote: Someone who does you an injury hurts you twice: first by the injury itself, and second by taking up your time afterward thinking about it.

principles.text: Check your real top idea by noticing what your thoughts return to in the shower.
principles.quote: just take a shower. What topic do your thoughts keep returning to? If it's not what you want to be thinking about, you may want to change something.

sources.title: Fundraising survival: how startups should handle raising money without losing morale or momentum
sources.summary: Paul Graham argues fundraising is the second hardest part of a startup because investors are few, random and herd-like. He gives survival techniques: expect deals to fail, keep building, take reasonable offers, stay flexible on amount, get ramen profitable, treat rejection analytically, and know where you stand.

principles.text: Assume every deal will fall through; low expectations protect morale, which is what kills startups.
principles.quote: At YC one of our secondary mantras is "Deals fall through." No matter what deal you have going on, assume it will fall through. The predictive power of this simple rule is amazing.

principles.text: Put the startup first; fit investor meetings around development, not the reverse.
principles.quote: Fit meetings with investors into the spare moments in your development schedule, rather than doing development in the spare moments between meetings with investors.

principles.text: Take reputable funding on reasonable terms, and close interested investors now or write them off.
principles.quote: if someone reputable offers you funding on reasonable terms, take it.

principles.text: Don't fix a raise amount; show you'll succeed regardless and money just makes it faster.
principles.quote: The message (and not just the message, but the fact) should be: we're going to succeed no matter what. Raising more money just lets us do it faster.

principles.text: Ramen profitability changes your bargaining position; investors love startups that don't need them.
principles.quote: There is nothing investors like more than a startup that seems like it's going to succeed even without them.

principles.text: Sort and analyze rejections instead of letting them pile up into demoralization; fix the pitch.
principles.quote: Don't let rejections pile up as a depressing, undifferentiated heap. Sort them and analyze them, and then instead of thinking "no one likes us," you'll know precisely how big a problem you have, and what to do about it.

sources.title: Superlinear Returns: why growth rate and exceptional work beat linear effort
sources.summary: Paul Graham argues that returns to performance are superlinear, driven by two causes: exponential growth and thresholds. He draws practical rules for founders and ambitious people: seek work that compounds, keep learning, focus on growth rate, do things that don't scale early, and follow curiosity into new fields.

principles.text: Returns to performance are superlinear, not linear: a product half as good as a competitor's gets no customers, not half.
principles.quote: If your product is only half as good as your competitor's, you don't get half as many customers. You get no customers, and you go out of business.

principles.text: Superlinear returns come from two causes: exponential growth and thresholds.
principles.quote: they reduce to two fundamental causes: exponential growth and thresholds.

principles.text: Focus founders on growth rate, not absolute numbers; it encourages them, guides focus, and tends to produce exponential growth.
principles.quote: Y Combinator encourages founders to focus on growth rate rather than absolute numbers. It prevents them from being discouraged early on, when the absolute numbers are still low.

principles.text: Seek work that compounds, directly (audience, brand, infrastructure) or by teaching you; always be learning.
principles.quote: The most obvious one is to seek work that compounds.

principles.text: Do things that don't scale: intense early effort on a tiny set of customers can kick off exponential word-of-mouth growth.
principles.quote: If you pay a ridiculous amount of attention to your tiny initial set of customers, ideally you'll kick off exponential growth by word of mouth.

principles.text: Replace products that are mediocre yet popular, but check for hidden reasons like monopoly, regulation or bad buying processes.
principles.quote: if you come across something that's mediocre yet still popular, it could be a good idea to replace it.

sources.title: How to Start a Startup: good people, what customers want, spend little
sources.summary: Paul Graham argues a startup needs three things: good people, a product customers actually want, and minimal spending. Ideas matter little; founders who watch users, ship early, grow slowly, stay cheap and avoid unnecessary hiring are most likely to win.

principles.text: Success needs three things: good people, something customers want, and spending as little as possible. All are doable.
principles.quote: You need three things to create a successful startup: to start with good people, to make something customers actually want, and to spend as little money as possible.

principles.text: The initial idea is worth little; the people matter. Good people can fix bad ideas, not vice versa.
principles.quote: What matters is not ideas, but the people who have them. Good people can fix bad ideas, but good ideas can't save bad people.

principles.text: Hire 'animals': people so good and obsessive at their job they cross from professional into obsessive.
principles.quote: It means someone who takes their work a little too seriously; someone who does what they do so well that they pass right through professional and cross over into obsessive.

principles.text: Get a prototype in front of users fast and refine from their reactions; initial plans are almost certainly wrong.
principles.quote: The only way to make something customers want is to get a prototype in front of them and refine it based on their reactions.

principles.text: Make technology easy to use; small ease-of-use gains can multiply sales.
principles.quote: A 10% improvement in ease of use doesn't just increase your sales 10%. It's more likely to double your sales.

principles.text: Get big slow: spending slowly buys time to learn from smart early users and keeps a culture of cheapness.
principles.quote: To make something users love, you have to understand them. And the bigger you are, the harder that is. So I say "get big slow." The slower you burn through your funding, the more time you have to learn.

sources.title: Hiring is Obsolete: why young hackers should start startups instead of taking jobs
sources.summary: Paul Graham argues that falling startup costs shift power from employers and investors to young hackers. Rather than being undervalued as employees, talented people can be valued directly by users and acquirers by building something people want. Big companies will increasingly buy early startups, fusing recruiting and product development.

principles.text: Cheaper startups reduce investors' power over founders, since their leverage comes from money.
principles.quote: Investors' power comes from money. When startups need less money, investors have less power over them.

principles.text: A startup's goal is to make something users want, not write cool software; look at users.
principles.quote: The goal in a startup is not to write a cool piece of software. It's to make something people want. And to do that you have to look at users-- forget about hacking, and just look at users.

principles.text: Successful startups solve a specific problem people already know they have.
principles.quote: Most successful startups not only do something very specific, but solve a problem people already know they have.

principles.text: Online, good products spread by word of mouth, so marketing spend matters less.
principles.quote: On the Internet, anything genuinely good will spread by word of mouth.

principles.text: Selling directly teaches developers more than focus groups do.
principles.quote: It's painful doing sales, but you learn much more from trying to sell people something than reading what they said in focus groups.

principles.text: Take big risks while young: risk and reward are proportionate, and most people avoid extreme choices, which reduces competition.
principles.quote: Extreme choices like starting a startup are so frightening that most people won't even try. So you don't end up having as much competition as you might expect, considering the prizes at stake.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In a short YC interview, Paul Graham argues that starting a startup is essentially unchanged despite AI. Founder quality (being "formidable", driven by fear of failure) and shipping speed still decide outcomes, and you can still start on little money by hitting milestones that unlock the next round.

chunks.heading: Founder ambition and why "formidable" is the key quality
chunks.text:
- Paul says he already knew before YC started that founders have to be really ambitious. He and his co-founders had run a startup themselves, so they knew it was grueling. Something has to drive a founder through the obstacles, and "being beautiful is not enough. The obstacles are too fearsome for mere beautifulness to do it." He calls that driver ambition.
- Ambition is mostly inborn. He says stories of founders who gain ambition during the batch are rare. Sam Altman "was extremely formidable the first time I met him before we even accepted him," and Paul says that is the rule, not the exception.
- The one exception he sees is a founder who has been trained not to show ambition. A young person in obedient situations, such as with pushy parents, may never have let themselves go. He argues that person was ambitious all along.
- "Formidable" was Maya's and Jessica's private word before YC. Paul's test is: someone who "gets what they want" in any situation. "How formidable are you if you don't get what you want?"
- Investors want formidable founders because interests align. If the founder gets what they want, the investor holding stock in the company gets what they want too.
- On the next trillion-dollar company, he says it comes "from the right founders," not from a particular idea. Ideas are mutable. Founders now look the same as they did 20 years ago, and he sees no reason that would change.

chunks.heading: What actually motivates founders day to day
chunks.text:
- Paul says founders are not mainly driven by the thought of becoming billionaires, even though that is the upside. At any given moment the motivator is fear of failure: disaster, looking like a fool, the server crashing.
- His example: if your online service's server is crashing, you are not thinking "if I fix this I'll become a billionaire." You are thinking "oh no, the server is crashing." He compares it to saving a model train set whose engine is falling off the table.
- Founders put their heads down on the "model train set" for 10 years, then look up and find that their shares at the last round's valuation make them a billionaire. It takes them by surprise.
- Paul sometimes does the math for founders himself: "Wait, according to your last round, you're a billionaire."

chunks.heading: Startups are a bad credential
chunks.text:
- Paul says people started applying to YC for prestige quite early in its history. He sees that as a mistake in how they think about startups.
- Harvard comparison: if you get into Harvard, you can choose an easy major and still leave with an impressive degree. A startup has no easy major. It is "like applying to Harvard and being forced to study theoretical physics."
- A failed startup is not much of a badge. A successful one is your life's work, so it is not a badge either.
- Starting a startup is "about the least efficient way" to seem cool. It is brutally hard, and you won't seem cool until after years of that hardness.

chunks.heading: Ambitious ideas and serious startups
chunks.text:
- Paul says YC startups today are more serious than in the "supposedly good old days." People have said YC "jumped the shark" since about 2008. Critics must admit it was once great, so they claim it has fallen.
- He notes that old-days companies like Reddit, however valuable, are "not exactly intercontinental ballistic cargo." He did office hours with an intercontinental ballistic cargo startup ("like an ICBM except instead of exploding, it lands").
- Cancer: he says to fund many approaches, since any one working would be good. One end is vaccines and the opposite end is therapies. A startup in the current batch does on-demand research for people with cancer. He likes that it inflicts "the death of a thousand cuts" on cancer, which may be how it is beaten.
- That startup's team helped Sid of GitLab with his cancer. Paul says Sid approached it like a startup, with them as de facto co-founders, and calls his "founder mode on my cancer" a good description. After that, Paul thought someone should do for everyone what Sid did for himself, and now the people who did it for Sid are doing it.
- He says his 2012 "frighteningly ambitious ideas" essay has largely come true. One idea was a new Google. His prediction was that you don't make a new Google by attacking them head-on. You wait until things change so much that their model is obsolete. That is what OpenAI is. After using it he realized he no longer used Google, because he wanted information, not web pages.

chunks.heading: Starting lean and what AI changes
chunks.text:
- Paul hasn't read *The Lean Startup* and isn't sure what "lean startup" means, so he answers on the narrower question of whether starting with little money is dead. He says no.
- Technology always gets cheaper. Token prices are high now only because of a GPU shortage. He says inference prices at a given quality level fall dramatically, "like 30x a year or something like that," and you also get higher-quality tokens over time.
- Even a rocket startup can start on little money. You adjust to the money you have. You can't build the rocket, but you can build a design, simulate it, and show it to experts. If it's convincing, investors give you a bit of money for the next stage. "You're always able to raise another round" as long as you reach some milestone.
- On StarCloud, a founder said they wrote a white paper and booked a launch. Paul says nothing is as convincing as booking a launch. But that founder is a huge famous expert with automatic credibility, so it's easier for him than for a recent graduate.
- Shipping speed: Paul says the best predictor of startup success is still the pace at which they ship. Many startups in the batch with powerful AI tools "are not shipping fast enough." Speed isn't just output rate, because you have to think of the ideas first.
- Almost everything about starting a startup is the same as before. The one new thing is cost structure. Salaries used to be the big cost, with laptops and people. Now companies face giant AI bills, "tens of thousands of dollars a day in tokens."
- He says most of starting a startup is always the same, whether the tech is microprocessors, AI or the internal combustion engine.

chunks.heading: Why a batch helps founders, and how YC came about
chunks.text:
- Paul gives three reasons the batch helps. Starting a startup is normally lonely, with full control but no colleagues, and the batch is like an office of colleagues who each work on their own startup. You can learn from other startups, such as asking someone who already hit your technical problem. And there is the "YC GDP": you can sell your product to other startups in the batch. They are the right users, early adopters who decide quickly and "have to at least listen to your pitch."
- Origin: the first idea was to be an angel firm. VCs did giant late-stage rounds and angels were individuals investing their own money. There were no angel firms. The idea was to be like a VC but invest small amounts earlier with standardized paperwork.
- They then decided they needed to learn to be investors, so they would fund many startups at once. College students got summer jobs at Microsoft, so YC would be an alternative to a summer job. That is why the batch runs in the summer. He says the length turned out to be perfect by accident.
- They expected undergrads wouldn't mind that YC wasn't a real investor, since they weren't real founders. In practice YC became real investors and the students became real founders quickly. The batch worked so well they kept it.
- On scale, YC has changed little: "the same thing but more of it." The startups' problems are the same. People complained about size back when there were 40 startups in a batch. Dividing YC into pods of 70 startups makes it like 2012, when a batch had 70.

chunks.heading: AI as Paul sees it
chunks.text:
- Paul studied AI in the 1980s, a kind of AI he says would never have worked. The expected path was a "perfect fly," then mice, cats, monkeys and humans, perfect at each level.
- What happened was the reverse: a full human-level but unreliable system. Early ChatGPT was like an undergrad bullshitting through a paper. Instead of starting perfect and working up to human, "you start with human and then work your way towards perfect." Nobody expected the first plausible AI to be a bullshitting undergraduate.
- He says it still has some of that flavor. AI is reportedly solving open math problems, yet he can't get it to say when restaurants are open. He calls this the "jagged frontier."
- On AGI, he says the Turing test is a good definition. One sign AGI was close was that he had to look up what the Turing test was. He expected AGI to be a clear finish line, but "the line had dimension." His best answer is that "we're on the smear."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Graham argues ambitious founders should spend time in the world's startup center for its peer density, serendipitous meetings, speed, investor competition and pay-it-forward culture. He says the best way to help Stockholm thrive is to go to Silicon Valley (ideally via YC) and then return, bringing back better startups, money and culture.

chunks.heading: Why Paul says ambitious founders should go to the center of their field
chunks.text:
- Paul argues that every intense pursuit has one global center at a given time: painting in Paris (1870), math in Göttingen (1900), movies in Hollywood (1950), startups in Silicon Valley now.
- His answer to "should I go?" is always the same: "Yes, you should. You can go there for a bit and then come back, but you should at least go."
- The logic is the same as moving from a village to a capital within one country. The reasoning "doesn't even know the dotted line is there" when the move crosses a border.
- What you get is the best peers. The talent pool is better and larger, and the people cluster. Paul says a YC batch feels like this: every dinner is full of ambitious people working on the same thing.
- Being among people working on the same hard thing also lifts morale. He cites a founder who said that on reaching Silicon Valley he "finally met his people."

chunks.heading: Serendipitous meetings and speed in the big centers
chunks.text:
- Paul says serendipitous meetings seem "enormously important." Biographies of people who did great things keep showing an unplanned meeting that changed their lives. He admits he isn't sure why.
- His candidate explanations:
  - There are simply more unplanned meetings, so more of the outliers are the unplanned kind.
  - Planned meetings are too conservative. They need a reason beforehand, which lops off outliers, "just like deliberately trying to find startup ideas lops off the outliers."
  - Unplanned meetings are self-selecting. After a few sentences you can decide whether to keep talking ("Oh, you're interested in that, too? We need to talk").
- Big centers also move faster. People are better and more confident, so they are more decisive. They "egg one another on," both encouraging and competing.
- In villages, people half have an idea and sit on it. Ten years later they say "I thought of that" about someone else's company.

chunks.heading: Why fundraising is faster in Silicon Valley
chunks.text:
- Paul says Silicon Valley investors decide much faster than European ones. The cause is partly confidence and partly competition.
- The more right an investor is about a startup, the less time they can wait, because the opportunity will time out. This is an unusual situation where being more right means you can wait less.
- Example: Yury Sagalov invested immediately on meeting Max, reasoning that anyone else who met him would invest too.
- Investors complain that valuations are too high and they are rushed. Paul notes that empirically it doesn't hurt them: Silicon Valley investors get better returns than European investors despite deciding so quickly.
- Moving to the center also raises your standing at home. Investors outside Silicon Valley implicitly assume any local startup is second rate ("no one is a prophet in their own country"). Leaving reverses the rule. Telling local investors you were accepted to YC often makes them "trip over themselves" to invest.
- Dropbox example (summer 2007, a Boston batch):
  - A large Boston VC firm had spent a year offering encouragement and advice, but no money.
  - YC flew Boston startups to Silicon Valley for a second demo day because Boston investors were "so lame."
  - Sequoia got interested in Dropbox. The Boston firm's opinion changed instantly and it faxed Drew a term sheet with a blank valuation.
  - It was too late. Drew went with Sequoia. Dropbox was the first YC company to go public, in 2018.

chunks.heading: What moving to the big pond does to you
chunks.text:
- Paul says the biggest advantage is not what the center does for you but what it does to you.
- In a small pond you can't tell how big a fish you are. In the big pond you measure yourself against known big fish. He says "surprisingly often, the news is good."
- Seeing people like Brian Chesky or Sam Altman up close, you can think "he's not a different species from me. I could do what he did if I worked that hard."
- He stresses the second half of that thought: you also see how hard they work. Startups are really hard, so meeting such a person "sets a new standard that you have to meet."
- The key point is that the goal stops looking impossible and becomes hard but definite. "For an ambitious person, there is nothing better than a high but definite threshold."
- He says it clears away the fog at the top of the mountain: the summit is visible and high, but not "invisibly high."
- He admits he half felt intimidated himself while calling law firms, but says that reaction is rarer than statistics would suggest.
- Part of the reason is that big founders who speak at YC batches try to be accessible and encouraging rather than intimidating.

chunks.heading: The pay-it-forward culture of Silicon Valley
chunks.text:
- Paul says "in Silicon Valley, people help you for no reason," in the way Swedish streets are clean for no reason.
- He asked a founder friend from England who had moved to Silicon Valley how it differed from expectations. Paul calls "How is it different than you expected?" the best question to ask anyone who has gone to a new place. The answer was how helpful everyone was, with nearly every conversation ending in "What can I do to help you?"
- This isn't politeness, since the English are more polite than Americans. It is a pay-it-forward culture.
- His origin story: Silicon Valley is where people go from nobody to billionaire fastest. Someone who liked being nice to nobodies ended up with powerful friends and probably got rich. Whatever calculation started it, the custom is about 60 years old and is now just how people behave.
- Ron Conway is his example. He helps people all day, doesn't track whether they are his portfolio companies, and doesn't remember most of the favors. Paul compares this to honesty: you don't have to track your lies.
- With many people doing this there is no conservation law for favors, "there's just more favors." Paul says he and Ron have traded favors for 20 years and he assumes Ron is ahead.
- Moving to Silicon Valley will make you more helpful to others.

chunks.heading: How Sweden can thrive as a startup hub: go, then come back
chunks.text:
- Paul says the answer to "how does Stockholm thrive as a startup hub?" is the same as the first question: founders should go to Silicon Valley for a bit, then come back.
- Precedent: 19th-century mathematicians didn't help their countries by boycotting Göttingen. The government gave fellowships conditional on leaving and studying math abroad.
- Returning founders help in three ways:
  - Their own startups are better, which raises the average quality locally.
  - They bring Silicon Valley investor money back.
  - They import a culture evolved over decades to suit startups. It is compatible with Swedish culture, with high trust, but without the "tall poppies" attitude, which Paul says Sweden should probably lose anyway.
- He admits this sounds like talking his own book, but says the optimal way to do it is YC:
  - It concentrates what is distinctive about Silicon Valley, like "a little super valley within the valley."
  - Everyone around you is a founder, you get instant colleagues, and the helpfulness norm is even stronger.
  - Investors decide even faster, "down to the minute."
  - It takes about four to six months.
  - It is funded by Silicon Valley investors, so it costs a government nothing. A government could just "call our API," with no sales process.

chunks.heading: Do founders who go home do worse, and the Silicon Valley of Europe
chunks.text:
- Paul says YC's data shows startups that go home after YC are only about half as likely to become unicorns as those that stay.
- He gives three reasons not to be discouraged:
  - Selection bias. The data also measures the confidence and determination of founders willing to move countries.
  - It measures valuation, and Bay Area companies raise at higher valuations.
  - Half as good is still very good. Having $500 million instead of $1 billion makes little difference (in Swedish, "5 billion kronor").
- He adds that "money isn't everything": once you have kids, you care more about them than the company, and where they grow up becomes the most important question.
- The upside is that Stockholm could become the Silicon Valley of Europe. He says that job is still open, since asking "where's the Silicon Valley of Europe?" has no obvious answer, unlike "where's the Silicon Valley of America?"
- Evidence that small, off-center places can win: Mountain View was a backwater in 1955, when Shockley Semiconductor was founded, yet it was the geometric center of Silicon Valley until 2012.
- His formula: "All you need is a place founders want to live and a critical mass of them." He thinks Stockholm is the kind of place founders want to live. Critical mass is only visible once you hit it, so Stockholm may be closer than it thinks.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Graham's 2012 keynote lists seven huge startup ideas (search, email, universities, Hollywood, a new Apple, the old Moore's law, ongoing diagnosis) and argues the biggest ideas frighten founders away. The way in is to start with a small, concrete thing a few users want, not a direct frontal attack.

chunks.heading: Seven startup ideas too big to look at directly
chunks.text:
Paul opens by arguing that the biggest startup ideas are frightening because they threaten your identity, not just because they are a lot of work. They say what the Being John Malkovich woman says: "if you ever got me you wouldn't have a clue what to do with me." He calls this one of the most important things to understand about startups: big ideas repel you, so you have to learn to tack into that wind. He gives seven ideas, each big enough to make a billionaire, and expects most listeners to retreat to something like a recipes site.

- Silicon Valley has no architectural center. The center is wherever the people who will make the next generation of stuff are concentrated at that moment.
- The best ideas sit "right on just the right side of impossible," and at the start you can't tell which side you're on.
- Avoiding them is not weakness. Arguably it is sanity.

chunks.heading: Start with the "dinosaur egg": the tiny thing that grows into the giant
chunks.text:
Paul's method for attacking gigantic ideas is to find the small seed that turns into the large idea.

- Example, the next Google: build a search engine that the top 10,000 hackers use, and nobody else. Get the first 20% of them in the room. He says this puts you in the same position Google had with its first 10,000 users.
- If you can build it, you are one of those 10,000 hackers, so build the search engine you want. This is a case where self-indulgence is good: make the queries Turing complete, optimize for code search at the expense of everything else, and don't worry about constraining your long-term future. "If you don't win in the short term there won't be a long term anyway."
- Even a UI that is hard to use doesn't matter if you get those first 10,000. He compares it to Facebook's Harvard undergrads: "5% of the way to an IPO" without realizing it.
- The opening he sees in search: Microsoft entering search showed it had lost its way, Google has drifted into social networks, and its results now feel personalized and cluttered with JavaScript, unlike the old Google that was "designed like a Unix utility."

chunks.heading: Replace email: a to-do list protocol, not a messaging protocol
chunks.text:
Paul says email was designed for people in one corridor at Bell Labs to send each other lunch invitations, and is now used as a to-do list.

- His inbox is a to-do list, and email is the protocol for putting things on it. It is a bad one because anyone can add to it.
- A better protocol would give power to the recipient: control over who can put things in your inbox, and a server that simply says it isn't accepting more. He calls the away message a sign something is wrong.
- Messages should carry what the sender wants done, whether it is physical-world action, the deadline, and when it expires. He cites conference invitations from 2007 still buried in his inbox.
- He says tweaking the inbox won't be enough. You need a new protocol that can degrade to the old one.
- He calls it an irresistible force meeting an immovable object. Entrenched protocols are impossible to displace, but he doesn't believe people in the future will live in the same email hell, so "if it's going to get replaced eventually why not now."
- Go-to-market: a friend, an early Google employee, said his only real problem was the volume of email. Powerful people in pain are an opportunity to make lots of money, and they can say "you want to put something on my to-do list, use this" without caring about interoperability. That solves the chicken-and-egg problem.
- Make it fast: Gmail "has become painfully slow." A Gmail equivalent that is much faster could pull users away on speed alone.
- Pricing: he would pay $50 a month without a problem, and would be justified paying $1,000 a month if it made his life better.

chunks.heading: Replace universities, kill Hollywood
chunks.text:
**Universities.** Paul doesn't expect them to disappear or be replaced wholesale. He expects them to be replaced by many small things that each do what the monolithic four years did, without people noticing.

- He calls them expensive country clubs that are not fun for students or professors, where you don't learn a lot.
- He cites Y Combinator as arguably one instance.
- Credentialing would have to be supplied separately, and a wave of secondary effects follows.
- Go after universities before high schools: high schools bring bureaucratic obstacles, and startups shouldn't take on things that slow them down.
- In Q&A he endorses the idea of getting a credential from a person (an adviser or lab) rather than an institution. That is how medieval guilds originally worked. "Eat away at that big lump of cheese."
- He agrees people must still meet in person, noting that YC moves founders to California and they shake hands. You can build things that involve meeting in person.

**Hollywood.** The idea came from Paul Buchheit; Paul wrote the RFS. Hollywood's mistake was being slow to embrace the internet, and he calls the winner of the entertainment delivery mechanism: the internet, not cable.

- Cable clients (TVs) are terrible; his own solution was to bolt an iMac to the wall.
- Attention can be stolen by social networks or games, but a residual demand remains for people who want to sit and watch a story unfold.
- The question is how to deliver drama over the internet. It will need to be larger scale than YouTube clips, with known characters and predictable length, or big movies known in advance.
- Two outcomes: a big company like Netflix or Apple becomes the app store for entertainment, or it is too restrictive and companies spring up to supply producers a la carte, creating a need for infrastructure companies.

chunks.heading: A new Apple, and the case that it must be a startup
chunks.text:
Paul says someone who knew Apple well told him the current leadership could not keep producing new things the way it did under Steve Jobs: "no, there will be no new stuff" beyond what is in the pipeline.

- His reasoning: existing players aren't run by product visionaries, and the only way a visionary becomes CEO is by starting the company and not getting fired. So the next Apple will have to be a startup.
- It sounds preposterously ambitious, but a founder now has Apple's example. Jobs showed what one person can do, and that you can do much better than a product manager choosing features and handing them to a designer.
- Jobs "unrolled the future like a carpet," and people had unconsciously signed up to use whatever Apple made. Now the future is open.
- The next Steve Jobs would not need to equal Jobs, only to be better than Samsung, HP and Motorola. He urges such founders to apply to YC.
- Q&A on hardware: don't start by competing with the iPad, and start with something for hackers, like Arduino, which doesn't look like a threat to Apple. Cheap consumer devices (a Jawbone-style headset) may be possible. He mentions a current YC startup that is a "print button" for circuit designs, with parts arriving from China.

chunks.heading: Bring back the old Moore's law: make many CPUs look like one fast one
chunks.text:
Paul says Moore's law actually said circuits get twice as dense, not twice as fast. The old version meant slow software could simply wait for faster processors. Now you must rewrite software to be parallel, which is far more work.

- The opportunity: a startup that makes many CPUs look to the developer like one big fast CPU.
- Most ambitious route: a compiler that automatically converts programs written the old way into programs for the new hardware. This is the "sufficiently smart compiler," a byword for impossibility. He asks whether it is truly impossible, and says if it isn't impossible but merely very hard, the expected value could be high.
- Why the value is high: with web services, users never see the processors, so software that restores the old convenience is indistinguishable from being the processor manufacturer, and Intel would be worried. Programmers like convenience and would flock to it.
- Less ambitious route: build from more parallelizable Lego blocks like Hadoop and MapReduce. The programmer still does most of the work, and he thinks there are many startup ideas there.
- Middle route: a semi-automatic version that looks like the smart compiler but has humans in the loop optimizing, either as employees or as a marketplace for optimization. Bots would likely start doing the optimizing, and if they did it all you would have created the sufficiently smart compiler that no one else has a copy of.
- Partner reactions were split: Robert Morris thought he would sound like an idiot, while Paul Buchheit and Aaron Iba said "maybe it'll work." Paul likes the idea for all the ways it is wrong: it runs against decades of software trends, and compilers are supposed to come from open source projects, not startups.

chunks.heading: Ongoing diagnosis, and the tactics for taking on huge problems
chunks.text:
**Ongoing diagnosis.** One of Paul's idea-generating tricks is to imagine how we will seem backward to people in the future. He expects it to seem barbaric in 50 to 100 years that we waited for symptoms to diagnose heart disease and cancer.

- Example: in 2004 Bill Clinton, with the best care available, felt short of breath and learned his arteries were over 90% blocked, then had a quadruple bypass three days later. He had to wait to learn that number.
- He expects eventually knowing such numbers the way we know our weight, via non-destructive testing, and likewise a "radar screen" for cancer. We may all have tens or hundreds of micro-cancers at any time without knowing.
- Obstacles are horrific: technical, bureaucratic, and going against thousands of years of medical tradition. Doctors dislike "fishing expeditions" and call discoveries "incidentalomas." He gives the example of a friend whose brain scan showed an apparent large tumor that was a harmless cyst, after weeks of terror.
- He thinks false alarms are an artifact of current limitations: with continuous scanning people will learn that something is just a birthmark.

**Tactical advice for huge problems.**

- Don't attack frontally or announce you're replacing email, or employees and investors will constantly ask "are we there yet" and haters will line up. Say you're building to-do list software; people notice later, as with iPads replacing Windows.
- Empirically the very big things start small: Microsoft began with a BASIC interpreter for a machine with a couple thousand users, and Facebook began as a site where Harvard undergrads could stalk one another.
- It is also for your own sake. Neither Bill Gates nor Mark Zuckerberg knew how big their companies would get; they knew they were on to something. Big initial ambitions take longer to realize, and the longer the projection the likelier you are wrong.
- Best model is Columbus: "there's something to the West, I'll sail westward." Start with something small that works, then move west when the opportunity comes. The popular image of the visionary with a precise view of the future is wrong; "it's probably better to have a blurry one."

chunks.heading: Q&A: property, copies, and funding ethics
chunks.text:
- On music and copyright: you can't practically charge for copies of stuff anymore. Property has historically been defined by what is convenient to make property (land was not property for hunter-gatherers). Files now move around like smells, so charging for them doesn't work. Some people will still pay, but you can't "print money" as the labels did in the 80s. He notes technology doesn't need copyright protection (Amazon Web Services isn't protected by copyright), and that writing books never made much money and was done mostly out of vanity.
- On funding things that could affect the human genetic code: he hadn't thought about it. YC tries to fund founders who seem likely to succeed, avoids ideas that are overtly evil, and plays it by ear. Paul Buchheit is the half-joking "official morality consultant." He notes that moral questions need other people's advice more than technical ones.
- On Hacker News: it was built by writing an HTTP server without reading the spec, and tweaking it until the browser got pages back. YC hired someone to make Hacker News faster.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Graham argues startups are counterintuitive, like skiing, so instincts mislead. Success comes from making something users want, not gaming the system or learning startup mechanics. Don't start one in college; instead learn powerful things and let ideas emerge unconsciously from side projects.

chunks.heading: Startups are counterintuitive, so don't trust instincts (except about people)
chunks.text:
- Paul argues startups are as unnatural as skiing: the instinct to lean back is wrong, so you need a list of counterintuitive rules to override your habits.
- At Y Combinator, "our function was to tell founders things they would ignore." Founders ignore warnings, then come back a year later saying "I wish we'd listened."
- Advice that matches your intuition is not worth much, which is why startup advisors exist the way ski instructors do.
- The exception: trust your instincts about people. Founders often say "I knew there was something wrong about that guy, but I ignored it because he seemed so impressive."
- Engineers wrongly assume a distasteful person is "normal for business." Paul says pick cofounders the way you pick friends: people you genuinely like and respect and have known long enough to be sure. Some people are good at seeming likeable "until your interests are opposed."

chunks.heading: What you need is expertise in your users, not in startups
chunks.text:
- Success comes from understanding your users, not startup mechanics. Mark Zuckerberg succeeded "despite being a complete noob at startups" (Facebook was first incorporated as a Florida LLC) because he understood his users.
- Learning the mechanics of an angel round is unnecessary and possibly dangerous, because it encourages "playing house": raising funding at a nice valuation, renting a nice office in SoMa, hiring friends, then realizing they neglected the essential thing, "make something people want."
- Paul traces playing house to a lifetime of training on artificial tests (extracurriculars, exam tricks). He admits he studied for exams by guessing the 20 or 30 likely exam questions and working out answers in advance.

chunks.heading: Growth hacks and fundraising tricks are bullshit
chunks.text:
- Young founders look for the trick, assuming fundraising is the measure of success. Paul's answer: the best way to convince investors is to start a startup that is doing well, growing fast, "and then simply tell investors so."
- On growth: "Whenever you hear anybody talk about growth hacks, just mentally translate it in your mind to bullshit." The way to grow is to make something users really love and tell them about it.
- Many partner-founder conversations start with the founder saying "how do I..." and the partner answering "just..."
- Gaming the system stops working in a startup. There is no boss to trick, only users, who are "like sharks": too stupid to fool, only caring whether the software does what they want.
- Faking can work on investors for one or maybe two rounds, but it is self-defeating since founders hold equity in a doomed company.
- Tricks exist but are "an order of magnitude less important." A founder who knows zero about fundraising but has users who love the product will raise more easily than one who knows every trick but has a flat usage graph.
- On fundraising bias (for example against women founders): the fix is the same, make the startup do really well. Paul once tweeted an anonymous, stupendous growth graph of a female-founded startup struggling to raise, noting "growth graphs have no gender."

chunks.heading: Startups are all-consuming, so don't start one in college
chunks.text:
- A startup takes over your life for years, maybe a decade or the rest of your working life. Every successful YC founder says "it never gets any easier"; the problems change but the total worry doesn't decrease.
- Paul compares it to having kids: a button that irrevocably changes your life. Most people in rich countries delay it, and he says startups should be delayed too.
- If you start at 20 and succeed, you lose the chance to do things best done in your early 20s: plunging into projects on a whim with no apparent payoff, or traveling cheaply with no deadline.
- A founder who waits is more likely to succeed. If a side project does take off at 20, running with it can be reasonable, but deliberately starting at 20 is "gratuitously stupid."
- Paul says you cannot reliably tell in advance whether you can handle it, because it changes you. Over nine years at YC he found little correlation between confident or doubtful attitudes and who became stars; he compares it to military recruits where swaggerers are no tougher than quiet ones.
- If you are absolutely terrified, probably don't do it; if merely unsure, the only way to find out is to try, just not now.

chunks.heading: Where startup ideas come from: don't try to think of them
chunks.text:
- Consciously trying to think of startup ideas yields ideas that are "bad and plausible sounding," fooling you and others.
- Yahoo, Google, Facebook and Apple all began as side projects that weren't supposed to be companies. The best ideas are outliers your conscious mind would reject as company ideas.
- Recipe: learn about things that matter, work on problems that interest you, with people you like and respect. The third part also gets you cofounders.
- Domain expertise is the real component of entrepreneurship. Larry Page became an expert on search because he was genuinely interested in it, not from an ulterior motive. Airbnb's Brian Chesky and Joe Gebbia were experts in design and in organizing people, not technology.
- Think of technology as a "fractal stain"; every point on the moving edge is an interesting problem. Get to the leading edge and "live in the future" (a phrase he attributes to Paul Buchheit), and ideas that seem prescient to others will look obvious to you.
- Example: a Harvard grad student wrote his own voice-over-IP software in the mid-90s to talk to his girlfriend in Taiwan without long-distance charges. He never tried to make it a startup, but that is how the best startups tend to happen.
- Heuristic for taste in interesting problems: if you find working on boring things intolerable, you likely have one.
- Best college preparation: learn powerful things out of curiosity, not a vocational entrepreneurship program. His two-word advice: "just learn." Starting a startup is "an ulterior motive for curiosity" best introduced at the end.

chunks.heading: Team, management and school Q&A
chunks.text:
- Non-technical founders: in a domain business like Uber, the domain expert (say, from limos) may do most of the work, recruiting drivers, while the technical founder builds the app. In a pure technology startup, the non-technical founder does sales.
- Business school is basically not useful for startups: it was designed to train the officer corps of large companies in management, a problem you only have if you succeed. Design school would serve better, but the real way to learn is to try it. He admits he was wrong to advise people to work at another company for a few years first.
- Early hires should be like founders: self-motivated peers who don't need managing ("not like The Office"). Airbnb took five months to hire its first employee, he notes (via Sam).
- On monoculture from hiring people you like: the benefits of hiring people you know and like far outweigh the blind spots. Empirically, the most successful startups hired "all their pals out of college."
- For a side project, you'll know it's becoming a startup when it takes over an alarming share of your life.
- For slow growth with some users, he points to his essay "Do Things That Don't Scale."
- No kind of startup should avoid YC unless it will fail or the founders are intolerable, since most startup problems are the same regardless of domain.

chunks.heading: Bubbles and what Paul would study
chunks.text:
- Paul distinguishes high prices from a bubble. A bubble is when people knowingly pay high prices hoping to unload on a greater fool, as VCs did in the late 90s by funding junk startups to take public. In 2014 he says valuations are high but it is not a bubble.
- Advice to founders: don't assume the next round will be as easy, and "assume the worst" about future recessions.
- Labs that spin off startups might work if the right people run them; Twitter began as a side project at Odeo (a podcasting company; he misspoke the name as Ideo).
- Paul says he would study physics in college, then notes that following your own curiosity is the point and "it'll turn out to be helpful."
- On efficiency, he says he works either under self-imposed forcing structures (YC's application deadlines made him read applications well) or on things so exciting he can't help working on them, and has no efficiency system.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Graham argues that "make something people want" plus "don't worry about money early" describes something that looks like a nonprofit, and that successful startups often behave that way. Benevolence boosts morale, attracts help and talent, and works as a decision compass. Startups should launch fast and stay hard to kill.

chunks.heading: Make something people want, and be benevolent while doing it
chunks.text:
- Paul's motto for Y Combinator is "make something people want". A month after YC started they stumbled on it, and he says that if he were choosing again today he would still choose it. He doesn't think it can be shortened to fewer than three words.
- The second most common advice to startups is not to worry too much about the business model at the start. Money is important, but it is much easier than making something great.
- Put together, the two ideas describe a nonprofit. Paul's conclusion is that this is a new discovery, not a bug: very successful startups often behave like nonprofits, and many nonprofit ideas would make good companies.
- Some ideas that look benevolent have to be built as companies to be done right. He once considered a free web email service with really good spam filters, and realized it would have to be a company. He thinks a purely benevolent project to index the web could not have come out much better than Google did.
- He won't say where the territory ends. He floats curing malaria as an extreme case: lifting that weight off a region could unlock growth, but he says explicitly it isn't a startup suggestion. His test for how far an idea extends is the point at which you'd be willing to bet against it, and betting against benevolence feels like betting against a technology.

chunks.heading: Craigslist, Google and Microsoft as models of early-stage niceness
chunks.text:
- Craigslist is not a charity but is run like one. Paul suspects, without having done the math, that it makes more money per employee than Google. Its employee count on the lists of most popular sites "looks like a misprint".
- He uses a sailing metaphor from Patrick O'Brian's novels: Craigslist has "the weather gauge" (it is upwind) of enormous revenues. It decides when and whether to engage, and its challenges would be "spin" challenges, unlike companies tacking upwind to force a crappy product on ambivalent customers while spending 10 times as much on sales as on development.
- He does not say startups should end up like Craigslist, but calls it a good model for the first phases.
- Google had no ads for its whole first year and looked like the limit of what a nonprofit web index would produce.
- Microsoft in the beginning was "like Robin Hood" next to IBM. IBM expected to make money selling PC hardware at high prices. Microsoft gained control of the PC standard, which let any manufacturer compete. Prices plummeted and many people who couldn't have afforded computers got them.
- Microsoft's stock rose like Google's back then and has been flat for years since it started frustrating and foisting on users. He suggests there may be a connection.

chunks.heading: Why small companies must charm and big ones can bully
chunks.text:
- When you're small you can't bully users, so you have to charm them. When you're big you can maltreat them at will, and tend to because it's less work.
- "You grow big by being nice, but you can stay big by being mean." You get away with it until the underlying conditions change and your victims all escape (his example: the record companies).
- He argues "don't be evil" may be the most valuable thing Paul Buchheit made for Google, more than Gmail, because it may work as "an elixir of corporate youth" that saves them from the laziness of Microsoft and IBM.
- The elixir is free to any company (no IP protection). The catch is that people will hold you to it, so he doesn't expect record labels or tobacco companies to adopt it.

chunks.heading: Three ways benevolence helps a startup
chunks.text:
Paul says investing in many startups gave him data on what happens inside them. He found three effects: it improves morale, makes other people want to help you, and above all helps you be decisive.

**Morale**
- Morale is so important that it is almost enough on its own to determine success. Startups are an emotional roller coaster, and the real problem with feeling doomed is that you stop working, which makes the downhill parts a self-fulfilling prophecy.
- If you feel you're really helping people, you keep working even when you feel doomed. Most people are naturally inclined to help someone who needs them.
- A product users come back to daily becomes "a giant Tamagotchi" you need to take care of. Blogger is his example: it ran out of money, everyone left, and Evan Williams came back the next day and was the only one there. Users needing him was part of what kept him going.
- This is one reason to launch quickly: once you launch, the Tamagotchi effect kicks in, and you are forced to figure out what users want, which is very valuable information.

**Confidence with investors**
- Chatterous's two founders decided what they were building was so important they would do it no matter what, even if they had to move back to Canada and live in their parents' basements. After that they stopped caring what investors thought, kept going to meetings, and investors got much more interested because they could tell the founders didn't need them.
- YC itself looks for startups that would do better with them, not ones that would die without them, because a startup that close to dying will probably die with them too.
- If you're really committed and your startup is cheap to run, you become very hard to kill. His model for a startup: "not WebVan, Craigslist, and cockroaches". He calls this the most valuable quality a startup can have, since nearly all startups, even successful ones, come close to death at some point, and you're lucky if it's only once.

chunks.heading: Benevolence makes people rally to you
chunks.text:
- Octopart, a search site for industrial components, is his example. Before it there was no good way to search for components online. Its founders dropped out of the physics PhD program at Berkeley after hitting the problem in their own research (they bought a lot of components).
- Digi-Key, the biggest distributor, tried to force Octopart to take prices off the site even though Octopart sent them paying customers for free. Paul's reading: Digi-Key's business model depends on overcharging people with incomplete information about prices, so they don't want search to work.
- Hearing about a big evil company trying to keep search broken made him spend more time on Octopart than on most funded startups. Investors, customers, other companies and potential employees all rally to a benevolent project.
- Employees may matter most in the long run. Good hackers are much more valuable pound for pound than mediocre ones, the best tend to be idealistic, can work anywhere, and choose projects that make the world better. A project that does so is a magnet for smart people, which was a huge advantage for Google.

chunks.heading: Being good as a compass and a stateless algorithm
chunks.text:
- A startup has thousands of things to do and two or three people to do them, and the one thing you can't do is vacillate. Paul's answer: "Just do whatever is best for your users." He says to hold on to it "like a rope in a hurricane".
- The loop: figure out what users want, make them happy, keep doing more of that.
- It also answers how to raise money. Most hackers aren't great salesmen, so go to investors through your customers. If users like the product enough to tell their friends, that is a recipe for exponential growth, and the traffic graph convinces investors (he shows Octopart's, which separates human from non-human traffic, with a dip at Christmas because "nobody buys components for Christmas presents").
- Being good is "stateless", like telling the truth. A liar has to remember everything said before to avoid contradiction, whereas a truth-teller remembers nothing. That matters in domains where things change fast.
- YC had invested in 80 startups, 57 still alive "for some definition of alive". Advising that many at once requires a stateless algorithm with no ulterior motives, since you couldn't remember them. Their rule is to do whatever is best for the startups, which may not be optimal for YC but is reasonably close. He says this is because it is the only algorithm that works at that scale, not because they're particularly benevolent.
- He adds that Google likely doesn't manipulate search results for the same reason: once you start, it doesn't scale.
- He says he is not a particularly good person and is suggesting benevolence "because it works", as corporate strategy and as a design spec for software, not as sanctimonious goody-two-shoes behavior. His closing line: "don't just not be evil, be good."

chunks.heading: Q&A: school, finding ideas, and what YC funds
chunks.text:
- **Dropping out for an idea:** Paul's view is there's no huge rush. College is also for fun, learning and friends, and the idea that seems so great you'd drop out may not turn out to be that great. If you wait until after school, you'll probably think of an even better one. (An audience member strongly disagreed, arguing that dropouts end up employing degree holders; Paul left it at "maybe".)
- **Finding startup ideas:** "Look for problems. Don't try and think of solutions." Look for things that seem broken and let the problems drive the solutions. Component search was broken and the Octopart founders noticed because they had to buy components in their research.
- **Why so many web 2.0 companies:** YC does fund infrastructure, including two database companies, which haven't launched because that kind of software takes so long to build. But they fund what people apply with, and most people apply with some form of Facebook or independent music. "You can only catch the fish that are floating down the stream."
- **Selection criterion:** YC tries to fund the founders it likes and who seem likely to succeed. A benevolent startup that doesn't succeed doesn't achieve its aims, so success is the limit on how benevolent YC can be. Founders it likes tend to do benevolent things because being good works.
- **Mottos:** Paul says encouraging startups to have mottos is a good idea, but not if making one delays launch by a couple of hours.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In a Startup School conversation with Geoff Ralston, Paul Graham recounts how ViaWeb started and distills lessons on co-founders, manual early work, launching a quantum of utility fast, and why determination beats smarts. He also covers competitors, pricing, raising too much money, and user interviews.

chunks.heading: Why startups are counterintuitive, and what YC actually does
chunks.text:
Paul says startups are "very, very counterintuitive," and that is why Y Combinator exists. If the right moves were obvious, YC "couldn't really add much by teaching people how to do it." He describes YC's job as telling founders things they ignore.

- Example: YC tells founders not to hire too fast. They hire too fast anyway, then come back and say they wish they had listened.
- Counterintuitive advice sounds wrong, so founders go with their gut and make the mistake, then hopefully catch it in time.
- He sees this in office hours "practically every day."

chunks.heading: Doing things that don't scale: Viaweb's manual start
chunks.text:
Paul argues founders should do things in a handmade, artisanal, painstaking way early on, even when they think "there's no way we can keep doing this and become giant." He says you have nothing to lose and you learn a lot.

- Viaweb was an online store builder. Customers said no to using the software, so the founders offered to use it for them. Customers agreed, and the founders built stores for them by hand.
- Paul used his own software to build customers' sites. When it was inconvenient, he changed the software mid-task, shipped it with the Unix `mv` command, and went back to the customer's site. This made the software much better.
- They signed up for every catalog to learn direct marketing and joined the Direct Marketing Association. The catalog business was then called the direct marketing industry.
- Early YC applications were an ASCII form answered by email. The partners printed them out, graded them on paper like exams, and sorted the pile. Software came later: "eventually you build software when you learn what software you ought to be building."
- Growth math: with 10 customers, a 10% weekly goal means finding about one more customer, which can be done manually. A constant growth rate is exponential growth, so "the base number will soon take care of itself."

chunks.heading: Where the Viaweb idea came from
chunks.text:
Paul says the idea was not a light bulb. He calls "light bulb" startup stories a cliché and false.

- Everyone then assumed writing software meant writing for the client, which meant Windows. His team knew Unix and refused to learn Windows.
- His first thought was an online store builder that you updated by email. He then asked: if you can use SMTP, why not HTTP? The software could run on the server and be controlled by clicking links in the browser.
- Netscape had already done the work of running on Windows, so the web was "a hole onto Windows."
- They did not foresee the benefits of web apps, which turned out to be great. They simply wanted to avoid learning Windows.
- The first version was clunky, but it worked.
- Ideas usually start as an inkling that you could do something nobody has done, probably a bad idea. Paul likes ideas that are implausible "in the right way," a bit naughty, as if something shouldn't be possible. He cites Facebook as an example.
- He told someone choosing between two ideas to pick the more outrageous one. He adds that laziness here means a gratuitous-work aversion that produces elegant solutions, not real laziness: "there's no such thing as a lazy founder that builds a big company."

chunks.heading: Picking co-founders and hiring
chunks.text:
Paul chose Robert Morris because he did everything with him and knew he could work with him. Morris was an exceptional programmer who "could program as fast as he could type."

- Morris was not enthusiastic about the startup. On the board he would respond to lowball acquisition offers by saying that at least it would mean they could stop working on this thing. Paul bet him an earring if he ever made a million dollars out of Viaweb. He did, and Paul and Trevor Blackwell frog-marched him to get one.
- Morris recommended Trevor Blackwell as the smartest person he knew in grad school. Blackwell disappeared for two weeks and came back having rewritten the software in Smalltalk. Paul told him they weren't using that.
- Hiring and co-founder rule: find someone you trust, then find someone they trust. This works for judging intelligence, because smart people can judge other smart people. It does not work for trustworthiness: trustworthy people are often fooled by untrustworthy ones.
- A recruiting trick at Viaweb: Morris had been kicked out of Harvard for a year after spending a semester reconnecting Harvard to the Internet instead of doing coursework. They put up posters at Harvard asking "Did you get kicked out working on some project of your own? We'd like to hire you." Paul says it got them a great programmer.
- Co-founders need to know one another well. The stress of a startup exposes any flakiness, uncertainty or disloyalty. He compares it to "a marriage only harder."
- Paul says he could not have started a company alone and calls solo founding lonely. Co-founders keep each other going when things go badly.
- On unequal commitment: ask whether you would rather have 30% of this person or 100% of someone else. He would rather have 10% of Robert Morris's brain than 100% of almost anyone else's.
- For firing a co-founder, talk to Carolyn Levy at YC and read YC's published material. He suggests one person hold slightly more equity, such as 51/49, to avoid deadlock.

chunks.heading: Determination, intelligence, and what founders get wrong
chunks.text:
Paul says determination matters more than intelligence. Take someone 100/100 on both and remove determination, and you quickly get "ineffectual but brilliant." Remove smartness from a very determined person and you eventually get someone who owns many taxi medallions but is still rich.

- Only one co-founder has to be super determined, as long as a tight bond lets that person drag the others along.
- A team also needs someone able to navigate as the idea evolves. Caring about users and following what makes them happy can substitute for creativity, "the way a scientist follows the truth."
- Competitors: of about 1,900 YC-funded companies, one was killed by a competitor. Founders have the same protection light aircraft have in clouds: "space is large." If another runner appears in your lane, run as fast as you can. What mostly kills companies is poor founder execution.
- He lists mistakes founders will make anyway:
  - They won't pay enough attention to users. They invent a "vision" in a cafe instead of finding anyone with a problem they will pay to fix. Best case is a problem the founder has.
  - They won't ship fast enough because they are embarrassed to ship something unfinished and dread the humbling feedback.
- Founder DNA: determination and willingness to try new things, plus negatives. Someone who has worked at a large company for twenty years is probably not a founder, since a good founder couldn't have stood it that long. Some companies' alumni make bad founders for this reason.
- He says a startup founder should not spend all their time thinking about fundraising.

chunks.heading: When to launch
chunks.text:
Paul says launch earlier than feels comfortable.

- Reid Hoffman's line he endorses: if you're not embarrassed by what you launched, you launched too late.
- He once told Geoff Ralston, who was working on a PR plan and finishing software six weeks before a summer batch, to "just launch now." They launched within a week.
- YC itself launched less than a week after having the idea, as a website plus an emailed form.
- Rule of thumb: launch as soon as you have "a quantum of utility," meaning at least one person in the world is glad you launched because they can now do something they couldn't before. If nobody would be happy, you are not ready.
- Ten people who really love the product is a good place to be, even if no one else cares.
- Launching in a private beta to a few people beats sitting with your idea in a cafe.
- Launching early is not riskless, but launching late has risk too.

chunks.heading: User interviews, building what people want, and pricing
chunks.text:
- Interviewing: find what is actually wrong, not what the user says is wrong. Ask what they would like to do that they can't. Their answer is often a symptom: someone who wants to mark email as unread is really using the inbox as a to-do list. Start with questions about their life, then ask hypotheticals ("what if you could do such-and-such").
- Need vs. want: build something people will choose to use or buy. Need is not the goal; people need healthy food but buy unhealthy food. Be careful with "need," because it often means what you think they need ("cleanse the world of sin"). Pick the solution you think can get usage quickest.
- Pricing: roughly guess what you should charge, or ask friendly early users what they would honestly pay. You can change prices later. Lowering draws no complaints. When raising, grandfather existing users, who are a tiny share if growth is exponential.
- In the early days you mostly need customers who will pay, and early customers teach you, not just pay you.

chunks.heading: Raising money, angels, and starting young
chunks.text:
- ICOs and large raises: Paul knows little about ICOs. He says raising too much is often wrong because you dilute more than needed and idle money "has a gravitational pull" that makes you spend it and do stupid things. He gives Magic Leap's $2.3 billion raise as a case that seemed to produce almost nothing.
- Finding angels: angels are looking for you, so go to startup events. The best route is to get one angel to invest, who then introduces you to others. Another tip: find people who work at startups and ask them to introduce you to their investors.
- High-school founders: YC has funded kids in high school, but only when they were already going. He does not encourage it. Between 18 and 22 people should be exploring options, and startups need one hundred percent commitment, not a dabbling fallback.
- He warns that starting a startup is "like catching a dragon by the tail," so be careful when in life you do it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Live office hours where Paul Graham and Sam Altman question three early startups (a coding game, a progress-video site, a customs brokerage). Recurring themes: don't over-optimize early, test the thing that matters, copy industry defaults, avoid pitching huge markets, and prefer founders who can't stand big-company jobs.

chunks.heading: Paul's rule: launch fast, test what matters, and let the product find its use
chunks.text:
- Paul and Sam interview three startups live. The first team (the multiplayer coding game) was told afterward that this was their YC interview, and they were accepted into the next batch.
- Paul's tests for the three companies are mostly empirical: does the product work with real users, will people share it, and have the founders actually tested the thing they say will drive growth?
- He pushes teams to launch and measure instead of polishing in private.

chunks.heading: Sam and Paul's read on a game that teaches programming
chunks.text:
- The company builds a multiplayer programming game: players write code to control units and fight. It is meant as a more engaging alternative to Codecademy.
- It launched the day before the office hours with a post on Reddit. About 15,000 people came and the server maxed out. Many users saw 404s ("hug of death") because the architecture couldn't scale.
- Paul asks how the game stays educational. Can advanced concepts "produce advanced weaponry"? The founders answer with levels that force recursion, restricted methods and performance limits.
- Beta lesson: the founders assumed too much prior knowledge. Formal notation was the single biggest obstacle for complete beginners.
- Paul's advice on open sourcing: look at what the games industry does and use that as the default starting point. He asks if the founders know the gaming business, and they say they are learning and have game designers advising them.
- The business model is recruiting: leads from coding challenges go to companies. Paul notes that "recruiters famously say all sorts of crazy stuff", so this is not yet validated.
- Paul on founder profiles: when reading applications, someone who worked a long time at a large company counts against them. "The best startup founders probably could not stand that."

chunks.heading: Why "Give 100" should test its sharing loop before the waitlist opens
chunks.text:
- Give 100 (give00.com, as written in the transcript) is a video site where people pick a skill and post a short video of their progress every day for 100 days. Clips are capped at 10 seconds.
- It was in private beta with 50 users and about 4,300 on a waitlist. The founder's own year-long video of learning to dance got about 3 million views and led to the idea.
- Reported numbers: about 1,000 views a day, 20 to 30 of the 50 beta users returning daily, and an average of about 18 videos per user. The longest streak was a beatboxer at about day 85.
- Paul and Sam press the founders on why they are holding back the waitlist. The founder wants social sharing features first.
- Sam's pointed critique: YouTube is the planned marketing channel, yet the beta never tested whether the clips get shared and watched there. "It seems like that would have been really important to test during the beta."
- Paul also asks what third parties would want to watch, as opposed to what the practicers do. He notes parents would love a record of a child's progress, since new memories overwrite earlier ones.

chunks.heading: Don't wire in an outcome too early
chunks.text:
- When the Give 100 founders are unsure whether dance, babies learning to walk, or something else will be the main use case, Paul says not to over-optimize early.
- His advice: "Let it grow into whatever it's going to grow into." The kids use case may become the big thing or not.
- He says to be empirical about it and not "wire in some outcome too early."
- Sam adds that a baby learning to walk is very different from someone teaching themselves to unicycle, so the product shouldn't be built around a single use case before the data points to one.

chunks.heading: Flexport: a customs brokerage as the entry point to logistics
chunks.text:
- Flexport is a licensed US customs brokerage built around a web app. Brokers are heavily licensed and need an FBI background check. A broker files up to about 120 forms per shipment, depending on the product.
- The founder has about 12 years in the industry. He has imported roughly 1,000 containers and has a customs worker on staff. His previous company sold a database of 300 million shipping manifests, which gives him a list of every importer in America.
- Traction: three customers and a waitlist of about 300. The first clearance was planned for November, delayed because the government shutdown held up the broker onboarding.
- Pricing and market: about $100 to $300 per shipment from incumbents, 30 million shipments a year entering the US. The founder plans to charge $100 per clearance regardless of size, with about 75% gross margin, and extra for FDA-type paperwork.
- The founder says that once he is the customs broker he knows the whole supply chain, and could later sell freight, warehousing, inspection and trucking.
- Paul and Sam probe why no one has done it: heavy regulation, and until 2007 a shipment could only be cleared at a local port.

chunks.heading: Paul on market-size claims
chunks.text:
- When the Flexport founder cites logistics as a "$2.3 trillion industry", Paul cuts in: "really big markets are bad for startups, not good."
- His reasoning: if you say too big a number, investors just don't believe it.
- Paul asks for the real number for the actual first product, the customs brokerage itself. The founder models about $30 million a year in profit at 1% share, with each customer worth roughly $200 to $3,000 a year. Paul and Sam do not agree on the market figure: the whole US customs clearance business is estimated at about $3 billion to $5 billion a year, and the founder concedes he lacks exact figures.
- Paul and Sam also ask how he will win customers from brokers with long relationships. The answer is his importer database and a plan to possibly hire sales staff, which he says "isn't that fun to manage" but works.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Graham explains how he evaluates early-stage founders (people over plans, determination via stories, real understanding), why YC interviews work in about 10 minutes, and how he pushes founders to think bigger. He also covers obsessing over missed companies and how fame arrived at YC unnoticed.

chunks.heading: Evaluating founders: people over plans
chunks.text:
- The earlier the stage, the more the investment is a bet on the founders. "It's location for real estate." Early-stage investors therefore need to be good judges of people.
- Paul says his wife Jessica Livingston is a much better judge of people and social protocol than he is. He puts part of that down to natural ability and part to caring less about those things.
- His own edge: he can tell whether someone actually understands an idea, especially a technical one, or only has a "reading the newspapers level of understanding."
