- Determination is hard to read from demeanor. Everyone walking into a YC interview thinks they must look tough, which is "painful to watch." He would rather they just be themselves.
- He judges determination through stories. He asks what happened to them, and looks at what they did when something went wrong: did they persevere instead of giving up?
- On Sam Altman, he sees a technical person who can also put the pieces together and run things: "a technical guy who also is very formidable, and that's a good combination."
- He is unsure the "great founders in their 20s" story is true. He plans to check with YC partners. His hunch is that hindsight is distorting it: "anybody who claims they knew early on that Patrick Collison was going to be a big star, show me the equity." Stripe's early rounds did not attract everyone.

chunks.heading: How YC interviews work and where they fail
chunks.text:
- The first 10 minutes of a YC interview is effectively the start of YC. You see what it's like to work with the founders by working with them for 10 minutes, and that is enough.
- He has studied the point where a decision stops changing. The chance of changing your mind is high after minute 1 or 2, and low after about minute 7. He says YC interviews could be 7 minutes rather than 10, and that 10 is "almost insultingly short" already.
- 7 minutes is where you are unlikely to change your mind if things are going badly. It does not mean 7 minutes tells you everything.
- Early flips are often a misunderstanding. The founders are near an idea YC knows is bad, YC assumes they're doing it, and then they say "no, we're doing this." They then earn extra credit for understanding why the bad idea is bad.
- YC tracks its failures obsessively. It keeps a list of companies that applied, were rejected and went on to succeed, and studies the common causes.
- Example fix: an email-sending company got a "C" and the comment "spam company" from the first reader (Robert Morris, the designated wet blanket). Nobody else saw it, and it later went public. YC then changed the software so every application is read by at least two people.
- This is also why he is "contemptuous" of university admissions: YC measures its misses and fixes them, while admissions offices don't.

chunks.heading: Making founders more ambitious
chunks.text:
- Founders are held back by fear of thinking big, because it seems like overreaching and like a lot of work.
- He compares his role to a fitness instructor. He can tell someone already working hard to "push harder" at no effort cost to himself, and surprisingly often they can.
- Introducing ambitious people to better peers and pulling them away from peers who aren't good enough is part of it, though he doesn't think it's the main thing.
- He says there is a real skill in "blowing up" an idea, meaning making it bigger: take an idea and ask how it could be bigger. YC interviews often do this, and founders walk out thinking their idea is much better than they thought, even though an interview is nominally a negotiation.
- Weak ambition isn't about ability. He is optimistic about the UK because people there "are not slack, they're not lazy and they're not stupid." Teaching British founders to aim for fast growth "is like teaching them a foreign language, but they do learn it."

chunks.heading: Founder heuristics and startup structure
chunks.text:
- The heuristic of preferring young founders with side projects is a way to match founders to ideas. Young founders with no experience of the world get things wrong when they sit down and brainstorm startup ideas. Older founders can start things like supersonic aircraft or geriatric care and get them right.
- Solo founders: he wouldn't start a company alone because of the weight involved. But it is hard to find a partner as good as you, so going solo is also easier in a sense.
- His advice to teens and people in their early 20s: don't sit around thinking up startup ideas. Work with other people on projects. You'll get a startup idea you'd never have thought of, and a co-founder, but "you can't get co-founders instantly. You got to have some patience."
- When technical founders hate sales, he tells them to do it in small steps. After a few months they get used to it, even if they never like it.
- He compares this to how he cured his fear of flying: he learned hang gliding gradually, starting by running on flat ground and moving up the hill, then took flying lessons. He says he never consciously used the lesson in selecting talent.

chunks.heading: Venture capital, Microsoft and the shape of the market
chunks.text:
- VC works where growth is high. Half the companies fail completely, so the winners need astonishing returns to compensate.
- VCs' ownership per round has shrunk. In the 1980s a round might buy 50% of a company, when YC started about 30%, and now around 10% for a given round size.
- Microsoft: his old essay was about Microsoft's culture and was not a claim that it wouldn't make money. He says Mark Zuckerberg was the founder puzzled that Microsoft could be a threat. Today no startup plans around the fear that Microsoft will enter its space.
- On Sam Altman's remark questioning "find product-market fit, then scale," he says OpenAI may be a special case because it needs giant warehouses of GPUs, so it may need advance planning. He says he doesn't know what goes on inside it.

chunks.heading: Florence, Harvard and building a talent magnet
chunks.text:
- Paul says Florence was good at art because it was the most progressive city, "New York City in 1450 with 60,000 people," not because of a special Florentine aesthetic. He says he realized he had gone to the place where the puck used to be.
- He sees YC as deliberately modeled on Harvard: a small area that draws talent in and produces many winners. YC's first office was within Harvard's footprint, and "we've consciously tried to make YC the Harvard of startups."
- Harvard's admissions are corrupt (Dean's favorites, legacies), but because other universities are similarly messed up, Harvard keeps its draw. He thinks only Caltech may do undergraduate admissions properly.
- On fame: he didn't realize how prominent YC had become until long after. YC itself stayed a few people doing the same thing each batch while its portfolio companies grew to thousands of employees. He calls this one of his biggest mistakes with YC: he didn't realize how many people were watching, or that some would be out to get it.

chunks.heading: AI, work habits and Lisp
chunks.text:
- On AI regulation he says he has no idea what it should look like. His one observation: safe AI is like a secure operating system or a fraud-proof tax code, built from patches in response to successful hacks, so any regulation will be wrong, with overregulation in some places and holes in others.
- He doesn't think AI makes programming more like painting, since you are still building something.
- AI optimists and pessimists differ mainly in which aspect they focus on. He holds both views at once: "unimaginably good and unimaginably bad."
- He thinks AI-code-trained AI won't converge on better code by itself, and recalls research where training on AI output "converges on crap." You need a large initial corpus of human-written examples in a language.
- Lisp is intimidating at the notation: an "initial hump" in front of people, and they will take a long detour to avoid even one obstacle. He says Clojure is successful and that JavaScript is, except for syntax, a Lisp.
- Activities with high interruption cost are those where you hold a "giant house of cards" mental model in your head, such as programming and math. Painting is less like that.
- Walking: he finds it best for learning from another person, less good for generating his own ideas. Classic YC office hours were walks down the block, which has the side benefit that people talk more freely when they aren't looking at each other. For solo thinking he suggests walking the same route somewhere undistracting.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: At a revenue bootcamp fireside chat, Paul Graham explains how YC picks founders (people who build things for love, not proven résumés), why he ignores revenue forecasts, why founders should be candid with smart investors, and how to spot the next platform. Mike Moritz of Sequoia adds the VC view.

chunks.heading: Early-stage investing: small checks, no revenue forecasts, and honest founders
chunks.text:
Paul runs Y Combinator, which invests in many startups at once. He funds roughly 25 or 30 startups twice a year, in batches. Each investment is about $20,000, and the group works intensively together for 3 months. At the end of the 3 months comes "demo day", where each startup gets 5 minutes to present to investors. YC is trying to be "first gear" money, and the aim is to help founders get the next round.

- He says the most useful thing YC does is "try and figure out what to build first".
- He also does things he wishes he didn't have to do, such as arbitrating conflicts between founders.
- YC has dinner with the founders once a week for the first 3 months. Until about a year before this talk, Paul cooked the dinners himself.
- Contact doesn't stop after the 3 months. Only the weekly dinners do.
- His expertise is the problems of the very beginning, not later-stage matters like IPOs. One example is that a two- or three-person founding team can lose a member in the first week.

chunks.heading: What Paul looks for in founders
chunks.text:
Paul doesn't look for a "proven" team, technology or market in the usual VC sense. He looks for four traits: determined, smart, a sense of design, and gets things done.

- The evidence he wants is that someone really likes to build things.
- His reasoning is that to be really good at something you have to actually like it, not do it out of duty for a job or a class.
- It is hard for someone who really likes programming to reach age 23 without having built something outside of school or work.
- So the big question YC asks is: "What have you made outside of school or work because you liked it?"
- If founders don't like building, he argues, they won't do well as startup founders.
- The ideal is founders building something they themselves want to use. The next best is something a close person, such as a spouse or sibling, wants to use. This gives a deep understanding of what is essential in the product that you can't get by intellectualizing.
- When Paul talks about hackers building for platforms they use, his example is iPhone development. Many YC companies build for the iPhone because founders own iPhones. Not one is building for BlackBerry because none of them use BlackBerrys.
- He treats this as the way to predict which platforms will be big: look at what hackers themselves use. He called it "really bad news" for RIM.

chunks.heading: Revenue forecasts and the "don't ask, don't tell" policy
chunks.text:
Paul says YC has a "don't ask, don't tell policy on revenue projections". They don't even ask for them.

- What he cares about is whether the founders are building something people really care about and want. If so, he argues, "the money will follow". If nobody cares, or it's like everything else, there won't be any money.
- It is fine for founders to say they don't know how to make money, as long as they treat it as a problem to solve. He frames it as: "We have no idea how to make money. We're worried about that. Talk to us. Let's figure out how to make money."
- He says you can't fake sincerity. Founders should care without saying so.
- The sentence to avoid is "we have no idea how to make money and it's not a problem".
- He thinks Dropbox was a good example of an early funding where the way to make money wasn't spelled out. The founders were two people from MIT, and the idea was clearly valuable.

chunks.heading: Being candid with investors, including about competitors
chunks.text:
Paul's advice on presenting competitors is that the smarter the investor, the more candid the founder should be.

- The typical mistake is a competitor grid where the founder's column is fully checked and every competitor's column is empty. He says no founder at the Garage event ever showed a grid where their own column wasn't fully checked.
- A smart investor will notice if you lie. So with the investors whose money you want, tell them what you would say among yourselves.
- His example wording: "We're worried about such and such company because of such and such, but we think we have an edge because of this."
- His analogy: the better the investor, the more it should be like going to the doctor. Don't lie about your symptoms. Tell them exactly what's going on.
- He lists generic language as a BS trigger. A specific one is describing your idea with the word "passion". His line: "You should show passion... you shouldn't say the word passion. You should just seem like you care."

chunks.heading: Founder age, and why YC funds young founders
chunks.text:
The average YC founder is about 25 or 26. Paul says the reason is not that young people are better. It is that more people start startups at that age.

- By the 30s, people have families and mortgages, and the friends they'd want to start a company with are more tied down.
- He calls this an "exponential effect of tied downness as people get older".
- 25-year-olds can say "What the hell, we'll try it."
- He says YC has funded some older founders, and that older founders can pitch and get a response.

chunks.heading: When to give up, and what founders can reasonably expect
chunks.text:
Paul's test for whether a startup should quit is whether the founders have given up.

- He says that as long as founders haven't given up, they can morph the company into anything. In the early phase, a couple of people in an apartment "eating beans and writing code" can turn things around tomorrow.
- When a founder asks him "Can I give up now?", he says the answer is probably yes. They have already decided and want his blessing.
- If founders say "we're a year in, our software still sucks, we have no customers, but we're not giving up", he says he'll keep helping them for as long as they keep fighting.

chunks.heading: Board seats, bad news, and how Paul sees the investor role
chunks.text:
Paul doesn't take board seats and says he never will.

- He argues you can do a lot of what a board member does without being on the board. Advice from a non-board member just has no formal standing. If it's good, he hopes they will listen.
- On founders bringing bad news, he says founders usually don't have good news when they ask to meet. In his experience, an email saying they "need to get together" means the VP of sales quit, a quarter was missed, or they are closer to running out of money than they thought.
- His observation is that bad things happen more suddenly than good things, in startups and in the news. Gradual improvement, like air safety getting better, isn't a headline.

chunks.heading: Valuation and ownership, and the competition for new platforms
chunks.text:
A founder in the audience, who had put in $500,000 of his own money, asked how a VC values an early company. Paul gave a joking rule of thumb for pre-money valuation.

- For every full-time engineer, add $500,000 of pre-money valuation. For every MBA, subtract $250,000.
- His example: three engineers and two MBAs is 3 x $500K = $1.5M, minus 2 x $250K = $500K, which gives $1M. He said this was how to figure it, "very simple".
- Paul framed this as a joke answer. Mike Moritz of Sequoia gave the serious ownership range.
- On predicting the next big wave, Paul says that if he knew, he would have every company YC funds do it. He argues the question can't really be answered.
- His practical version is the platform rule above: watch which platforms hackers use themselves.
- His source of good ideas: think of something you needed at a company you worked for that didn't exist, where you'd say "if somebody would just make blank, we'd pay a lot for that". If you can fill in the blank, he says you are "onto a gold mine".
- On how much of a prototype to expect from founders: YC gives them about 3 weeks between inviting them to interview and the interview itself, which is the time to get plane tickets. He says that in that time they ought to throw together something to look at, unless they're building hardware or something that takes a long time.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: At YC Startup School Stockholm, Graham argues ambitious founders should move to the center of their field, at least for a while. The big center gives better peers, serendipity, faster decisions, a calibrated sense of your own ability, and a culture of helping. Going and returning also strengthens your home hub.

chunks.heading: Why go to the center of your field
chunks.text:
- Paul says that whenever many people work intensely on something, one place is its center: Paris for painting in 1870, Göttingen for math in 1900, Hollywood for movies in 1950. Ambitious people there always ask "Should I go?"
- His answer is always yes. "You can go there for a bit and then come back, but you should at least go."
- The logic is the same as moving from a small village to the capital. It doesn't change when you cross "a dotted line on a map."
- What you get is the best peers. The talent pool grows in two ways: the people are better and there are more of them, and they cluster together.
- He compares a YC batch to a room like the one he's speaking in: "every dinner feels like this," every week for 3 months.

chunks.heading: Serendipitous meetings and speed
chunks.text:
- Paul says serendipitous meetings are "enormously important." Biographies of people who did great things constantly feature an unplanned meeting that changed their life.
- He is unsure why unplanned meetings beat planned ones. His candidate explanations:
  - There are simply more of them, so more outliers are the unplanned kind.
  - Planned meetings are too conservative. Needing a reason beforehand "lops off the outliers," like deliberately trying to find startup ideas.
  - Unplanned meetings involve more selection. You can decide after a few sentences whether to keep talking.
- In a big center you have more of these meetings with people working on the same ambitious thing.
- Things also move faster in centers. People are better and more confident, so more decisive, and they egg one another on, both encouraging and competing.
- In villages, people "half had" ideas and never acted. Years later, when a big startup appears, they say "I thought of that."

chunks.heading: Why Silicon Valley investors decide faster
chunks.text:
- Paul says Valley investors decide much faster than European ones, partly because they are more confident and partly because there is much more competition.
- Investors there can't sit on a good idea: "the more right this investor is, the more likely that opportunity is to time out." The more right you are, the less time you can wait.
- Example: Yuri Sagalov invested immediately on meeting Max because "anybody else who meets this guy is going to invest in him."
- Investors complain about high valuations and being rushed. Empirically it doesn't hurt them: Silicon Valley investors get better returns than European investors despite deciding so quickly.

chunks.heading: Respect back home, and the Dropbox story
chunks.text:
- Paul says investors outside Silicon Valley implicitly assume any local startup is second rate ("No one is a prophet in their own country"). He says it's not uniquely Swedish.
- Going to Silicon Valley reverses this, and you rise in local investors' opinion. Sometimes you only need to announce you've been accepted to Y Combinator.
- Dropbox, summer 2007, was in a Boston batch. A big Boston VC firm had watched them for a year, giving encouragement and advice but no money.
- Boston investors were so lame that YC flew Boston startups to Silicon Valley for a second demo day so they could raise money.
- Dropbox came to Sequoia's attention there. When the Boston firm heard, it faxed founder Drew a term sheet with a blank valuation: "Let us invest."
- It was too late. Drew went with Sequoia. In 2018 Dropbox was the first YC company to go public.

chunks.heading: Seeing how big a fish you are
chunks.text:
- Paul says the biggest advantage of a center is what it does to you. In a small pond you don't know how big a fish you are. In a big pond you can measure yourself against known big fish.
- Surprisingly often the news is good. You meet someone like Brian Chesky or Sam Altman and think: impressive, but "not a different species from me. I could do what he did if I worked that hard."
- He calls this the most important part, and the condition matters. It's "I could be like that guy if I worked as hard." Startups are really hard.
- Seeing such people sets a new standard you have to meet. It makes the goal seem "no longer... an impossible goal, just a hard one." For an ambitious person, "there is nothing better than a high but definite threshold."
- He uses Max (a Swedish founder at the event, whom he jokingly calls "the Swedish fish") as the example: he is about as big a fish as they get, and you can see how hard he works.
- Big fish who speak at YC try to seem accessible and encouraging, not frightening. That's why fewer people than expected conclude "I could never do what they do."

chunks.heading: Pay-it-forward culture
chunks.text:
- Paul says in Silicon Valley "people help you for no reason." Saying so there would sound as odd as saying "in Sweden the streets are clean for no reason."
- He asked a founder who had just moved from England how it differed from expectations. He recommends this as the best question to ask anyone who has tried something new: "How is it different than you expected?"
- The founder said the surprise was how helpful everyone was. Every conversation seemed to end with "What can I do to help you?" In England, apparently not. Paul says this is not politeness, since English people are more polite than Americans.
- His explanation for how it evolved: Silicon Valley is where people go from nobodies to billionaires fastest. Someone who was kind to nobodies ended up with powerful friends, and probably rich. Even if it started as calculation, it no longer is. The custom is about 60 years old and now seems like how everyone behaves.
- Ron Conway is his example. He helps people all day, doesn't track whether they're his portfolio companies, and doesn't remember most favors. That lets him operate on a much larger scale, like honesty: you don't have to track lies.
- With many people doing this "there is no longer a conservation law for favors. There's just more favors." Paul and Ron have traded favors for 20 years and he assumes Ron is ahead.
- He says moving to the Valley will make you more helpful to others.

chunks.heading: How Sweden can thrive as a startup hub
chunks.text:
- Paul says both questions have the same answer: go for a bit, then come back. Coming back is one of the best things you can do for Stockholm as a startup hub.
- He says it isn't controversial. It would not have helped 19th-century mathematicians to boycott Göttingen and stay to develop national math. Government fellowships of the time were conditional on leaving and studying abroad.
- Going to Silicon Valley and returning helps Sweden in three ways:
  - Your own startup improves, raising the average quality of local startups.
  - You likely bring back money from Silicon Valley investors.
  - You import Silicon Valley culture, which evolved over decades to be optimal for startups. He calls it compatible with Swedish culture, since it has the high-trust part.
- He thinks Sweden should lose the "tall-poppy thing" anyway.
- He admits it sounds like "talking my own book," but says the best way to spend time in the Valley is to do YC, which is designed to concentrate these advantages.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A 2014 fireside chat where Graham explains why he handed YC to Sam Altman, how YC's early model was a summer-job accident, and what he has learned from 632 startups. Key themes: co-founder relationships, brute focus on the one bottleneck, starting with a small intense fire of users, and why determination beats raw intelligence.

chunks.heading: How YC started and the summer-program origin
chunks.text:
- Paul says YC started for two reasons: he felt guilty he hadn't gotten around to Angel Investing, and Jessica was talking to a Boston VC fund about becoming their VP of marketing. The VCs took so long to decide that he said "[ __ ] them we'll just start our own thing."
- The first batch (summer 2005, Cambridge) was pitched as a summer program for undergraduates. Compared to a regular summer job ("work in a cubicle", "work on not what you would want with people you don't want to work with"), it was a great deal: work on whatever you want with whoever you want, get paid, and get dinner once a week.
- Hundreds of applications came in, more than expected. The first batch included Sam Altman (Loopt), Reddit, Kiko (founders went on to Justin.tv/Twitch) and Aaron Swartz (Infogami, which merged with Reddit).
- The three-month length exists because that was summer vacation. Weekly dinners were modeled on the Society of Fellows at Harvard. Demo Day was only decided about halfway through the first batch.
- Paul's summary: "a bunch of accidents that turned out to be good." Three months "turned out to be just about right."
- After Foo Camp he concluded someone would start the YC of Silicon Valley "and it better be us," so they moved the next batch across the country. They ended up in Mountain View because a friend, Trevor, had a building. The application form said the location (Cambridge or Silicon Valley) was undecided.

chunks.heading: Deal terms and why YC is not an old-style incubator
chunks.text:
- The deal was modeled on Paul's own startup (Viaweb). A lawyer, the husband of his painting teacher, gave them $10,000, incorporated them and sat on the board. He "saved us from stepping in a bunch of dog poops" (landmines). Paul first thought it was a great deal for the lawyer (10% for $10k), then realized it was a great deal for the founders too.
- YC thought 10% was too much, so it asked for 6%, which later became 7%.
- The cash amount came from asking an MIT professor what MIT grad students got for the summer: $2,000 a month. So YC gave $6,000 per founder, because you could live on that in Cambridge.
- The 1990s incubators were the model of "what not to do." They took 30-40% (or more), had you work out of their building, and ran your accounting, so you were "almost like a subsidiary" and "very much like an employee."
- Paul had been a founder and asked himself whether he would have taken that deal. He saw it as an adverse selection filter: the best founders would refuse.
- YC was meant to be "first gear," after which founders raise money at market rates from whoever they like. He notes the word "incubator" now effectively means YC.

chunks.heading: Spotting good founding teams
chunks.text:
- Paul says the patterns visible across 632 startups are "astonishing." The big one: founders must get along. "You don't know how good friends you are with somebody until you try to start a startup with them." Founder conflict shows up in a class often, and Apple had three founders, not two.
- Interview tells that a team is dysfunctional:
  - One founder looks in terror at the other before answering.
  - A founder rolls their eyes while the co-founder speaks.
  - A founder doesn't show up and the other says "I don't know, he was supposed to be here." (All of these have happened.)
- He is skeptical of the business-school founder who has an idea and recruits a meek 20-year-old CS major to build it. That is a poor founding team.
- Working model for strong teams: each founder is king of their own domain. Wozniak built the Apple I and Jobs sold it; Jobs didn't change what Woz built. Each is master of their own domain and they don't step on each other's toes.
- On solo founders: YC prefers more than one founder. Drew Houston applied to YC as a solo founder; YC told him to get a co-founder, and he did before the interview (about two weeks). Paul's reaction to someone pitching an idea: "who's your co-founder? That's what I care about."
- MBAs are not automatically penalized. Rescale's CEO has an MBA but also deep domain expertise in the aircraft industry.
- A signal he has changed his mind on: people who are very smart but ineffectual. "We used to have more faith in brains." Now: "you can be surprisingly stupid if you're sufficiently determined." Being "fearsomely effective" matters more than raw smarts.

chunks.heading: Interviews, decisions and the "unpredictable" winners
chunks.text:
- YC does about 20 ten-minute interviews a day and must decide right after each one, while memory is fresh. After years the partners can signal "this person is in" with their eyes. There are a few borderline cases, and many clear yes or clear no cases.
- Dropbox, Airbnb and Stripe were all no-brainers: "we didn't even need the full 10 minutes."
- Paul does not claim he predicted they'd be worth billions: "you cannot predict that, that is unpredictable." Drew Houston's application answered the old question "how much would you take if someone wanted to buy you after YC?" with far less than $10 billion, so YC dropped the question as predicting nothing.
- Many billion-dollar companies get there partly because acquirers' M&A people are not smart enough to pick them off early.
- Valuation is not value: if a company hasn't raised for a year or two and grows about 5x a year, its last valuation is off by something like 25x after two years. He called Dropbox (about $10 billion at the time) and Airbnb peers by value, and said Stripe is in that group too.
- A rejection lesson: one company (applied to YC, later successful elsewhere) was read by only one partner, Robert Morris, who gave a harsh grade and the comment "Spam company." YC now has a second person review any application Robert grades badly, and about 10 people read applications.
- Companies who come to YC already launched are not predictably better or worse: Airbnb had been live a year but flatlined before YC.

chunks.heading: Scaling YC: the N-squared mistake
chunks.text:
- The summer 2012 batch (80-something startups) felt too big. The cause: until then every partner had to know what every startup was doing, and office hours were assigned FIFO to whoever was in the queue longest.
- Paul's diagnosis: "an N squared algorithm" and "we're all computer science people and we made this mistake." Some startups were halfway through the batch before he knew what they did.
- Fix: shard it. YC now has three silos, each overseen by a group of Partners, "basically three little Y combinators." With sharding, 68 startups per batch is "no problem."
- On the $150K-style uncapped note given to every startup: it caused fights over money when founders split, since "$150,000 is a lot of money" and a departing founder would demand "my $75,000" (it was the company's money). He considered eliminating the notes but polled startups; about 80% said the money helped significantly, so YC kept a smaller version.
- Org changes: Sam Altman takes over as president because YC has to grow and Paul is "no good at running giant things." Paul will do office hours a couple of days a week, which is about a tenth of what he used to do. The rest was internal overhead. He would stop reading applications and doing interviews, and expected to get his brain back after being unable to stop thinking about YC "in the shower in the morning."

chunks.heading: Advice on focus and fundraising
chunks.text:
- "The most important thing for startups to do is to focus." Of the thousand things you could do, one is the most important. It works like optimizing software: find the current bottleneck and work on that.
- Founders usually know the answer but don't ask themselves. At office hours YC asks "which one is the most important?" and then "so why aren't you doing that?"
- Fundraising: shift into fundraising mode, raise, and stop. Do not "promiscuously meet with investors in the middle of the day" just because they email "let's grab coffee."
- Funding climate (2014): valuations are high, but that isn't a bubble. A bubble means people believe they can sell the overpriced thing to a greater fool later, and that needs a public-market bubble, which he didn't see. Prices move like a sine wave, so high prices will likely come down somewhat.
- Valuation advice is not a blanket rule. For some startups, if anyone offers money you should take it on any terms.
- Being YC-funded does not automatically get you customers, unless you sell to startups. A consumer product still has to earn its users.

chunks.heading: How to grow: the small intense fire
chunks.text:
- Start with "a small intense fire." You can't make something a large number of people want a lot, so find a small number who want it a lot. That is how Apple and Facebook started.
- Example: the Apple I, about 500 units. Find those first users, know how you'll get them, then "just sit down and have a party with those first few users" and make them super happy.
- A mobile app might need 5,000 rather than 500, but the principle holds.
- Example from the current batch: a team building a mobile email client whose beta group is one user, Sam Altman. His demands make him a good mold; if they satisfy him they can satisfy many.
- Tactic for extreme cases: act like a consultant hired by that one user (it could even say his name at the top of the screen).
- The test of product-market fit: the user "would be bummed if you stopped working on this." Friends saying "oh yeah it's good, I'll use it" is not the test.
- On Google Wave as a launch lesson: it was launched "like New Coke" as a thing that would change everything, doing so much it seemed to do nothing. Paul says it should have launched as an apparently inconsequential real-time typing tool and let users see how much bigger it could be. YC funded EtherPad (real-time collaborative writing) four times and thinks the idea will happen.
- Starting a startup is painful. "There's a conservation law there": don't expect it to be easy and also a great way to get money. He says if it isn't a certain amount of painful, "you're probably not trying hard enough."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Podcast hosts discuss Paul Graham using clips of him speaking. He argues good ideas come from side projects rather than brainstorming, that expertise in users beats startup mechanics, that founders matter more than ideas, and that doing things manually and iterating quickly with users beats polish.

chunks.heading: Don't try to think of startup ideas; build a brain that produces them
chunks.text:
- Paul argues that consciously trying to come up with startup ideas yields ideas that are "not only bad but bad and plausible sounding," so you and everyone else get fooled and waste a lot of time before seeing they are no good.
- His alternative is to take a step back and turn your brain into the kind that has startup ideas unconsciously, so unconsciously that you don't realize at first that they are startup ideas.
- Yahoo, Google, Facebook and Apple all started this way. None were supposed to be companies at first; they were side projects.
- The very best ideas almost have to start as side projects, because they are such outliers that your conscious mind would reject them as ideas for companies.
- Three ways to get a brain that produces ideas:
  1. Learn a lot about things that matter.
  2. Work on problems that interest you.
  3. Work with people you like and respect. This is also how you get co-founders, at the same time as the idea.

chunks.heading: Expertise in your users matters more than expertise in startups
chunks.text:
- Paul says what you need to succeed is not expertise in startups but expertise in your own users.
- Mark Zuckerberg succeeded despite being "a complete noob at startups." Facebook was first incorporated as a Florida LLC. He won because he understood his users very well.
- Paul worries that learning the mechanics of starting a startup is not merely unnecessary but possibly somewhat dangerous.
- The characteristic young-founder mistake is going through the motions of a startup:
  - Come up with a plausible-sounding idea.
  - Raise funding at a nice valuation.
  - Rent a nice office in SoMa.
  - Hire a bunch of friends.
- While imitating all the outward forms, such founders neglect the one essential thing: "make something people want."

chunks.heading: What a startup actually does: make people's lives better
chunks.text:
- Paul says a successful startup, whether it ends in an IPO or just a great business, has to "make something that actually makes people's lives better."
- He thinks it is "funny how straightforward it is." People assume business needs trickery, like cornering a market, but you just have to improve people's lives.
- His model of value is a rectangle. One side is the number of people, the other is how much better you make each person's life. "Big rectangle big value you're rich it's really that simple."

chunks.heading: Co-founders: friends who know each other's capacities
chunks.text:
- The YC team looks for founders who have been friends for a while and have worked on things together, so they know one another's capacities.
- It dislikes teams that came together only for the purpose of doing the startup. In that case the startup is the only thing holding them together.
- Almost every startup hits a point where it seems doomed and worthless. If nothing but the startup binds the founders, they quit and go do other things.
- Friends keep working on it so as not to let the other down. It turns out they were wrong that it was worthless. Paul's summary: continuing out of "misplaced loyalty to your pal" is oddly a good thing.

chunks.heading: Fund the founders more than the idea
chunks.text:
- YC has learned that, at the stage it funds, the founder is much more important than the idea.
- Its application form used to ask many questions about the idea. It now asks far fewer about the idea and many more about the founders and the relationship between them.

chunks.heading: Early on, do things by hand and get customers
chunks.text:
- Paul says doing things very manually for early customers is so important that "if you have to do a ton of manual stuff that's okay you'll learn a lot from it."
- He and his co-founders did this themselves and thought they were doing it wrong ("this is so lame"). It was exactly the right thing.
- Their company made an online store builder:
  - They asked prospective customers if they wanted to use the easy online store builder, and the answer was no.
  - They asked "you want an online store right?" and the answer was yes.
  - They then offered to use their own software to build the store for the customer, and the customer said all right.
- Paul's takeaway: they could not get anyone to use the software, but people would let them use it for them.
- He says many of the things YC teaches startups are things he did himself without realizing they were common lessons.

chunks.heading: What kills startups, and the iteration loop
chunks.text:
- Paul's answer to what kills startups: they make something users don't like. "They make dog food the dogs do not like to eat. That is the killer of all startups."
- The first version does not have to be good, as long as you get it out very quickly.
- Putting it out starts a conversation with users, who say things like "I sort of like this but I wish you would do such-and-such."
- You do such-and-such and repeat that process roughly 200 times, "and then you have something really good."

chunks.heading: Counterintuitive advice founders ignore
chunks.text:
- Paul says what Y Combinator does is tell founders things they ignore. The advice is counterintuitive, not obvious.
- His example is "don't hire too fast." Founders hire too fast anyway, then come back later and say they wish they had listened.
- Counterintuitive advice "sounds wrong," so founders go with their gut and do the wrong thing, and hopefully catch the mistake in time.

chunks.heading: A startup takes over your life, so weigh the timing
chunks.text:
- Paul warns that a startup will take over your life "to a degree that you cannot imagine." If it succeeds, it does so for several years at the very least, maybe a decade, maybe the rest of your working life, so there is a real opportunity cost.
- Larry Page is his example. He started running as fast as he could at 25 and has not stopped to catch his breath since.
  - Every day something happens within Google that only the emperor can deal with.
  - A week of vacation creates a backlog.
  - As the company's "daddy" he can never show fear or weakness, and a billionaire gets zero sympathy for complaining.
- The difficulty of founding a successful startup is concealed from almost everyone who has done it, like Olympic 100-meter winners who make it look easy.
- Paul frames the real problem as "how to have a good life." A startup can be a component of that, but the early 20s are not necessarily the optimal time. Two things work better then than before or after: plunging deeply into projects on a whim with no obvious payoff, and traveling super cheaply with no deadline.
- For ambitious people this is "a really valuable sort of exploration." If you start a startup at 20 and succeed, you never get to do it. He says Zuckerberg will never get to bum around a foreign country, because success has "taken a lot of the serendipity out of his life."
- Serendipity also gives you more options to choose your life's work from.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: At a Revenue Boot Camp fireside chat with Mike Moritz and Guy Kawasaki, Paul Graham explains what YC looks for in early founders. He stresses people who build because they love it, candor with smart investors, and building something people want over spreadsheet forecasts.

chunks.heading: Who Y Combinator funds and how it works
chunks.text:
- YC invests in 25-30 startups at a time, twice a year, "in batch mode". Each batch works intensively for three months.
- The batch ends with demo day, where each startup gets about five minutes to present to investors. The hope is that they then raise the next round.
- Paul says the main useful thing YC does is "try and figure out what to build first". He also arbitrates conflicts between founders, which he wishes he didn't have to do.
- Everyone has dinner together once a week for the first three months. Paul used to cook it himself until about a year earlier.
- YC stays in touch after the 90 days. Only the weekly dinners stop.
- Paul focuses on the problems of the very beginning (for example, a founding team shrinking from three to two). He says he knows nothing about IPOs.

chunks.heading: What Paul looks for in founders
chunks.text:
- Paul wants founders who are "determined, smart, have a sense of design, and get things done".
- The "proven" he cares about is evidence that someone likes to build things, not a track record as a proven entrepreneur.
- The key question is "what have you made outside of school or work because you liked it?" To be really good at something you have to like it, not do it out of duty. Paul says someone who really likes programming rarely reaches 23 without building something on their own.
- Ideal founders build something they want to use themselves. The next best is something a person very close to them, such as a spouse or sibling, wants. That gives a deep sense of what is essential in the product, which "you can't intellectualize".
- He doesn't treat a founder couple as a plus or minus. What matters is that both would have been in the startup even if they weren't married. He warns against dragging in a spouse only because they're a spouse.

chunks.heading: Why most YC founders are young
chunks.text:
- The average founder YC funds is about 25 or 26.
- Paul's explanation is not that youth is better. More people start startups at that age. By their 30s, people have families and mortgages, and the friends they'd start with are tied down too.
- 25-year-olds can say "what the hell, we'll try it".
- Paul says YC has funded some older founders. His answer to "should I recruit a 25-year-old" was not to do that. Mike answered that older founders should email him or Paul directly.

chunks.heading: Revenue forecasts and pitching
chunks.text:
- YC has a "don't ask, don't tell" policy on revenue forecasts. Paul says "we don't even ask".
- A founder who doesn't know how to make money can say so. Paul's example: "we have no idea how to make money, we're worried about that, we know that's a problem, talk to us, let's figure out how to make money".
- Paul's BS detectors are generic language and buzzwords. He says never use the word "passion"; just seem like you care.
- On competitive analysis, the grid where the founder's column is all checked and the competitors' columns are empty is a bad sign. His advice is to be candid, and the smarter the investor, the more candid you should be.
- Tell investors what you'd say among yourselves, for example "we're worried about such-and-such company because of X, but we think we have an edge because of Y". Paul compares it to a doctor: "don't lie about your symptoms".
- A smart investor will notice if you lie.

chunks.heading: Early-stage expectations on product
chunks.text:
- With tools like MySQL, Drupal and Rails, Paul expects a founder to show up with some kind of demo.
- Between the interview invitation and the interview, YC gives about three weeks, enough to book a cheap plane ticket. In that time they should be able to throw together something so the conversation isn't only talk. A working demo is "a good sign if they do".
- The exception is something that takes a long time to build, such as a hardware device.

chunks.heading: When to give up
chunks.text:
- Paul says that as long as the founders haven't given up, they can morph the company into anything. In the early phase, a couple of people eating beans and writing code can turn it around tomorrow if they want.
- When founders ask him "can I give up now?", he says "probably the answer is yes". If they're asking, they've usually already decided and want him to be okay with it.
- If they say "we're a year in, our software still sucks, we have no customers, but we're not giving up", his answer is "keep going, I'll help you". He helps as long as they keep fighting.
- Founders often call an urgent meeting, with "need to get together" in the email, to deliver bad news: a missed quarter, or running out of money sooner than expected. Paul says he has never heard anyone say "I really need to come see you to tell you how great everything's going".
- He notes that bad news tends to arrive suddenly and good news gradually, as with plane crashes versus slowly improving air safety.

chunks.heading: Boards and predicting the next platform
chunks.text:
- Paul has never been on a board and says he never will. YC doesn't take board seats.
- He says he can give any advice a board member could without the formal standing. If it's good, "they'll listen, one hopes".
- Nobody can predict the next big wave. If you could, you'd be funding those companies. Paul's practical heuristic is to look at which platforms hackers themselves use, because they build for the platforms they use.
- His example: many startups were building for the iPhone because their founders all had iPhones. None were building for the BlackBerry, which had market share but not among startup founders.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Paul Graham reminisces with Jessica Livingston and Carolyn Levy about how Y Combinator grew with no deliberate marketing: alumni told their friends. He also explains how he coached demo day pitches, expanded founders' ideas, and why founder needs remain the best source of startup ideas even with AI.

chunks.heading: How YC grew and why it spread
chunks.text:
- Paul says YC never made a conscious marketing effort to get applicants. It set an application deadline, announced it, ran Startup School every year, and applications grew each cycle.
- His essays carried a link: "Interested in starting a startup? Apply to Y Combinator." He thinks that probably brought in some applicants.
- Hacker News began around 2007, so it was not a factor in the first couple of years.
- He thinks the main driver was word of mouth from founders. "I think we actually helped the startups a lot. And so they would tell one another."
- His analogy: friends tell you to go to a restaurant when the food is good. Alumni told friends that YC helped them get investment, incorporate, and more.
- He calls this "a recipe for exponential growth": each new founder becomes another person telling others it helped.
- Young programmers know each other from school and hang out together, so "if you please that group, word spreads quickly."
- Alumni also helped by dropping by dinners, introducing new startups to their investors, and sometimes becoming customers.

chunks.heading: Press only matters if your audience reads it
chunks.text:
- The New York Times article ("a hatchery for startups") described YC as a new phenomenon in the investment world. Paul called it a useful historical article.
- His rule: for YC, the only publicity that counts is whether potential applicants know about you, meaning 22-year-old programmers.
- If those people don't read the outlet, "it might seem to you you've gotten a lot of publicity, but actually it didn't really help much."
- Parents also mattered. In 2005 parents would freak out that their kids were leaving school with no job, so it looked like unemployment rather than founding.
- Once YC had a brand, founders could say, "Look, Mom, I'm not just working on my loser startup. I got into YC."
- YC needed a consumer-style brand, because it takes open applications from people just out of college and is not "just doing series A's". Paul says this visibility also made YC a target for press and online mobs.

chunks.heading: Real advice he gave startups
chunks.text:
- **Airbnb:** he told them to focus on New York, one initial market, "cuz you need to get this ball rolling." He says it made all the difference, and that they were effectively dead when they arrived, though YC didn't know it.
- This is the dream case. Usually "you would tell people something and they would ignore you. And then they would fail."
- **Time spent:** YC spends most of its time on knotty problems from companies that never amount to much. Airbnb was one of about 25 startups in its batch and got about 1/25 of the time. Trouble caused is inversely proportional to eventual size.
- **Expanding ideas:** in roughly a third of his office hours he and the founders figured out how to make the idea much bigger. He still does this, often early in a batch, when there is room to expand.
- **Naming:** he helps startups find names, often at instant domain search on the kitchen island. He cites Imgix and Phind as names he is proud of.
- **Advocacy:** the partners sometimes had to talk to a startup's investors, like parents of kids in a fight, when someone was mistreating a startup.

chunks.heading: Demo Day: the "vertebrae" method
chunks.text:
- Investors see 50 startups, now closer to 300, so their brains are wiped clean by the end. At best they remember about five sentences.
- So decide the five sentences in advance. These are the "vertebrae" of the pitch, and "the rest is just filler."
- The five sentences should each do a job. His example chain: it's a giant market; we already solve the problem better than anyone; it's ours to lose; at scale there are network effects, so it's winner takes all.
- "Demo day presentation shouldn't be like fast-talking marketing speak. They should be almost like logical proofs of why this company is good to invest in." If the investor agrees with each step, the expected value comes out high.
- Process: he did vertebrae office hours, founders built slides saying exactly that, then practiced at YC while he sat in the audience "like a playwright" cutting lines and changing words.
- Pacing: YC was always trying to get people to talk slower.
- At Demo Day he watched from the audience taking notes, hoping each founder would land specific lines he already knew were coming.

chunks.heading: Inflection point office hours and "palliative care mode"
chunks.text:
- Inflection point office hours were for startups in terrible shape. Several partners met with the founders to work out how to save the company.
- This was for startups whose founders still looked promising.
- If the startup seemed doomed and the founders would be better off with jobs, the partners went into "palliative care mode": just be really nice, so they were cheerful as it died. No tough love.
- Tough love was reserved for cases where it might work.
- Paul says he worked harder than anyone at trying to save failing startups, and his attitude was "This time will be different."
- On feedback, he says YC treated food complaints as a good sign: if the only complaint is the Tuesday food, "we're doing it right." Carolyn adds the post-batch survey was how they checked.

chunks.heading: Choosing and handing over the YC president
chunks.text:
- Paul knew Sam Altman from the first batch. He says it was instant: "this must be what Bill Gates was like when he was 19." Sam was the class president type, raised serious money, and got Sequoia to invest.
- Paul's reasoning for picking him: Sam gets whatever he wants, so "if the only way he can succeed is by making Y Combinator succeed then Y Combinator cannot fail."
- His mistake: he should have said Sam could only do YC and nothing else. His view is that Sam would have accepted at that stage.
- On OpenAI, Paul says YC would have been "psyched" if Sam had picked someone else for AI and focused on YC. "All we wanted was him to pick." He denies that YC fired Sam.
- Succession: the partners told Sam he couldn't do both and agreed to find a successor. They chose Jeff, an established YC partner, who served 3 years.
- Garry then took over. Paul likes that Garry had done YC himself, so he knows what founders feel when raising, chasing growth, or facing Demo Day. LPs also trusted him from his results at Initialized.
- Paul says it is good for the president to have gone through YC. He says YC is now the best he has felt about it in about 10 years, with no nagging worry.

chunks.heading: Hacker News and the cost of side projects
chunks.text:
- Paul says Hacker News was a huge stress, "more than half of the total stress of running YC." Servers ran out of file space, there were denial-of-service attacks, and users fought on the site.
- He says that in retrospect it was like running a startup alongside YC, and "maybe that was a mistake."
- He wrote every bit of YC's software and every word on the website. The one exception was the up and down arrow JavaScript on Hacker News, which PB wrote.
- The Peter Thiel episode: part-time partners were unpaid experts who did office hours. YC was facing pressure to remove Thiel for being openly Republican.
- Sam had planned to drop him anyway because he had done few office hours. Paul told Sam not to set a precedent of firing someone for supporting the wrong political party, so YC kept him.
- Paul says doing the job was less stressful than being attacked for it. He says outsiders knew only YC, so problems were blamed on Silicon Valley and then on him.

chunks.heading: Paul's view of startups in the AI era
chunks.text:
- AI progress surprised him. He did not expect this in his lifetime, and he notes how quickly people adjusted.
- So far AI's main effect is as a source of startup ideas and as leverage to displace incumbents. He says starting a startup is not structurally different yet.
- He sees a possible risk that model companies copy startups, like the Samwer brothers did, joking about "the Sams instead of the Samwers."
- His encouraging point: the best source of startup ideas is your own needs (Facebook, Google, Airbnb). "AIs don't have any needs," so they may not replace human founders.
- Other surprises: founders keep getting younger (17 or 18 and skipping college), and Demo Day valuations are "like $60 million now." He has heard of multiple startups raising at a $60M cap, about 20 times Airbnb's post-money valuation.
- He opposes skipping college, wants founders to go back, and is thinking of writing an essay "Go to College."
- B2B is where he sees age as a handicap: 18-year-olds will struggle to convince a CIO to buy seat licenses. They could work on the idea meanwhile and start later.
- On "it'll be too late if I don't start now," he asks whether people were right about that 2 years ago.
- His energy for office hours comes from interest, not benevolence: founders bring a "constant stream of new puzzles."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Startups take off because founders push them, usually through unscalable work: recruiting users one at a time, over-delivering on experience, and starting in a narrow market. Big launches and partnerships rarely work. The unscalable effort also shapes company culture for the better.

chunks.heading: Startups take off because founders push them, so recruit users manually
chunks.text:
- Paul rejects the belief that startups either take off on their own or the market must not exist. He says "startups take off because the founders make them take off."
- His metaphor is the hand crank on pre-electric-starter car engines. Once the engine runs it keeps going, but getting it going is a separate, laborious process.
- The most common unscalable task is recruiting users one at a time. "You can't wait for users to come to you. You have to go out and get them."
- Even Stripe, whose problem was urgent, was famous within YC for aggressive early user acquisition. YC calls the technique the "Collison installation": when someone agreed to try Stripe, the Collisons said "Right then, give me your laptop" and set them up on the spot. Diffident founders instead say "we'll send you a link."
- Airbnb's early version was going door to door in New York, recruiting users and helping existing hosts improve their listings. About 30 days of in-person engagement made the difference between success and failure. Paul says marketplaces are so hard to start that you should expect "heroic measures."
- Reasons founders resist:
  - Shyness and laziness. At least one founder (usually the CEO) must spend a lot of time on sales and marketing. You can't avoid sales by hiring someone to do it. Do it yourself first, then hire a real salesperson to replace you.
  - The absolute numbers look too small. He says this underestimates compound growth.
- Manual recruiting usually works if the market exists. Start manual, then gradually switch to less manual methods.

chunks.heading: Measure weekly growth and expect compounding
chunks.text:
- Paul encourages every startup to measure progress by weekly growth rate.
- Example: with 100 users, you need 10 more next week to grow 10% a week. 110 doesn't look much better than 100, but at 10% a week you reach 14,000 users after a year and 2 million after 2 years.
- Growth must slow eventually, and you'll do different things when acquiring users a thousand at a time.
- Size starts to help growth. He quotes Patrick Collison: "At some point, there was a very noticeable change in how Stripe felt. It tipped from being this boulder we had to push to being a train car that in fact had its own momentum."

chunks.heading: Early startups are fragile; ask how big they could get
chunks.text:
- Almost all startups are fragile at first. Inexperienced founders, investors, reporters and forum commenters judge "larval" startups by the standards of established ones, like looking at a newborn and concluding it can't accomplish anything.
- Outsiders dismissing you is harmless. Investors will change their minds when they see growth. The real danger is the founders dismissing their own startup. Paul says even Bill Gates returned to Harvard for the fall semester after starting Microsoft, which he wouldn't have done if he'd seen how big it would get.
- The right question is not "is this company taking over the world?" but "how big could this company get if the founders did the right things?" The right things often seem "both laborious and inconsequential at the time."
- Examples: Microsoft was a couple of people in Albuquerque writing Basic interpreters for a few thousand hobbyists. Airbnb's founders were taking "professional" photos of their first hosts' apartments.
- Finding users to recruit:
  - If you build for your own problems, you only need to find your peers.
  - Otherwise, do a comparatively untargeted launch, see which users are most enthusiastic, and seek out more like them. Ben Silbermann saw that many early Pinterest users were into design, so he went to a conference of design bloggers to recruit users, and it worked well.
  - For things like enterprise software with no connections, you'd rely on cold calls and introductions. He asks whether you should be working on such an idea at all.

chunks.heading: Delight users and make the experience insanely great
chunks.text:
- Take extraordinary measures to make early users happy, not just to acquire them. Wufoo sent each new user a hand-written thank-you note for as long as it could, which was surprisingly long. Early users should feel signing up was one of their best choices.
- Why founders resist:
  - Engineers aren't trained in customer service.
  - They worry it won't scale. Paul says a larval startup has nothing to lose, and having too many users to delight would be a great problem. Delight scales better than expected, partly because it will have permeated the culture.
  - They've never experienced such attention, because their standards come from big companies. "Tim Cook doesn't send you a hand-written note after you buy a laptop. He can't. But you can."
- "I have never once seen a startup lured down a blind alley by trying too hard to make their initial users happy."
- Garry Tan's trap: founders imitate big companies' flaws, like indifference to individual users, to seem "professional." Paul says to embrace being small and use its advantages.
- He borrows Steve Jobs's "insanely great." In a larval startup it isn't the product that should be insanely great but "the experience of being your user." The product is one component. You can give an insanely great experience with an early, incomplete, buggy product if you make up the difference with attentiveness.
- Over-engaging with early users is a necessary part of the feedback loop that makes the product good.
  - The first thing you build is never quite right.
  - Except where mistakes carry big penalties, don't aim for perfection. In software, get something in front of users once it has "a quantum of utility," then see what they do.
  - "Perfectionism is often an excuse for procrastination," and your initial model of users is always inaccurate, even if you're one of them.
- Direct feedback from your earliest users will be the best you ever get. Later you'll wish you could watch users in their homes and offices instead of using focus groups.

chunks.heading: Start in a deliberately narrow market (the contained fire)
chunks.text:
- Paul compares it to keeping a fire contained at first to get it really hot before adding more logs.
- Facebook began only for Harvard students, a market of a few thousand people. Because they felt it was really for them, a critical mass signed up. It then stayed college-by-college for a long time. Zuckerberg told Paul that creating course lists for each school was a lot of work but made students feel the site was their natural home.
- Marketplaces usually must start in a subset of the market, but it works for other startups too. Always ask whether there's a subset where you can reach critical mass quickly.
- Most founders do this unconsciously by building for themselves and friends who are early adopters. The danger is discarding part of the pattern, for example if you come from the corporate world and your friends aren't early adopters.
- Best early adopters among companies are other startups. They're open to new things, haven't made all their choices yet, and grow fast when they succeed. This gives B2B startups an instant market among YC companies.
- If choosing between the segment that signs up quickest and the segment that pays most, usually pick the quickest. They're probably early adopters, influence the product better, need less sales effort, and you don't need much money early on to hit your target growth rate.

chunks.heading: Consult, use your own software, and do things manually
chunks.text:
- Consult for one user (for B2B). Pick a single user and act like a consultant building just for them. "The initial user serves as the form for your mold." Tweak until it fits their needs, and you'll usually find others want it too. One user who really needs something and can act on it is a toehold.
- Don't be paid for it. It's safe while you're a product company being extra attentive. Once they pay by the hour, "they expect you to do everything." He doesn't worry about building something useful to only one user, since those cases are usually obvious.
- Use your software on users' behalf. At Viaweb, some merchants who declined the software let them build a store for them, so they did, selling luggage, pens and men's shirts. It taught them how merchants would feel using the software. Sometimes feedback was near instant: mid-build Paul would find a missing feature, spend a couple of hours implementing it, then resume building the site.
- Be the software. With few users, do by hand what you plan to automate later. You launch faster and know exactly what to build because of the muscle memory. Stripe delivered "instant" merchant accounts by manually signing users up for traditional merchant accounts behind the scenes.
- Some startups could be entirely manual at first: solve a real problem by hand, then gradually automate the bottlenecks. Paul says this is less frightening than "having something automatic that doesn't yet solve anyone's problems."

chunks.heading: Hardware: pull a Meraki
chunks.text:
- Hardware startups face a catch-22. Minimum factory runs usually cost several hundred thousand dollars, and without a product you can't generate the growth needed to raise the money to make it.
- "Pulling a Meraki" means assembling the product yourselves. Meraki's founders, Robert Morris's grad students, assembled their routers themselves. Paul didn't fund them.
- Pebble assembled the first several hundred watches itself. Paul says without that phase they probably wouldn't have sold $10 million worth of watches when they went on Kickstarter. Crowdfunding (more precisely, preorders) has helped, but he still advises pulling a Meraki if you can.
- Being the factory lets you tweak the design faster and learn things you'd never otherwise know. Eric Migicovsky of Pebble learned "how valuable it was to source good screws."

chunks.heading: Big launches and partnerships usually don't work; think of ideas as vectors
chunks.text:
- Big Launch: founders who think startups are projectiles that need high initial velocity, such as launching in 8 publications with embargoes on a Tuesday. Paul says that all you need from a launch is an initial core of users. "How well you're doing a few months later will depend more on how happy you made those users than how many there were of them." Ask how many launches of successful startups you remember.
- He suspects an inverse correlation between launch magnitude and success. He remembers only flops like the Segway and Google Wave, and thinks Wave was a great idea partly killed by its overdone launch.
- Founders believe in launches out of solipsism and laziness. Getting users is always gradual, because great things are novel and users have other things on their minds.
- Partnerships usually don't work, especially for starting growth. Inexperienced founders think a big-company partnership will be their big break. Six months later they say it was far more work than expected and got them practically nothing. Google grew on the back of Yahoo, but Yahoo was its customer, not a partner.
- "It's not enough just to do something extraordinary initially. You have to make an extraordinary effort initially." Any strategy that omits the effort is "ipso facto suspect."
- Think of a startup idea as a vector: what you'll build, plus the unscalable things you'll do initially to get going. Usually the second part is recruiting users manually and giving them an overwhelmingly good experience.
- An idea with an empty second component, such as no way to find users to recruit manually, is probably a bad idea for those founders.
- Best case, the unscalable work becomes company DNA. Aggressive user acquisition when small tends to continue when big, and so does working hard to delight users.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Paul Graham argues a startup is a company designed to grow fast, and everything else (funding, acquisitions, technology) follows from growth. Founders should know their weekly growth rate, pick a target, and use it to make every decision, letting growth pressure evolve the idea.

chunks.heading: A startup is a company designed to grow fast
chunks.text:
- Paul defines a startup as "a company designed to grow fast." Growth is the only essential trait. Technology, venture funding and an "exit" are not required, and being newly founded does not make a company a startup.
- Most new companies are service businesses such as restaurants, barbershops and plumbers. They are not startups. A search engine is designed to grow fast, and a barbershop is not.
- "Designed" means two things: intended, since most startups fail, and different by nature. He compares a redwood seedling with a bean sprout. Google was different from the beginning and was not "a barbershop whose founders were unusually lucky and hard-working."
- Growth works as a compass. If a founder knows growth is the goal, "you can use growth like a compass to make almost every decision you face." If you get growth, "everything else tends to fall into place."
- "Startup" is "a pole, not a threshold." Starting one is at first a declaration of ambition. It is like an actor who starts out as a waiter going to auditions.

chunks.heading: Two requirements for growing big: what people want and how to reach them
chunks.text:
- To grow really big, a company must (a) make something lots of people want and (b) reach and serve all of those people. Most businesses are tightly constrained on (a) or (b). Successful startups are not.
- A barbershop does fine on (a), since almost everyone needs a haircut. It fails on (b) because it serves customers in person and few will travel far.
- Software solves (b) but can still be limited on (a). Software to teach Tibetan to Hungarian speakers reaches most of its market, but the market is small. Software to teach English to Chinese speakers is "startup territory."
- Strictly, what matters is a big market: customers times what they pay. Having too few customers is dangerous even if each pays a lot. Individual customers' power over you can turn you into "a de facto consulting firm." Paul advises erring toward the broadest type of product for the market.
- He thinks most people should not try to start startups. It is fine to build a software company constrained on (a), the way a restaurant is constrained on (b).

chunks.heading: Why startup ideas are hard to find
chunks.text:
- The market is "(fairly) efficient." Big-market ideas draw ferocious competition because the prize is larger. Tibetan-for-Hungarians has little competition. English-for-Chinese has a lot.
- The constraints on an ordinary business protect it and define it. A bar in a neighborhood is "a sufficient idea for a small business." A search engine competes with the whole world. The biggest protection is not from competitors but from the difficulty of coming up with a new idea.
- Obvious ideas for large markets are already taken, so a startup usually has to work on something everyone else has overlooked.
- Paul says successful startups mostly don't start by consciously hunting for overlooked ideas. Founders are different enough that ideas few others see seem obvious to them. Later they may notice they are in a blind spot and deliberately stay there. Y Combinator helps founders step back and see what they found intuitively.
- Examples:
  - Wozniak wanted his own computer in 1975, an unusual problem then. He could build one, and chip advances made it affordable.
  - Page and Brin could tell existing search engines were not as good as they could be, and they knew how to improve them. As the web grew, their problem became everyone's.
  - In both cases the company was entrenched by the time the market was obvious to ordinary people.
- Technological change creates startup ideas in two ways. It changes solubility (Apple) or bigness (Google's web). Technology also makes formerly bad ideas good without anyone noticing, so being good at technology and facing problems it can solve is a strong combination.
- Startups create new ways of doing things, and Paul counts these as new technology in the broad sense. He corrects "How to Make Wealth": a startup is not only a small company taking on a hard technical problem.

chunks.heading: Measure growth rate, not absolute numbers
chunks.text:
- A successful startup's growth has three phases:
  1. A slow or no-growth period while it figures out what it's doing.
  2. Rapid growth once it knows how to make something lots of people want and how to reach them.
  3. Slowing as it becomes a big company, from internal limits and market limits.
- Together these form an S-curve. The ascent defines the startup, and its length and slope set how big the company gets.
- "If there's one number every founder should always know, it's the company's growth rate." Without it you don't know if you're doing well or badly.
- "We get about a hundred new customers a month" is not a rate. What matters is the ratio of new customers to existing ones. A constant number of new customers each month means the growth rate is falling.
- At YC, growth is measured per week. Time before Demo Day is short, and early startups need frequent user feedback.
- Benchmarks during YC:
  - 5-7% a week is good.
  - 10% a week is exceptional.
  - 1% a week suggests the founders haven't yet figured out what they're doing.
- Revenue is the best thing to measure. For startups not yet charging, active users is the next best, since revenue will probably be a constant multiple of active users.
- Caveats:
  - Companies building a Facebook or Twitter-style product with no clear way to make money need a higher growth rate, because they need huge numbers of users to succeed at all.
  - Watch for fast spread with high churn. Net growth looks good until the potential users run out, then it stops suddenly.
  - Weekly measurement suits startups that have launched or can launch during YC. A startup building a new database probably won't do it. Launching something small and using growth rate as evolutionary pressure is valuable enough that any company that can start this way probably should.

chunks.heading: Use a weekly growth target as a decision rule
chunks.text:
- YC advises startups to pick a growth rate they think they can hit and "just try to hit it every week." Hitting it means the week was a success. Missing it means failing at "the only thing that mattered," and founders should be alarmed.
- This turns starting a startup into an optimization problem, like optimizing code. It reduces a "bewilderingly multifarious problem" to one. Paul says programmers will find the narrow focus effective and surprisingly fast.
- Decisions get settled by the target: "anything that gets you the growth you need is ipso facto right." He lists these questions as examples:
  - Spend two days at a conference?
  - Hire another programmer?
  - Focus more on marketing?
  - Court a big customer?
  - Add feature x?
- Weekly measurement doesn't limit thinking to one week ahead. Missing a target makes founders want to avoid future misses. They might hire a programmer who won't help this week but will ship a feature in a month. He sets two conditions:
  - The distraction of hiring won't make them miss short-term numbers.
  - They are worried enough about whether they can keep hitting the numbers without the hire.
- "It's not that you don't think about the future, just that you think about it no more than necessary."
- Local maxima are a theoretical risk that "in practice never happens." Having to hit a number every week forces action, and "acting versus not acting is the high bit of succeeding." He says that nine times out of ten, sitting around strategizing is procrastination. Founders' intuitions about which hill to climb are usually better than they realize. Fairly good ideas are usually adjacent to better ones.
- Growth can discover the idea. If you modify your plan to keep hitting something like 10% weekly growth, you may end up with a quite different company, and "anything that grows consistently at 10% a week is almost certainly a better idea than you started with." Follow the growth constraint wherever it leads, as a scientist follows the truth.
- Paul warns against believing a successful startup is "the embodiment of some brilliant initial idea." Look for an idea that can evolve into a great one. Early adopters have different needs from the rest of the market. The idea that evolves into Facebook "is a site for Harvard undergrads," not a subset of Facebook.
- Don't cheat the metric. Within YC, "ipso facto right" excludes:
  - Buying users for more than their lifetime value.
  - Counting users as active when they're not.
  - Bleeding out invites at an increasing rate to manufacture a perfect growth curve.
  - Even if these fool investors, they throw off your own compass.

chunks.heading: Why small differences in growth rate matter
chunks.text:
- Weekly rate and yearly multiple:

| Weekly | Yearly |
| :-: | :-: |
| 1% | 1.7x |
| 2% | 2.8x |
| 5% | 12.6x |
| 7% | 33.7x |
| 10% | 142.0x |

- A company making $1000 a month (a typical number early in YC) and growing 1% a week makes $7900 a month four years later. That is less than a good programmer's Silicon Valley salary. At 5% a week it makes $25 million a month after four years.
- A company growing 1% a week for 19 years would match one growing 5% a week for 4 years. Paul says such slow trajectories may be common in real estate development but are rare in technology, where slow growers tend not to grow as big.
- Human intuition is poor at exponential growth, so fast growth surprises even founders.
- "Small variations in growth rate produce qualitatively different outcomes." This is why startups behave differently from ordinary companies, such as raising money and getting acquired, and why they fail so often.

chunks.heading: Expected value, failure rates and why investors and acquirers want startups
chunks.text:
- Expected value:
  - If a success could make a founder $100 million, a 1% chance of success gives an expected value of $1 million.
  - For the right people, such as the young Bill Gates, the odds might be 20% or even 50%.
  - In an efficient market, the number of failed startups should be proportionate to the size of the successes.
  - Most startups at any time are working on something that will go nowhere.
