- Paul says to judge startups by the average outcome, not the median. Judging by the median makes the concept look like a fraud and requires inventing a bubble to explain why founders and investors act as they do.
- Utility of money varies by person. Younger or more ambitious founders have a flatter utility function, which may be part of why the most successful founders tend to be young.
- Why VCs like startups:
  - The return-to-risk ratio is good.
  - VCs are paid by getting capital back through an IPO or acquisition. An investor taking dividends from ordinary private companies would have to scrutinize the books closely, because controllers can funnel revenue to themselves, for example by buying overpriced components from a supplier they control.
  - Startup investments are easy to oversee because "the founders can't enrich themselves without also enriching the investors." This holds for the biggest winners, where all the returns come from.
- Why founders take VC money:
  - If you have a scalable idea and grow too slowly, competitors will grow instead. This is especially dangerous with network effects.
  - Raising money is like buying insurance. The most successful startups raise even when they are or could be profitable, because "raising money lets you _choose_ your growth rate."
  - The best startups can get money on terms they'd be crazy to refuse, because VCs need them more than they need the VCs.
- Why acquirers want startups:
  - A fast-growing company is valuable, and also dangerous because it might expand into the acquirer's territory. Most product acquisitions "have some component of fear," so acquirers often pay more than ordinary investors.
  - His example: it was a good thing eBay bought PayPal, since PayPal is responsible for 43% of eBay's sales and probably more of its growth.
  - Instagram was bought by Mark Zuckerberg because it was valuable and dangerous, and growth made it both.
  - Acquisitions are either of the business or just of the employees. He calls the latter "HR acquisitions" and says acquirers see them as closer to hiring bonuses.

chunks.heading: Starting a startup means searching for a rare fast-growth idea
chunks.text:
- Growth explains the whole ecosystem. It is why startups usually work on technology, why starting one is a rational economic choice, why VCs invest, why top startups raise money they don't need, and why they get acquisition offers.
- Paul says understanding growth is what starting a startup "consists of." You are committing to solve a harder type of problem than ordinary businesses do: searching for one of the rare ideas that generates rapid growth. Because these ideas are so valuable, finding one is hard.
- The startup is "the embodiment of your discoveries so far."
- He compares founding to becoming a research scientist: you don't know which problems are soluble, but you commit to discovering something no one knew. A founder is "an economic research scientist. Most don't discover anything that remarkable, but some discover relativity."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Paul Graham argues you shouldn't try to think up startup ideas. Become someone at the leading edge of a fast-changing field and notice problems, ideally ones you have yourself. Good ideas are narrow, deep "wells" that a small group wants badly. Ignore the schlep and unsexy filters, and worry about users rather than competitors.

chunks.heading: Start with a problem you have, not an idea you invent
chunks.text:
- Paul's core claim: "The way to get startup ideas is not to try to think of startup ideas. It's to look for problems, preferably problems you have yourself."
- The best ideas share three traits: the founders want it themselves, they can build it themselves, and few others realize it is worth doing. He says Microsoft, Apple, Yahoo, Google and Facebook all began this way.
- Working on your own problem guarantees the problem exists. He calls solving problems no one has "by far the most common mistake startups make."
- His own example: in 1995 he started a company to put art galleries online. Galleries did not want to be online. He spent 6 months on it because he "didn't pay attention to users" and worked from an invented model of the world. He only noticed when he tried to get users to pay.
- Test he asks YC founders: "Would you use this thing yourself, if you hadn't written it?" The answer is often no.
- The need must be strong. Any made-up idea can be described after the fact as something you need. Compare it to how much Drew Houston needed Dropbox, or Brian Chesky and Joe Gebbia needed Airbnb.

chunks.heading: "Sitcom" ideas and why plausible ideas are dangerous
chunks.text:
- YC calls made-up ideas "sitcom" startup ideas. A TV writer has to invent a startup idea, and it sounds plausible but is bad.
- Example: a social network for pet owners. Friends with pets do not say "I would never use this." They say "Yeah, maybe I could see using something like that." Summed across a population, that reaction yields zero users.
- Trying to think up ideas is doubly dangerous: it yields few good ideas, and bad ones that sound plausible enough to fool you.
- Portal-for-x and social-network-for-x ideas are "stone soup": you post a sign saying "this is the place for people interested in x" and expect them to show up. The statistics on millions of interested people mislead, because one person may have 20 affinities and will not visit 20 communities regularly.
- Paul does not claim to know the pet idea is bad. He knows it the way he knows randomly generated DNA would not produce a viable organism. The set of plausible ideas is many times larger than the set of good ones, and many good ones do not sound plausible. If all you know is that it sounds plausible, assume it is bad.

chunks.heading: Build a well, not a broad shallow hole
chunks.text:
- At launch, some users must need the product urgently, not just "see themselves using it one day." That initial group is usually small, because anything many people urgently needed and a v1 could deliver would probably already exist.
- Choose between something a large number of people want a little and something a small number want a lot. Paul says choose the latter: "nearly all good startup ideas are of that type."
- Picture a graph with how many people want it on x and how much on y, with y inverted so companies are holes. Google is an immense crater. A new startup digs either a broad shallow hole or a narrow deep well.
- Examples of wells: Microsoft's Altair Basic (only a couple thousand Altair owners, who otherwise programmed in machine language) and the first Facebook (exclusive to Harvard students, a few thousand of them who wanted it a lot).
- Question to ask: who wants this right now, so much that they will use a crappy v1 from an unknown two-person startup? If you cannot answer, the idea is probably bad.
- Depth is what you need. Narrowness is a byproduct of optimizing for depth and speed.
- Activation energy matters. Enterprise software sold through traditional channels has very high activation energy, so you would need to be far better. Switching to a new search engine has low activation energy.
- A well is not sufficient. It needs a fast path out. Facebook worked because colleges are similar, so what works at Harvard works at any college, then you let everyone else in. Microsoft's path: Basic for Altair, Basic for other machines, other languages, operating systems, applications, IPO.
- Paths out are hard to see, even for experienced people. Airbnb's founders initially only planned to rent floor space during conventions.

chunks.heading: Live in the future and build what's missing
chunks.text:
- Paul says startup ideas should be "noticed," not "thought up." The recipe: "Live in the future, then build what's missing" (combining Paul Buchheit's "live in the future" with Pirsig).
- If you are the right sort of person at the leading edge of a fast-changing field, your hunches are more likely to be right. "The way to have good startup ideas is to become the sort of person who has them."
- You can be at the leading edge as a user, not only a builder. Mark Zuckerberg already lived online in 2004, when most 40-year-olds would have been horrified at publishing their lives semi-publicly.
- Organic ideas come from an external stimulus hitting a prepared mind: Gates and Allen hearing about the Altair, Drew Houston forgetting a USB stick. Many people had those stimuli; only the prepared acted.
- Apple, Yahoo, Google and Facebook were not even supposed to be companies at first. They grew from things founders built because there was a gap.
- Anyone reasonably smart can reach an edge of programming (e.g. building mobile apps) in about a year. A startup consumes at least 3-5 years, so a year of preparation is a reasonable investment.
- Programming is not necessary but is "for the foreseeable future sufficient." It lets you think "I'll try building an initial version tonight." It is best when you are also the target user, since the build-and-test cycle happens in one head.
- Give it time. Houston worked on an SAT prep startup before Dropbox, a much better idea and a better fit for his skills. Sam Altman's point: taking time to find an idea is like an undervalued stock, because few founders do it, while many compete over mediocre made-up ideas.
- Preparation gets harder with age, because the walls between career paths get higher.

chunks.heading: How to notice ideas: turn off the filters
chunks.text:
- Once living in the future, look for what seems missing. Turn off every other filter, especially "Could this be a big company?" Apply that test later.
- The most powerful filter is taking the status quo for granted. Question things: why is your inbox overflowing, because of volume or because it is hard to get email out? Is an inbox the optimal tool?
- Pay attention to things that chafe you. Annoyance can mean you are living in the future.
- A good problem should feel obvious to you. At Viaweb, online stores were hand-built HTML pages, and it was obvious to the programmer founders that they should be generated by software.
- Keep a background process running: work on hard problems out of curiosity while a second self notes gaps and anomalies. Possible journal: each night, list the raw gaps and anomalies you noticed, not startup ideas.
- Work on projects that seem cool. Things dismissed as "toys" often become important: microcomputers (then "hobbyists"), BackRub, the Facebook. YC is excited when startups look like something forum know-it-alls would dismiss as toys.
- Refined version: "Live in the future and build what seems interesting."
- Paul Buchheit's trick for bad ideas: tell founders to go sell the product ASAP before building it. They learn nobody wants it and "very often come back with a real idea that they discovered in the process."

chunks.heading: Schlep and unsexy filters
chunks.text:
- Most programmers want to write brilliant code, push it to a server and get paid, avoiding tedious real-world problems. This preference is so widespread that convenient ideas have been "stripped pretty clean." Messy, tedious ideas are "just sitting there."
- Stripe is his example of turning off the schlep filter. Thousands of programmers knew payments were painful but unconsciously shrank from them. Stripe's schlep was tolerable, and because others stayed away, users were "desperately waiting," so Stripe did not have to try hard to be heard in user acquisition.
- The unsexy filter blocks problems you despise rather than fear. He and his cofounders overcame it for Viaweb: they were not interested in ecommerce per se but saw it needed solving.
- The schlep filter matters more, because it is more likely an illusion and a worse form of self-indulgence. Any sufficiently good idea has as many schleps (investors, hiring, firing).
- The unsexy filter is partly useful: at the leading edge, what you find sexy correlates with what is valuable, and you work harder on ideas you like.
- Strategy: seek out ideas that are unsexy or involve schleps. "Don't try to start Twitter... Make something unsexy that people will pay you for."

chunks.heading: Competition and picking an idea when you need one now
chunks.text:
- A good idea feels obvious, so you feel late. Worrying you are late is a sign of a good idea. Ten minutes of web searching usually settles it. Startups are so rarely killed by competitors that you can almost discount it, unless a competitor has lock-in that stops users choosing you.
- Rule: focus on users, not competitors. If you have something no competitor does and some users urgently need it, you have a beachhead. A small beachhead is big enough if its people do something many more will do later (e.g. a product that only works on the newest phones).
- Err toward ideas with competitors. Inexperienced founders give them too much credit; success depends far more on you. "Better a good idea with competitors than a bad one without."
- A crowded market signals demand and that existing solutions are not good enough. You need a thesis about what incumbents overlook, more precise than "an x that doesn't suck." Best is that they lacked the courage of their convictions, as with search engines before Google, which shied away from the fact that the better they worked, the faster users would leave.
- Any success either enters an existing market with a secret weapon (Google) or a market that looks small but is big (Microsoft).
- Plan B recipes if you need an idea now (more discipline required, because you will see many bad ideas):
  - Stay in areas where you have expertise, since you can judge quality there.
  - Start with things you need. Ask: in a previous job, did you say "Why doesn't someone make x? If someone made x we'd buy it in a second"?
  - Look at what is unusual about you, especially if you are different in a way people will increasingly be. Being young (under 23, say) helps understand peers; Hotmail began as a tool for talking about the founders' previous startup idea.
  - Talk to many people about gaps, tedium and annoyances in their work, without forcing it.
  - For a blurry need that is not yours, act like a consultant retained to solve one user's problem. Nearly all the code will be reusable, and you start certain you have reached the bottom of the well.
  - Make others' problems your own: Rajat Suri of E la Carte took a job as a waiter before writing software for restaurants.
  - Ask what you wish someone else would build and what you would pay for right now.
  - Look at dying industries and imagine what will later be called a replacement. Replacements usually come in "from the side," starting with a small, important market the big players ignore, ideally with disdain. Example: HP turned down Wozniak's computer partly because it used a TV as a monitor, which was "intolerably déclassé."
  - Look for waves (e.g. falling gene sequencing and 3D printing costs). Looking for waves simulates the organic method: "you don't have to look for waves; you are the wave."
- Warning: when an idea you came up with deliberately feels like an inspired "just knew" idea, you are probably mistaken.

chunks.heading: Advice for students
chunks.text:
- Paul advises students to ratchet themselves into the future rather than learn "entrepreneurship," which you learn by doing. Classes only teach "the words for things."
- Clash of domains is fruitful. A programmer learning another field (e.g. genetics, or a summer job at a biotech company) will see software-solvable problems, since that domain's people are less likely to have solved them with software and the newcomer does not take the status quo for granted.
- Or just build things, preferably with other students. That produces organic ideas with organic founding teams, "empirically... the best combination." Do not worry about making them startups; "that's premature optimization."
- Microsoft and Facebook both started in January, which at Harvard is Reading Period with no classes. The best a college can do is "leave them alone in the right way."
- Beware of research. A project undergrads' friends all start using is likely a good idea; a PhD dissertation almost never is (for IT startups; biotech differs). Research is too narrow a constraint to also solve users' problems.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Paul Graham argues that any startup older than 8-9 months should know whether, at current expenses and growth, it reaches profitability on its remaining money. Not knowing leads to the fatal pinch. The main way to avoid being default dead is not to hire too fast, and to seek growth through product evolution and doing things that don't scale.

chunks.heading: "Default alive or default dead" as the first question for any startup older than 8-9 months
chunks.text:
- When Paul talks to a startup that has operated for more than 8 or 9 months, the first thing he wants to know is whether they make it to profitability on the money they have left. The assumptions are that expenses stay constant and revenue growth stays what it has been over the last several months.
- If yes, the startup is "default alive". If no, it is "default dead".
- The rest of the conversation depends on the answer. Default alive: talk about ambitious new things they could do. Default dead: talk about how to save it, since the current trajectory ends badly and they need to get off it.
- He says half the founders he talks to don't know which one they are. Trevor Blackwell built a calculator to find out (growth.tlb.org).
- Founders don't ask because the question is meaningless early on, "any more than it makes sense to ask a 3 year old how he plans to support himself." As the company ages it turns critical, and that switch often takes people by surprise.
- His fix is to start asking too early rather than too late. Worrying early that you're default dead is "probably not that dangerous", but worrying late is "very dangerous".

chunks.heading: The fatal pinch
chunks.text:
- The fatal pinch is default dead + slow growth + not enough time to fix it.
- Founders end up in it by not realizing that's where they're headed.
- Paul covered this in an earlier essay, "the fatal pinch" (paulgraham.com/pinch.html).
- Asking the default alive/dead question early is meant to set off the alarms soon enough to avoid it.

chunks.heading: Don't count on investors saving you
chunks.text:
- Founders skip the question because they assume it will be easy to raise more money. Paul says that assumption is often false, and "the more you depend on it, the falser it becomes."
- Separate facts from hopes instead of thinking of the future with vague optimism. Say it explicitly: "We're default dead, but we're counting on investors to save us." He expects that sentence to set off the same alarms in the founder's head that it does in his.
- Investor interest is, as a rule, a function of growth. With revenue growth steeper than about 5x a year, you can start to count on investors being interested even if you're not profitable.
- Steep usage growth also interests investors, since revenue will ultimately be a constant multiple of usage. But investors discount merely predicted revenue, so if you measure usage you need a higher growth rate to impress them.
- Investors are fickle, so you can only ever "start to count on them". Something about your business can spook them even when growth is great.
- Fundraising is therefore never more than a plan A, however good the growth. Always have a plan B:
  - Know, and write down, precisely what you'll do to survive if you can't raise more money.
  - Know, and write down, precisely when you'll have to switch to plan B if plan A isn't working.

chunks.heading: Spending and growth are weakly connected
chunks.text:
- Growing fast versus operating cheaply is "far from the sharp dichotomy many founders assume it to be."
- In practice there is surprisingly little connection between how much a startup spends and how fast it grows.
- Fast growth usually comes from the product hitting a nerve, meaning it hits some big need straight on.
- High spending usually comes from a product that is expensive to develop or sell, or from simple waste.

chunks.heading: Hiring too fast is the biggest killer of funded startups
chunks.text:
- To avoid being default dead, Paul's answer is: don't hire too fast. He calls hiring too fast "by far the biggest killer of startups that raise money."
- Founders say they need to hire in order to grow, but most overestimate that need. His reasons:
  - There is so much work to do that naive founders think enough hires will get it all done.
  - Successful startups have lots of employees, so it seems like what one does to succeed. He thinks the large staffs of successful startups are "probably more the effect of growth than the cause."
  - Founders with slow growth don't want to face the usual real reason: the product is not appealing enough.
- Startups that don't raise money are saved from hiring too fast because they can't afford to. That still isn't a reason to avoid raising money, "any more than that total abstinence is the only way to avoid becoming an alcoholic."
- He quotes Sam Altman: YC's most successful companies have never been the fastest to hire, and one of the marks of a great founder is being able to resist this urge.
- He also quotes Paul Buchheit on premature scaling. Founders take a small business that isn't really working (typically bad unit economics) and scale it up for impressive growth numbers. This makes it much harder to fix once it's big, and they bleed cash fast.

chunks.heading: VC incentives push founders to overhire
chunks.text:
- Founders who have just raised money are often encouraged by their VCs to overhire.
- Kill-or-cure strategies are optimal for VCs because the portfolio effect protects them. "VCs want to blow you up, in one sense of the phrase or the other."
- A founder's incentive is different: "You want above all to survive."
- Paul wouldn't be surprised if pushing founders to overhire isn't even in the VCs' own interest. They don't know how many of the companies killed by overspending might have done well had they survived, and he guesses a significant number.

chunks.heading: The common death spiral, and what to do instead
chunks.text:
- The pattern Paul describes:
  1. The founders make something moderately appealing and get decent initial growth.
  2. They raise a first round fairly easily, because they seem smart and the idea sounds plausible.
  3. Growth is ok but not great, since the product is only moderately appealing. The founders and their investors agree that hiring a bunch of people will boost growth.
  4. The growth never comes, and they are rapidly running out of runway.
  5. They hope further investment will save them, but high expenses plus slow growth make them unappealing to investors. They can't raise more, and the company dies.
- What they should have done is address the fundamental problem, that the product is only moderately appealing. Hiring is rarely the way to fix that, and more often than not it makes it harder.
- At this early stage the product needs to evolve more than to be "built out", and that is usually easier with fewer people.
- Asking the default alive/dead question can push founders to seek growth in other ways instead of overhiring. His examples are doing things that don't scale (paulgraham.com/ds.html) and redesigning the product "in the way only founders can." He says for many if not most startups these are the paths to growth that actually work.
- Example: Airbnb waited 4 months after raising money at the end of Y Combinator before hiring its first employee. The founders were terribly overworked, but they were overworked evolving Airbnb into the "astonishingly successful organism it is now."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Paul Graham distinguishes the manager's schedule (one-hour slots) from the maker's schedule (half-day blocks at least). A single meeting can wreck a maker's afternoon and even the morning before it. He explains how Y Combinator copes with office hours clustered at the end of the day, and why speculative meetings are only cheap for managers.

chunks.heading: The two schedules
chunks.text:
Paul describes two ways of using time. The manager's schedule is the traditional appointment book, with each day cut into one-hour intervals. It is the schedule of bosses and "the schedule of command", and most powerful people use it. The maker's schedule is common among programmers and writers, who "generally prefer to use time in units of half a day at least."

- He says "you can't write or program well in units of an hour. That's barely enough time to get started."
- On the manager's schedule, meeting someone is "merely a practical problem": find an open slot, book it, done.
- Each schedule works fine alone. Problems arise "when they meet."

chunks.heading: Why meetings wreck a maker's day
chunks.text:
- A single meeting can blow a whole afternoon by splitting it into two pieces, each too small to do anything hard in.
- A maker also has to remember the meeting. A manager always has something coming on the next hour, so there is nothing extra to think about.
- Paul says a meeting is "like throwing an exception." It changes the mode in which you work, not just the task.
- The effect cascades. If he knows the afternoon will be broken up, he is slightly less likely to start something ambitious in the morning.
- His reasoning: ambitious projects are close to the limits of your capacity, so "a small decrease in morale is enough to kill them off." A maker's spirits rise at the thought of an entire day free of appointments, so they sink when there isn't one.

chunks.heading: What powerful people should do
chunks.text:
- Most powerful people run on the manager's schedule, so they can make everyone "resonate at their frequency" if they want to.
- Paul says the smarter ones restrain themselves when some of their people need long chunks of time.
- He suggests founders may increasingly be able to resist, or at least postpone, turning into managers. He compares this to founders starting, a few decades earlier, to resist switching from jeans to suits.
- He notes that nearly all investors, including every VC he knows, operate on the manager's schedule. Y Combinator runs on the maker's schedule. Paul, Rtm and Trevor do because they always have, and Jessica mostly does because she got in sync with them.

chunks.heading: Simulating a manager's schedule inside a maker's: office hours
chunks.text:
Paul's method for advising many startups on a maker's schedule is office hours.

- Several times a week he sets aside a chunk of time to meet funded founders.
- The chunk sits at the end of his working day.
- He wrote a signup program that clusters all appointments within a given set of office hours at the end.
- Because the meetings come at the end of his day, they are never an interruption. In busy periods they can get long enough to "compress the day", but they "never interrupt it."
- The founders chose the appointments, so presumably each one is worth it to them even if it cuts into their own day.

chunks.heading: Splitting the day into two workdays
chunks.text:
When Paul and his partners worked on their own startup in the 90s, he used another trick.

- He programmed from dinner until about 3 am, because at night no one could interrupt him.
- He slept until about 11 am, then came in and worked until dinner on what he called "business stuff."
- In effect he had two workdays each day: one on the maker's schedule and one on the manager's. He did not think of it in those terms at the time.

chunks.heading: Speculative meetings and the coffee problem
chunks.text:
- On the manager's schedule you can have speculative meetings, meeting someone "just to get to know one another." An empty slot costs nothing, so "why not?" They are so common that there is distinctive language for proposing them, such as "grab coffee."
- On the maker's schedule speculative meetings are "terribly costly."
- Because everyone assumes YC is run like other investors, people introduce them to contacts or propose coffee. Paul says they then have two bad options: meet and lose half a day's work, or avoid the meeting and probably offend the person.
- His proposed third option is to explain the two types of schedule so the conflict becomes widely understood, and hopefully less of a problem.
- His compromise: makers accept that they have to have some number of meetings. "All we ask from those on the manager's schedule is that they understand the cost."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Graham argues there are two ways to run a company: founder mode and manager mode. Standard advice to hire good people and give them room is how to run a company you didn't found, and it damages founder-led companies. Founder mode breaks the rule that CEOs deal only with direct reports, and is still poorly understood.

chunks.heading: Two modes: founder mode vs. manager mode
chunks.text:
- Paul argues there are two distinct ways to run a company: "founder mode" and "manager mode."
- Most people in Silicon Valley have implicitly assumed that scaling a startup means switching to manager mode.
- He infers founder mode exists from the dismay of founders who tried manager mode and from the success of their attempts to escape it.
- As far as he knows, there are no books specifically about founder mode, and business schools don't know it exists. All that exists so far are the experiments of individual founders figuring it out for themselves.
- He hopes that within a few years founder mode will be as well understood as manager mode.
- The trigger was Brian Chesky's talk at a YC event. Paul says Chesky's conclusion was that conventional wisdom about running larger companies is mistaken.

chunks.heading: Why the standard scaling advice backfires
chunks.text:
- As Airbnb grew, well-meaning people told Chesky he had to run the company a certain way to scale. Paul summarizes the advice as "hire good people and give them room to do their jobs."
- Chesky followed it and "the results were disastrous." He then worked out a better way, partly by studying how Steve Jobs ran Apple.
- Paul says it seems to be working: Airbnb's free cash flow margin is now among the best in Silicon Valley.
- Many of the most successful YC-funded founders in the audience said the same thing had happened to them. They got the same advice, and it damaged their companies instead of helping.
- Paul's explanation: that advice describes how to run a company you didn't found, i.e. how to run it as a professional manager. That mode is so much less effective that to founders it feels broken. "There are things founders can do that managers can't, and not doing them feels wrong to founders, because it is."

chunks.heading: What manager mode looks like and where it fails
chunks.text:
- Paul likens the way managers are taught to run companies to modular design. You treat subtrees of the org chart as black boxes: you tell direct reports what to do, they figure out how, and you stay out of the details because getting involved would be micromanaging.
- "Hire good people and give them room to do their jobs" sounds great described that way. In practice, going by founder after founder, he says it often turns out to mean "hire professional fakers and let them drive the company into the ground."
- Paul's footnote concedes one upside of the modular approach: it limits the damage a bad CEO can do.

chunks.heading: Founders being gaslit, and why to trust your own instinct here
chunks.text:
- A recurring theme in Chesky's talk and in Paul's conversations afterward was founders feeling gaslit from both sides: by people telling them to run like managers, and by the people working for them once they do.
- Normally, when everyone around you disagrees, your default should be that you are mistaken. Paul says this is one of the rare exceptions.
- Two reasons:
  - VCs who haven't been founders don't know how founders should run companies.
  - C-level execs, as a class, "include some of the most skillful liars in the world."
- His more diplomatic phrasing: experienced C-level execs are often very skilled at managing up.

chunks.heading: Skip-level engagement and Jobs's retreats
chunks.text:
- Paul predicts founder mode will break the principle that the CEO engages with the company only through direct reports. "Skip-level" meetings will become the norm rather than a practice unusual enough to have a name.
- Once that constraint is dropped, there are "a huge number of permutations to choose from."
- Example: Steve Jobs ran an annual retreat for the 100 people he considered most important at Apple, who were not the 100 highest on the org chart.
- Paul notes the force of will this would take at the average company, and says it could make a big company feel like a startup. He presumes Jobs wouldn't have kept doing it if it didn't work.
- He has never heard of another company doing this and says it's unknown whether it's a good idea: "That's how little we know about founder mode."
- Footnote idea: if such retreats became widespread even at politics-dominated mature companies, you could measure a company's senescence by the average org-chart depth of those invited.

chunks.heading: Delegation limits and what to expect from founder mode
chunks.text:
- Paul is clear that founders can't run a 2000-person company the way they ran it at 20. "There's going to have to be some amount of delegation."
- Where the borders of autonomy fall, and how sharp they are, will vary by company and over time within one company as managers earn trust.
- So founder mode will be more complicated than manager mode, but it will also work better, which we already know from founders groping toward it.
- Prediction: once founder mode is understood, we'll find that many individual founders were already most of the way there, but were regarded by many as eccentric or worse.
- The goal is to tell founders how to run their companies "like Steve Jobs instead of John Sculley." Paul finds it encouraging how little is known, since founders have achieved so much against a headwind of bad advice.

chunks.heading: How "founder mode" will be misused
chunks.text:
- Paul predicts people will misuse the concept once it's established.
- Founders who can't delegate even things they should will use founder mode as an excuse.
- Non-founder managers will decide to act like founders. That may work to some extent, but when it doesn't the results will be messy.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Paul Graham explains why startups defy instinct and how to prepare. Expertise in your users and problem beats expertise in startup mechanics. Gaming the system stops working; only making something people want matters. Good ideas come from learning deeply and following interesting problems, not from brainstorming startup ideas.

chunks.heading: Counterintuitive nature of startups
chunks.text:
Paul argues that startups are so counterintuitive that trusting your instincts produces a lot of mistakes. He compares it to skiing: the instinct to lean back when you want to slow down makes you fly out of control, so you have to learn to suppress it.

- When he ran Y Combinator he joked that YC's function was "to tell founders things they would ignore." Founders ignore the partners' warnings, then come back a year later and say "I wish we'd listened."
- Counterintuitive ideas contradict your intuitions, so they seem wrong. You only need advisors for advice that surprises you. That is why there are many ski instructors and few running instructors.
- Some founders listen more than others, and this predicts success. He remembers how intently the Airbnb founders listened during YC.
- The exception is instincts about people. If you have misgivings about a cofounder, employee, investor or acquirer (they seem slippery, bogus or a jerk), trust your gut. A common young-founder mistake is ignoring misgivings because someone "seemed so impressive."
- Work with people you genuinely like and have known long enough to be sure.

chunks.heading: Expertise: be an expert on users, not on startups
chunks.text:
- The way to succeed is not to be an expert on startups but to be an expert on your users and the problem you are solving for them. Mark Zuckerberg succeeded despite being "a complete noob at startups" because he understood his users really well.
- Mechanics like how to raise an angel round can be learned when needed and forgotten afterward.
- Knowing everything about convertible notes, employee agreements and class FF stock sets off alarms for him. It is a sign of "playing house," where founders imitate the outward forms of a startup: a plausible-sounding idea, money raised at a good valuation, a cool office, a bunch of hires. They neglect the one essential thing, making something people want.

chunks.heading: Gaming the system stops working
chunks.text:
- Young founders go through the motions because that is what they were trained to do their whole lives. Paul admits he gamed college exams himself: he listed the 20 or 30 ideas shaped like good exam questions and worked out answers in advance.
- Founders look for the trick at every step. Fundraising looks like the measure of success, so they ask for tricks to convince investors. YC says the best way to convince investors is to build a startup that is growing fast and tell them. Then they ask for tricks to grow fast, and the answer is to make something people want. Partner conversations often go "How do we..." / "Just..."
- Starting a startup is "where gaming the system stops working." There is no boss to trick, only users, and "Startups are as impersonal as physics." You prosper only to the extent you make something people want.
- Faking does work somewhat on investors. A good talker can fool them for one or even two rounds. It is not in your interest, because the company is doomed and you just waste your time riding it down.
- Tricks exist but are an order of magnitude less important than solving the real problem. A founder who knows nothing about fundraising but has made something users love raises money more easily than one who knows every trick but has a flat usage graph. That founder also goes on to succeed after the raise.
- Startup schlep work is "merely unglamorous, not bogus." If your true calling is gaming the system, he says, go into management consulting.

chunks.heading: Startups are all-consuming, so don't start one in college
chunks.text:
- A startup takes over your life to a degree you cannot imagine, for several years at least, maybe a decade or the rest of your working life.
- Larry Page started running at 25 and hasn't stopped. Every day brings problems only the CEO can handle, a week's vacation creates a week's backlog, and as "the company's daddy" he can never show fear or weakness. The difficulty is concealed because billionaires get "less than zero sympathy."
- Every YC founder of a big success says the same thing: it never gets easier. The problems change but the total volume of worry never decreases, and if anything it increases.
- He compares it to having kids: a button that changes your life irrevocably, and many things are easier to do before.
- Universities can teach about startups, but that is not what you need to know. You need to learn your own users' needs, and you can't until you actually start. If you have significant numbers of users, you have started the company whether or not it is incorporated.
- You can't start a startup for real as a student, because you are then no longer really a student. His advice is blunt: "Do not start a startup in college."
- Starting a startup is "like a brutally fast depth-first search"; at 20 most people should still be searching breadth-first.
- Early-20s freedom (plunging into projects on a whim, traveling cheaply with no deadline) is valuable for ambitious people. Darwin was 22 and so unoccupied it alarmed his family when he got the HMS Beagle invitation. Zuckerberg will never get to bum around a foreign country.
- Waiting costs nothing, because you are more likely to succeed if you wait. If a side project takes off like Facebook did, running with it may be reasonable. But the usual way startups take off is founders making them take off, and doing that at 20 is "gratuitously stupid."

chunks.heading: You can't tell if you're up to it, so try later
chunks.text:
- Starting a startup is really hard, and you can't tell in advance if you can handle it. It will change you, so what you are estimating is what you could grow into.
- Over 9 years, his job at YC was predicting who would have what it takes. Intelligence was easy to judge. Toughness and ambition were hard to predict. His conclusion on how much an expert can know: "not much," and he kept a completely open mind about which startups in each batch would be stars.
- Founders' initial attitudes, whether swaggering confidence or fear of being found out, had little correlation with results. He has read the same is true in the military: swaggering recruits are no more likely to be tough than quiet ones.
- His rule: if you are absolutely terrified, probably don't. If you are merely unsure, the only way to find out is to try, "just not now."

chunks.heading: How to get startup ideas without trying to think of them
chunks.text:
- Before a startup you need only an idea and cofounders, and the method for getting both is the same. The way to get startup ideas "is not to try to think of startup ideas."
- Deliberately generated ideas are "not merely bad, but bad and plausible-sounding," so you waste time before realizing it.
- Instead, turn your mind into the type that ideas form in unconsciously, so you don't even realize at first they're startup ideas. Apple, Yahoo, Google and Facebook all began as side projects, not meant to be companies. Great ideas are such outliers that your conscious mind would reject them as company ideas.
- His recipe: (1) learn a lot about things that matter, (2) work on problems that interest you, (3) with people you like and respect. The third part also gets you cofounders at the same time as the idea.
- The prescription isn't limited to technology. Brian Chesky and Joe Gebbia were good at design and at organizing groups and making projects happen. What matters is working on problems demanding enough to stretch you.
- His test for real problems is that they are interesting, and he works on interesting things even if no one else cares ("especially if no one else cares"). He did YC itself only because it seemed interesting.
- A heuristic for whether you have the taste: do you find known boring ideas intolerable? Could you endure studying literary theory or working in middle management at a large company?

chunks.heading: Live at the leading edge and just learn
chunks.text:
- Think of technology as a fractal stain spreading. Every moving point on the edge is an interesting problem. Getting to the leading edge of some technology, to "live in the future" (Paul Buchheit's phrase), makes ideas that look uncannily prescient to others seem obvious to you.
- Example: in the mid 90s at Harvard, a grad student who knew networks wrote his own voice over IP software to talk to his girlfriend in Taiwan without paying long distance. He never turned it into a startup, but "this is exactly the way the best startups get started."
- The best preparation in college is not a vocational "entrepreneurship" program but classic education for its own sake: learn powerful things by following genuine curiosity.
- The component of entrepreneurship that matters is domain expertise. Becoming Larry Page meant becoming an expert on search, driven by curiosity and not an ulterior motive. "At its best, starting a startup is merely an ulterior motive for curiosity," best introduced toward the end of the process.
- Students can stick closer to a liberal education, without worrying about how courses look to employers or shying from hard classes for GPA. Users don't care about your GPA, he has never heard of investors caring, and YC never asks about classes or grades.
- His advice in two words: "just learn."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Graham gives founders a simple rule set for phase 2 (seed) fundraising: stay out of fundraising until you decide to raise, talk to investors in parallel ranked by expected value, treat anything short of a firm offer as a no, and accept acceptable offers quickly. Fundraising is a means to an end; the real test is revenue, so get it over with and get back to making things and talking to users.

chunks.heading: Funding stages and what this essay covers
chunks.text:
- Paul describes a typical path in three phases: (1) a few tens of thousands from something like Y Combinator or individual angels, (2) a few hundred thousand to a few million to build the company, (3) later rounds to accelerate growth once the company is clearly succeeding.
- Reality is messier: some companies raise twice in phase 2, some skip phase 1, and YC sees more companies arriving with hundreds of thousands already raised.
- This advice is for phase 2, the round startups raise on Demo Day.
- Fundraising is hard like lifting a weight (convincing people to part with large sums is irreducibly hard) and hard like a puzzle (an alien world to most founders). He wants to remove the puzzle part.
- Investors are pinched between fear of backing startups that fizzle and fear of missing startups that take off. Because winners grow fast, "if you wait till a startup is obviously a success, it's too late." Investors would like to wait, but if they wait too long others take the deal, so they all wait as long as they can and then rush at once.
- Investors are often opaque and sometimes deliberately misleading, which combines badly with founders' wishful thinking. His "rule number zero": the rules exist because powerful forces push you the other way, and inexperienced founders cannot trust their intuitions.

chunks.heading: When to raise, and fundraising mode
chunks.text:
- Rapid growth, not fundraising, is what makes a company a startup. Raise only if outside money would help you grow faster and your growth potential makes it easy to attract. If you wouldn't want to grow faster, or money wouldn't help, don't raise.
- Don't raise before you can convince investors. You waste time and burn your reputation with those investors.
- Fundraising is distracting because it becomes "the top idea in your mind," not because of the hours. Early-stage growth comes mostly from founders making it happen, so growth drops sharply if they look away. A startup should be either in fundraising mode or not, and when raising, give it your whole attention, finish fast and get back to work.
- Outside fundraising mode, take money only if it needs no convincing (zero time on meetings or materials) and no negotiation. Example: a reputable investor on a standard-paperwork convertible note, uncapped or capped at a good valuation.
- If an investor says they're ready but wants you to come in for one meeting with partners, say no politely while not in fundraising mode: "that's fundraising." Say you're focusing on the company and will get back to them when you're raising.
- Investors try to lure you into fundraising early to get a shot before everyone else. A cold email from an associate at a VC firm is not worth a meeting even in fundraising mode: "I don't know of a single VC investment that began with an associate cold-emailing a startup." Associates have no decision-making power, and partners discriminate against deals that reach them that way.
- Delay "just chat" meetings with partners too. "Investors never just want to meet and chat." Avoid casual conversations with potential acquirers as well; they can distract even more than fundraising.
- Tacking on a few investors after you leave fundraising mode is fine if they need no convincing or negotiation.

chunks.heading: Getting intros and reading investors
chunks.text:
- In phase 2 you need introductions. Best: a well-known investor who just invested in you, so ask each committed investor to introduce you to others they respect (a suggestion from Joshua Reeves: ask for two more intros each). Next best: founders of companies the investor funded. Also lawyers and reporters. Don't ask investors who said no for intros; it is often an anti-recommendation.
- AngelList, FundersClub and WeFunder are auxiliary sources. Raise first from leads you get yourself, which are on average better investors, and it is easier to raise on those sites once you've closed well-known investors.
- "Hear no till you hear yes": treat investors as saying no until they give a definite offer with no contingencies. Investors lead you on right up to the no, and some never say no and just stop replying, hoping for a free option if you turn out hot. Some use language that sounds like a commitment but isn't, and wishful founders meet them halfway.
- If you think an investor committed, get them to confirm it in writing. Till they do, regard them as saying no. YC built a protocol for this.
- Know where you stand by actions, not words. Never leave a meeting without asking what happens next: what they need to decide, whether another meeting, what internal steps, how long. Vague or resistant answers mean assume the worst; serious investors are already running through the path to wiring money.
- If you're inexperienced, confess it and ask how their process works and where you are in it. "Larry and Sergey were noobs at fundraising." Another signal (Ian Hogarth): serious investors expend resources on you after the first meeting.
- Don't imitate a smooth salesperson. A founder who ended meetings with "So, can I count you in?" pulled it off, but "nothing is more unconvincing" than a nerdy founder delivering lines meant for a smooth one. Be a good nerd.

chunks.heading: Running the process: parallel, expected value, first commitment, closing
chunks.text:
- Talk to investors in parallel, not serially, as breadth-first search weighted by expected value. Parallel saves time and gives each investor the pressure of the others.
- Expected value = probability they say yes × how good it would be. An eminent hard-to-convince investor can equal an easy-to-convince obscure angel. An obscure angel who invests little and needs several meetings has very low expected value; meet such investors last if at all. Some of the most useless investors are also the highest maintenance.
- Be disciplined assigning probabilities: don't let how much you want an investor inflate your estimate of how much they want you. This also makes you drift away from flaky investors at the same rate they drift from you.
- Packing meetings tightly is good, but too tight leaves less time for the pitch to evolve. Some founders schedule a few lame investors first to debug the pitch.
- The biggest factor in most investors' opinion of you is the opinion of other investors, so the first substantial commitment can be half the total difficulty. $50k from a well-known VC or angel is usually enough to get things rolling; friends and family money usually doesn't count.
- Signalling risk (a prestigious VC's small seed makes others read a later pass as a sign you suck) rarely matters in practice. If you can choose, excluding VC firms plays it safe, but it isn't critical.
- "It's not a deal till the money's in the bank." Founders say "We've raised $800,000" with zero in the bank. Investors are prone to buyer's remorse, and events (a competitor appears, a C&D, a cofounder quits, market shocks) cluster around fundraising. After a yes, get the timetable and babysit it until the money arrives; you may have to hunt angels down for a check. Inexperienced investors are likeliest to welch, though even top-tier VCs have.
- Competitor lawsuit threats timed to your raise: be forthright with investors. Experienced ones know the trick, and evasiveness alarms them more than disclosure.

chunks.heading: Investors who won't "lead," and the amount you raise
chunks.text:
- Some investors say "I want to invest, but I don't lead," or "I'll invest once you have a lead." Paul calls this a "contemptible subspecies." The term originally meant the lead negotiated terms in a round with shared paperwork. Series A rounds still work that way, but earlier raising now happens investor by investor, so "lead" now just means their interest is a function of other investors' interest.
- Translate "I don't lead" as "No, except yes if you turn out to be a hot deal," which is every investor's default view of every startup, so it tells you nothing. Their initial expected value is zero; talk to them last if at all. It's fine if "lead" means they invest unilaterally and also help raise more. Claims that they'll only invest if you raise $x elsewhere because you'd otherwise be "undercapitalized" are "almost always bullshit."
- Investors who decide quickly are extra valuable early because getting the first yes matters most.
- When investors ask how much you're raising, it is like a salesperson asking your budget: they check fit with their check size and judge your ambition, reasonableness and progress. You shouldn't have one fixed number. Have multiple plans: e.g. profitable with no more money; a few hundred thousand lets you hire one or two smart friends; a couple million, a whole engineering team. Match the plan to the investor: a series-A-only VC gets your most expensive plan; an angel writing $20k checks to a first-time raiser gets the cheapest.
- Upper limit rule of thumb: people you want to hire × $15k × 18 months. Example: 20 people × $15k × 18 = $5.4 million. $15k per person per month includes benefits and office space and is deliberately high as a margin of error; don't actually spend that much. Add other costs like manufacturing at the end.
- Underestimate how much you want. If you want $500k, say $250k: at $150k you're more than half done, which signals you're doing well and must be decided on quickly; at a $500k target you'd be under a third done and read as stalling. Saying $250k doesn't cap you; most very successful fundraisers end up raising more than planned. He says not to lie, just lower initial expectations. Metaphor: angle of attack. Announce a $5 million series A out of the gate without a very strong position and "you not only won't get that but won't get anything"; start low, build speed, then raise the angle.

chunks.heading: Profitability, valuation and terms
chunks.text:
- Be profitable if you can. Include a plan for raising zero dollars: "We'll succeed no matter what, but raising money will help us do it faster." Fundraising resembles dating: "No one wants you if you seem desperate," and the best way not to seem desperate is not to be. This is why YC urges low expenses and ramen profitability before Demo Day.
- Paul distinguishes type A fundraising (you don't need the money) from type B (you do). Inexperienced founders see famous startups doing type A and raise without a path to profitability, doing type B, then find it hard and unpleasant. Without profitability, fundraising from strength needs other advantages like extraordinary growth or exceptionally formidable founders, and gets harder over time. One YC founder said he'd leave up-front-capital-intensive ideas to founders with established reputations.
- Don't optimize for valuation. Priorities: (1) get the money you need, (2) good investors, (3) valuation, "at best third." Fundraising is not the test; revenue is. Being proud of your valuation is "like being proud of your college grades."
- Evidence: Dropbox and Airbnb, the most successful companies YC had funded at the time, raised after YC at pre-money valuations of $4 million and $2.6 million.
- The first committing investor sets your default asking price. Raise later investors at higher prices if there's interest. If the price was set too high you can lower it (give earlier investors the same terms), but you may lose leads. To avoid being stuck with an over-eager investor's high price, take their money on an uncapped convertible note with an MFN clause, so the cap is set by the next investors. Also a convertible-note warning: a very high valuation from an eager investor can set an impossible target for the next round.
- Lower prices are easier to close even though they shouldn't be: phase 2 prices vary at most 10x while big successes return at least 100x, yet many investors care about price. A startup investors like but won't back at cap $x may close at $x/2.
- Yes/no before valuation: if an investor pushes you to name a price before you've closed anyone, say valuation isn't the priority, you haven't thought much about it, you want partners, and you should first discuss whether they want to invest at all. Closing the first investor is the priority. YC usually tells founders to give the first committing investor as low a price as they need to, provided they handle "valuation sensitive" investors correctly (YC partners can estimate a market price if an investor insists you set it).
- "Valuation sensitive" investors are compulsive negotiators who eat time. Never approach them first; approach near the end and say "this is the price everyone else has paid; take it or leave it." If one pops up early, slow down your interactions. If you get a lowball offer, treat it as a backup offer and delay responding; lowballing "is a dick move that should be met with the corresponding countermove."

chunks.heading: Accepting offers, dilution and team
chunks.text:
- Accept offers greedily (like a greedy algorithm that doesn't look ahead). If someone makes an acceptable offer, take it; with multiple incompatible offers, take the best. Don't reject an acceptable offer hoping for a better one. As you near your target, the threshold for "acceptable" rises. Roll up investors as they say yes.
- Offers last for stretches of time. With an acceptable offer that is incompatible with others, tell other investors you have an offer good enough to accept and give them a few days. Exploding offers: three working days is acceptable; shorter signals a sketchy investor and you can usually call the bluff. The best investors explode less (Fred Wilson never gives exploding offers). Respond promptly to clean offers with no deadline.
- "Get the best investors" rarely conflicts with greedy acceptance if you talk in parallel and push back on short deadlines. The best investors are the most selective and reject nearly everyone, so trading a definite offer from an acceptable investor for a potential offer from a better one is a bad average-case trade. In phase 1 they do conflict, because incubators stagger schedules; apply so the ones you want most decide first.
- If a series A investor starts talking, keep taking smaller investments until they give a termsheet. Convertible notes convert into the A. Tell the A investor about each smaller investment as it happens; you owe them cap table updates, and it pressures them to act. They can't legitimately ask you to stop until they give a termsheet with a no-shop clause. Relax a little only if the investor has a great reputation, is clearly moving fast, and a third party like YC is involved.
- Don't sell more than 25% in phase 2, on top of under 15% in phase 1. Above about 40% total sold, VCs worry about founder motivation and an A gets harder. On uncapped notes, guess the eventual valuation conservatively. Tentatively assume the path to huge passes through an A; Weebly skipped it, reaching profitability on a $650k seed after bad terms in fall 2008.
- Have one person handle fundraising, the CEO and most formidable founder, even if another founder is the salesperson. Insulate the others from the details. Bring all founders only to meet an investor who will invest a lot, as a final step ("like introducing a girl/boyfriend to your parents"). A single founder in the room also lets you say "I need to circle back with my co-founder" instead of negotiating in real time against professional negotiators.
- Growth still matters during the raise: if numbers grow between meetings investors get hot to close; flat or down numbers give them cold feet.
- You need a one-page executive summary: matter-of-fact language on what you'll do, why it's a good idea, and progress so far, to remind investors who saw many startups. A deck is traditional (Sequoia describes contents), but Paul is ambivalent and many successful phase 2 startups never make one. Materials will leak; treat it as a cost of business (he can't name a startup whose outcome it affected). Don't send a deck or summary before a meeting; requesting it is a sign they're not interested.

chunks.heading: Stopping, pitfalls, and being nice
chunks.text:
- Stop fundraising when "you start to get a lot of air in the straw," like drinking through a straw near the end of the liquid.
- Don't get addicted: good fundraisers can enjoy lunches with famous investors more than listening to users complain about bugs, and start to feel already successful and lose their taste for schleps. "When I see a startup with young founders that is fabulously successful at fundraising, I mentally decrease my estimate of the probability that they'll succeed." The opposite risk is demoralization from rejection.
- Don't raise too much. A company's valuation is expected to rise each round, so a $30 million post-money in phase 2 means the next round needs at least $50 million pre-money, and "you have to be doing really, really well" for that. More money also means more spending and more people, which hurts profitability and makes it harder to change direction. If you raise a huge amount, don't spend it.
- The bar is higher next time: "Assume the money you raise in phase 2 will be the last you ever raise." Investors now spray money at early startups and ruthlessly cull at the next stage. In phase 3 the experiment must have worked, usually shown by profitability, so phase 3 is usually type A fundraising.
- Two ways startups hose themselves between phases 2 and 3: being too slow to become profitable (raise two years' money, make no effort for a year, then can't), and letting expenses grow too fast by hiring too many. Don't hire 8 people right after raising; wait for growth to justify them. VCs tell you to spend too much, partly because they solve problems with money and partly because they want to sell you more of your company later. "Don't listen to them."
- Be nice. Playing hardball per these rules (refusing meetings, slowing slow investors, treating contingent offers as no, leaving some out) requires cushioning with soft words. Blame YC or "PG said startups shouldn't ___, and since we're new to fundraising we feel like we have to play it safe." Never seem arrogant, especially when you're doing well: "pride goeth before a fall."
- Be nice to investors who reject you too. The best aren't wedded to their first opinion and often invest in phase 3; those who spent time deciding probably came close, often with an internal champion needing a bit more evidence. Treat a rejection as the start of a relationship.

chunks.heading: The one-sentence version
chunks.text:
- "Avoid investors till you decide to raise money, and then when you do, talk to them all in parallel, prioritized by expected value, and accept offers greedily."
- Don't add complicated optimizations or let investors introduce complications. Fundraising is a means; the goal is to get it over with and return to "making things and talking to users." His closing line: "don't leave the path."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Paul Graham argues that founders unconsciously avoid ideas involving painful schleps, so great ideas like Stripe sit unexploited in plain sight. Schleps are what business consists of, and scary, ambitious ideas face less competition. Ignorance, and asking what problem you wish someone else would solve for you, are the antidotes.

chunks.heading: Schlep blindness: what it is and why it hides the best startup ideas
chunks.text:
Paul defines a schlep as "a tedious, unpleasant task." *Schlep blindness* is his name for the way people fail to see startup ideas that involve painful schleps. The aversion is largely unconscious: "Your unconscious won't even let you see ideas that involve painful schleps." Great ideas lie around unexploited because the mind filters them out before they are ever considered.

- He compares it to physical fitness. Most people don't consciously decide against being in Olympic shape. Their unconscious mind decides for them by shrinking from the work.
- Nobody weighs "fix payments or build a recipe site?" and picks the recipe site. The hard option never makes it onto the list.

chunks.heading: Schleps are what business consists of
chunks.text:
Paul says hackers dislike schleps most. They hope to write clever software, put it on a server and watch the money roll in, without talking to users, negotiating with other companies or dealing with other people's broken code. He says he hasn't seen that work.

- YC teaches hackers that schleps are inevitable: "No, you can't start a startup by just writing code."
- He went through this himself. In 1995 he was still trying to convince himself he could start a company by just writing code. Experience taught him that "schleps are not merely inevitable, but pretty much what business consists of."
- "A company is defined by the schleps it will undertake."
- His advice is to treat a schlep like a cold swimming pool and "just jump in."
- He does not say to seek out unpleasant work for its own sake. The point is to never shrink from it when it is on the path to something great.

chunks.heading: Stripe as the clearest example
chunks.text:
Paul calls Stripe, or rather Stripe's idea, the most striking example of schlep blindness he knows.

- For over a decade, every hacker who had processed payments online knew how painful it was. Thousands of people must have known about the problem.
- Many of them still started recipe sites or aggregators for local events. These were problems few care about and no one will pay for, when they could have fixed "one of the most important components of the world's infrastructure."
- The schleps that scared people off:
  - Making deals with banks, with no obvious way to do it.
  - Fraud, and people trying to break into your servers, because you are moving money.
  - Regulations to comply with.
- Starting this kind of company is far more intimidating than starting a recipe site, so the idea was in plain sight but never seen.

chunks.heading: Why scary ideas are more valuable
chunks.text:
Paul argues that the scariness of an ambitious idea is itself a source of value.

- Ambitious ideas have intrinsic value, and in addition they are "like undervalued stocks" because there is less demand for them among founders.
- Pick an ambitious idea and you face less competition, because everyone else was frightened off by the challenges.
- He notes this is also true of starting a startup in general.

chunks.heading: Antidote one: ignorance, and why young founders win
chunks.text:
Paul says the most valuable antidote to schlep blindness is probably ignorance.

- Most successful founders would say that had they known the obstacles ahead, they might never have started.
- This may be one reason the most successful startups so often have young founders.
- In practice, "the founders grow with the problems," but no one seems able to foresee that, not even older, more experienced founders.
- Young founders make two mistakes that cancel out: they don't know how much they can grow, and they don't know how much they'll need to. Older founders make only the first mistake.

chunks.heading: Antidote two: ask what you wish someone else would solve
chunks.text:
Ignorance can't solve everything, because some ideas obviously involve alarming schleps that anyone can see. For those, Paul recommends taking yourself out of the picture.

- Don't ask "what problem should I solve?" Ask "what problem do I wish someone else would solve for me?"
- Anyone who had struggled with payments before Stripe, and asked that question, would have put Stripe among the first things they wished for.
- He says it is too late to be Stripe, but "there's plenty still broken in the world, if you know how to see it."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Paul Graham defines ramen profitability as a startup making just enough to pay the founders' living expenses. It buys time and independence from investors, and it is not the destination. He lists four advantages (better terms, investor appeal, morale, no fundraising distraction) and warns about sliding into consulting.

chunks.heading: Ramen profitability: definition and what it is for
chunks.text:
- Paul defines ramen profitable as a startup making "just enough to pay the founders' living expenses."
- This differs from traditional profitability. A hardware company might spend $50 million over 5 years before turning profitable, then earn $50 million a year. That kind of profitability means the startup has succeeded.
- Ramen profitability can arrive after 2 months, at $3000 a month of revenue, when the only employees are a couple of 25 year old founders who can live on almost nothing. That revenue does not mean the company has succeeded.
- What the two share is that the company doesn't need to raise money to survive. Ramen profitability "buys you time."
- It only recently became feasible. It is not feasible for most biotech startups, but it is for many software startups because they are now so cheap. For many, the only real cost is the founders' living expenses.
- "Ramen" means instant ramen, the cheapest food available. Paul says not to take it literally, since it is unhealthy, and suggests rice and beans cooked in a rice cooker.

chunks.heading: The investor advantage: not being at their mercy
chunks.text:
- A startup that is still losing money must eventually raise more or shut down. Once ramen profitable, "this painful choice goes away." You can still raise money, but you don't have to do it now.
- Not needing money gets you better terms. Investors who know you need money sometimes take advantage of you. Some deliberately stall, because they know you become "increasingly pliable" as you run out of money.
- Ramen profitability also makes you more attractive to investors, because it shows:
  - (a) you can get at least someone to pay you,
  - (b) you're serious about building things people want,
  - (c) you're disciplined enough to keep expenses low.
- Paul says these address three of investors' biggest worries. Companies with smart founders and a big market usually fail because:
  - (a) people wouldn't pay for what they made, for example because it was too hard to sell or the market wasn't ready,
  - (b) the founders solved the wrong problem instead of paying attention to what users needed,
  - (c) the company spent too much and burned through its funding before making money.
- A ramen profitable company is already avoiding these mistakes.

chunks.heading: Morale and the weight of responsibility
chunks.text:
- A new company feels theoretical. It is legally a company, but "you feel like you're lying when you call it one." When people start paying you significant amounts, it starts to feel real.
- Covering your own living expenses is the milestone you feel most, because "the future flips state. Now survival is the default, instead of dying."
- Paul argues the moral weight of running a startup is what makes it hard. He dismisses the usual explanations:
  - Financial risk is not the barrier, since plenty of 25 year olds save nothing anyway.
  - Long hours are not the barrier, since plenty of people in regular jobs work just as long.
  - What keeps people from starting startups is "the fear of having so much responsibility," and the fear is not irrational.
- Anything that takes some of that weight off increases your chances of surviving.
- He says a startup that reaches ramen profitability "may be more likely to succeed than not." That is notable given the bimodal distribution of startup outcomes, where you either fail or make a lot of money.

chunks.heading: Fundraising is a distraction; choose when to raise
chunks.text:
- Paul calls not interrupting the company to raise money the fourth advantage, "the least obvious but may be the most important."
- Raising money is "terribly distracting." You're lucky if your productivity is a third of what it was, and it can last for months.
- Startups YC funded usually "grind to a halt" when they switched to fundraising. Paul only remembered why when YC raised money itself.
  - It was comparatively easy, since the first people he asked said yes.
  - Working out the details still took months, and he got hardly any real work done.
  - The reason: "I thought about it all the time."
- At any time a startup has one most urgent problem, the one you think about falling asleep and in the morning shower. Fundraising takes over that slot. "You only take one shower in the morning, and if you're thinking about investors during it, then you're not thinking about the product."
- If you can choose when to raise, you can pick a time when you're not in the middle of something else and probably insist that the round close fast. You may even avoid having the round occupy your thoughts, if you don't care whether it closes.

chunks.heading: What ramen profitability does not imply
chunks.text:
- **Not bootstrapping.** It doesn't mean you will never take investor money. Paul says empirically that doesn't seem to work well: "Few startups succeed without taking investment."
  - The money is there waiting to be invested. If startups need it less, they get it on better terms, which makes them more inclined to take it, so an equilibrium emerges.
- **Not Joe Kraus's rule** of putting your business model in beta when you put your product in beta, getting people to pay from the start.
  - Paul thinks that is too constraining. Facebook didn't do it and did better than most startups. Making money right away was probably not just unnecessary but harmful for them.
  - He still finds the rule useful for many startups. When founders seem unfocused, he sometimes suggests they try to get customers to pay for something, hoping the constraint prods them into action.
- **Not the final business model.** A ramen profitable company "doesn't have to be making money the way it ultimately will. It just has to be making money." The most famous example is Google, which initially made money by licensing search to sites like Yahoo.

chunks.heading: The main danger: sliding into consulting
chunks.text:
- Paul says the biggest downside is that ramen profitability might turn you into a consulting firm.
- Startups must be product companies, "making a single thing that everyone uses." Their defining quality is that they grow fast, and consulting can't scale the way a product can.
- It is easy to make $3000 a month consulting. That would be a low rate for contract programming. The temptation is to tell yourselves you're a ramen profitable startup "when in fact you're not a startup at all."
- A little consulting-type work at first is fine, since startups usually have to do something weird early on.
- Paul's reminder: "ramen profitability is not the destination. A startup's destination is to grow really big; ramen profitability is a trick for not dying en route."
- A startup could in theory grow big by transforming consulting into something that scales, but then it would really be a product company.

chunks.heading: Investor power and the venture business (side argument)
chunks.text:
- Paul thinks a shift in power from investors to founders could actually increase the size of the venture business.
- He believes investors currently "err too far on the side of being harsh to founders." Forced to stop, the whole venture business would work better, like the increase in trade you see when restrictive laws are removed.
- His chain of reasoning: investors are one of the biggest sources of pain for founders. If they caused less pain, being a founder would be better, and more people would do it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Paul Graham distills seven counterintuitive startup lessons he finds himself repeating to YC founders. The core themes: release a minimal v1 fast, keep shipping small improvements, obsess over users and conversion, fear other startups and self-inflicted wounds instead of big companies, stay determined but flexible, and never count on a deal until it closes.

chunks.heading: Release early, then pump out features
chunks.text:
- Paul's most-repeated recipe: "get a version 1 out fast, then improve it based on users' reactions."
- "Release early" means minimal, not buggy. "Users hate bugs, but they don't seem to mind a minimal version 1, if there's more coming soon."
- He has repeated this about software since 1993. He has seen many startups die from releasing too slowly, "and none because they were too quick." Startups can die from a buggy release that isn't fixed fast, but he knows of none that died from a stable, minimal, very early release followed by prompt improvement.
- Reasons to release early:
  - Web startups don't know their users (Reddit had almost half a million unique visitors a month and "they have no idea" who they are), so guessing what users want is dangerous. Release and let them tell you.
  - Wufoo released its form-builder before the underlying database. 83,000 people came, and Linux users complained about too much Flash, so Wufoo rewrote the software to avoid it. Waiting would have buried the problem deeper.
  - The first release is a shakedown cruise. A bad idea or founders who hate each other get exposed by the stress of shipping, and you want that early.
  - It makes you work harder. Unreleased, "problems are intriguing"; released, "problems are alarming." People delay because they know they'll have to work harder after release.
- Second half of the rule: "pump out features." Starting minimal only works if you improve fast, and this applies for as long as you want to be considered a startup.
- A "feature" means "one unit of hacking, one quantum of making users' lives better," not added complexity. Improve the system in some small way every day or two.
- Improvements beget improvements, like running: the more ideas you implement, the more you have.
- Constant improvement is also marketing. Users expect a site to improve, and judge a site as an animation of many frames, not a snapshot. Paul says the rate of improvement matters more to users than the current state.
- Improving in response to comments creates "fanatical loyalty" because customers are used to being ignored. "You won't need to advertise, because your users will do it for you."
- Teams stop improving because they get used to the product and its current features become its identity (few at Yahoo or Google imagined better webmail until Paul Buchheit showed them).
- Fix: assume the product is far short of what it could be and keep asking what you would change. If it seems finished, "(a) it is finished, or (b) you lack imagination. Experience suggests (b) is a thousand times more likely."

chunks.heading: Make users happy: convert casual visitors
chunks.text:
- Startups can't force anyone to use their software or do deals, so "a startup has to sing for its supper." That is why successful ones make great things.
- Paul's wind metaphor: users are the most powerful wind. They can loft you up (as with Google) or leave you flat, and "if they take you up, no competitor can keep you down." The rational move is to "curl yourself into a shape the wind will catch."
