- Design for the casual majority, not the people who care and will find things themselves. The median visitor arrives "with their finger poised on the Back button," trained by the web that most links are lame.
- Two things make people pause:
  1. Explain concisely what the site is about. A startup should describe what it does in one or two sentences, for users and also investors, acquirers, partners, reporters and employees. Paul says you probably shouldn't start a company whose product can't be described compellingly in one or two sentences.
  2. Give people everything you've've got right away. Put the impressive stuff on the front page, since most visitors only see that. The paradox is that pushing good stuff forward makes visitors explore further.
- Best case: show instead of tell. "Nothing will explain what your site does so well as using it."
- Don't make users register to try the site. They've been trained to expect that registration-gated things suck.
- Caveat: a startup need not always tell users plainly what it is. MySpace, basically a replacement mall for mallrats, was wiser to pretend at first that it was about bands.
- The job of the site is "conversion," turning casual visitors into users. Measure it by growth rate: "If you have decent growth, you'll win in the end, no matter how obscure you are now. And if you don't, you need to fix something."

chunks.heading: Fear the right things
chunks.text:
- Paul often says "don't worry about this; worry about that instead." Startups are right to be paranoid but fear the wrong things.
- Visible disasters are normal and won't kill you unless you let them: a founder quits, a patent covers your idea, servers crash, an insoluble technical problem, a forced name change, a deal falls through.
- Big companies are not the threat, not even Google. Their people are no smarter than you, are less motivated because one failed product won't put Google out of business, and face bureaucracy.
- Fear other startups you don't know exist yet. They are more dangerous than Google because "like you, they're cornered animals."
- Compete against what someone else could be doing, not only visible competitors. Having no visible competitors is no reason to relax: "No matter what your idea, there's someone else out there working on the same thing."
- Paul disagrees with Caterina Fake that more people starting startups makes it a bad time to start. Most college graduates still think they need a job.
- More startups hose themselves than get crushed by competitors. The three main ways, each enough to kill you: internal disputes, inertia, and ignoring users. Ignoring users is the worst.
- The recipe for a dying startup: founders with a great idea they know everyone will love, which they will build "no matter what."
- Almost every initial plan is broken. If companies had stuck to initial plans, Microsoft would sell programming languages and Apple would sell printed circuit boards. In both cases customers told them what the business should be and they listened.
- Paul quotes Feynman ("the imagination of nature is greater than the imagination of man"). You find better product ideas "by smashing a beam of prototypes into a beam of users" than by thinking alone.

chunks.heading: Determination beats intelligence
chunks.text:
- Paul says the most important quality in a founder is determination, "not intelligence." He would like to believe Viaweb succeeded because of smarts, but concluded otherwise, partly from years in New York.
- "You can lose quite a lot in the brains department and it won't kill you. But lose even a little bit in the commitment department, and that will kill you very rapidly."
- VCs overinvest in eminent professors. That may work in biotech, but in software back students: Microsoft, Yahoo and Google were founded by people who dropped out. Students make up for lack of experience with dedication.
- Running a startup is "like walking on your hands." An ordinary employee asked to do a founder's job would be indignant: code ten times faster while also answering support calls, administering servers, designing the site, cold-calling customers, finding office space and fetching lunch, amid constant disasters. Disasters give anyone inclined to quit an excuse.
- Commitment shows. People who deal with startups give little attention to ambivalent founders, so good things happen to competitors and not to you, and you feel unlucky. Committed founders are "a local, not just a tourist."
- Y Combinator sometimes mistakenly funds teams who plan to try for three months and stay only if something great happens (an acquisition or millions in investment). That attitude makes "something great" unlikely, since acquirers and investors judge you by commitment.
- Acquirers who think you'll stick around may buy sooner, since your price rises as you grow. Paul says investors, even big VCs, are motivated "not [by] the hope of good returns, but the fear of missing out." Show you'll succeed regardless and only need them to go faster.
- Why VCs behave this way: in a typical fund half the companies fail, most others return little, and one or two "make the fund," so missing a few top deals can sink it.
- "You can't fake this." You must actually be ready to fight to the death.
- Be determined, not stubborn. Be "determined, but flexible, like a running back": improvise, run around obstacles, even briefly run the wrong way, but never stand still.

chunks.heading: Don't get your hopes up: protect yourself in deals
chunks.text:
- This was practically the corporate motto at Viaweb. Treat optimism like a nuclear reactor core: a power source that needs shielding, pierced only in a few places.
- Draw the line between expectations of yourself and of others: "It's ok to be optimistic about what you can do, but assume the worst about machines and other people." Startups push limits, so things change suddenly and usually for the worse.
- On deals, assume it won't happen. "The VCs who say they're going to invest in you aren't. The company that says they're going to buy you isn't. The big customer who wants to use your system in their whole company won't." Then you can be pleasantly surprised.
- The point isn't avoiding disappointment but avoiding leaning the company on something that will fall over.
- Tactic: when someone says they want to invest, you tend to stop looking for other investors, and the person proposing the deal wants you to stop. Doing deals is a pain and raising money is a huge time sink, so force yourself to keep looking.
- Keep looking even if you take the first deal, because you get better terms. Deals have many subsidiary questions after the handshake, and if the other side senses you need it, they will be tempted to squeeze you in the details.
- VCs and corp dev people are professional negotiators, trained to exploit weakness, and do it more often than you. Don't try to bluff them. "The only way a startup can have any leverage in a deal is genuinely not to need it."
- Y Combinator never negotiates valuations, because it isn't made of professional negotiators and doesn't want to become one.
- Hypnotic suggestion: when you hear "we want to invest in you" or "we want to acquire you," think "don't get your hopes up" and keep running as if the deal didn't exist. "Nothing is more likely to make it close."
- Focus on getting lots of users and "keep walking swiftly toward it while investors and acquirers scurry alongside trying to wave money in your face."

chunks.heading: There is always room for new startups
chunks.text:
- Paul rejects "tapped out" thinking. A founder told him the social thing was tapped out, but he doubts the only social sites in a hundred years will be Facebook, MySpace, Flickr and Del.icio.us.
- People adjust to how things are and assume that's how they must be. Even a better search engine than Google seems crazy, yet he doubts people will search the same way in twenty or a hundred years.
- On the claim that startups will be disappointed because Google and Yahoo can only buy so many: no one says there is a limit to jobs in an economy of big companies of a couple thousand people, so why a limit for small companies of ten? The only limit is people willing to work that hard.
- The real limit is the wealth that can be created, since startups "make things people want." He sees no limit short of cosmological ones: "I still don't even have a flying car."

chunks.heading: Startups are about speed, not money
chunks.text:
- Founders all say it was harder than expected.
- Paul regards making money as "a boring errand to be got out of the way as soon as possible" and says it's ridiculous to take business too seriously.
- Economically, a startup is "not... a way to get rich, but... a way to work faster": a way to finish making a living quickly instead of dragging it through your whole life.
- Life is short; Paul cites Franklin: "if you love life, don't waste time, because time is what life is made of."
- Compressing the dull task of earning a living into the smallest possible time "show[s] respect for life."
- A footnote notes two ways to do work you love: make money then work on what you love, or get paid to work on what you love. Early phases of both are mostly unedifying schleps, and the second is less secure in its later phase.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Paul Graham surveyed 100+ YC founders on what surprised them about starting a startup, which amounts to asking what he got wrong. The surprises (cofounder character, persistence, slow deals, minimal launches, talking to users, luck, clueless investors) were all things he already says, because people unconsciously model a startup on a job.

chunks.heading: Cofounders are the foundation, so pick on character and commitment
chunks.text:
- Paul reports "the surprise mentioned by the most founders" was how carefully cofounders must be chosen and how hard the relationship must be maintained.
- Founders who failed wished they had weighed character and commitment over ability. His lesson: "don't pick cofounders who will flake."
- Character is tested harder in a startup than anywhere else. One founder: "You haven't seen someone's true colors unless you've worked with them on a startup."
- One founder preferred a friend over a higher-output stranger, because the emotional and social support outweighs the lost output.
- YC's application has more questions about the founders' commitment and relationship than about their ability.
- Successful founders talked less about choosing and more about maintaining the relationship. Several said it turns from friendship into a marriage, which Paul explains by the greater stress and by founders being the whole company at first. "It's the basis of everything."

chunks.heading: A startup is not a job: it takes over your life and swings emotionally
chunks.text:
- Running a startup never stops, unlike a job or being a student. Founders spend nearly every waking moment working or thinking about it, and time seems to stretch so that a month feels huge.
- Total immersion can feel exciting and never like "work", though Paul notes the founder who said this was only a few months in.
- The emotional swings are larger than founders expect, from "the next Google" to pondering failure within hours. The lows, and keeping the team motivated through them, are the hard part.
- Keeping going without major success "is siphoned from the founders themselves". If you can't continue, Paul says it's not the end of the world, since plenty of famous founders had earlier failures.
- The highs are real too. Many founders found it fun and more fulfilling than friends' jobs, mainly because of the freedom.
- Paul deliberately doesn't oversell this: starting a startup is fun "the way a survivalist training course would be fun", and not at all if you're not into that. YC's application weeds out people who wouldn't like it.

chunks.heading: Persistence and a long-term view matter more than intelligence
chunks.text:
- Founders were surprised by how much persistence is required and by how often persistence alone dissolved obstacles, even problems like immigration.
- Several said persistence matters more than raw intelligence. Paul extends this to ability in general, which is why character matters in cofounders.
- Everything takes 2-3x longer than expected, especially dealmaking. Paul's cause: fast-moving founders hit "shocking amount of shear stress" wherever they touch bureaucracies like big companies or VC funds, which is why fundraising and the enterprise market kill so many startups.
- Founders are also overconfident. Told only 1 in 100 successful startups has a YouTube or Facebook trajectory, "they all think 'we're going to be that 1.'"
- A successful founder's view: for most successful startups it's "at least 3 years and probably 5+."
- Thinking long-term helps. Working patiently is less stressful and produces better work, and things improve at ramen profitability when you can "shift into a different mode of working".
- Tactic from his notes: don't put a slow organization on the critical path. Fork off separate processes to deal with them, and avoid depending on closing a deal to move forward.

chunks.heading: Launch something minimal, talk to users, and change the idea
chunks.text:
- Success comes from lots of little things, not one magic idea or killer feature. "There is no such thing as a killer feature. Or at least you won't know what it is." Hacker-founders won't get to program all day: "If you spend all your time programming, you will fail."
- Because you don't even know which basket is best, the strategy is to try lots of different things.
- Launch "the absolute smallest thing that can be considered a complete application." Pride is the usual reason people launch late. Paul: "If your first version is so impressive that trolls don't make fun of it, you waited too long to launch" (a variant of Reid Hoffman's embarrassment principle).
- Over-engineering "is poison": it's like telling a lie you then have to remember so you don't contradict it.
- Product development is a conversation with users that doesn't start until launch. Before launch you're like a police artist before showing the witness the first sketch. Treat the first version as a trick for getting users talking.
- Customers reveal what they value and will pay for. They often won't like what you built, but there are other things they'd like that are trivially easy to implement.
- Treat the idea as "a hypothesis rather than a blueprint". Determination without flexibility is "a greedy algorithm" that finds a mediocre local maximum.
- One founder's advice: find a problem that's easy for you to solve, since "you can make enormous gains playing around in problem-space." Fast iteration is key.
- Judging startup ideas, especially your own, is very hard, and experienced founders keep an open mind. Paul applies this to YC itself, which is "a decent hypothesis".

chunks.heading: Competitors are rarely the threat, but getting users is hard
chunks.text:
- Worrying about competitors is mostly a false alarm. Apparent competitors usually have a different goal, and scares are forgotten weeks later.
- People overreact because they overvalue ideas. Execution is what usually matters.
- Hype doesn't create satisfied users for something as complicated as technology: "Competitors riding on lots of good blogger perception aren't really the winners."
- Getting users is harder than founders expect. When it fails, it's hard to tell whether the problem is exposure or a bad product, and even good products can be blocked by switching or integration costs. Small companies asking other companies' developers to do work aren't seen as urgent.
- Paul's note: the test for what you've built isn't whether it's good but whether it's good enough to supply the activation energy required.
- The sharpest criticism of YC was too little focus on customer acquisition cost. Paul concedes this may be true, especially for games.
- Technically challenging products can rely on word of mouth, as Google did. Other types of startups may win more through deals and marketing than features.

chunks.heading: Deals and investors: expect the worst, and sell yourself
chunks.text:
- Deals fall through constantly. Startups are powerless and good ideas generally seem wrong, so everyone is nervous about closing with you.
- Paul's pessimistic advice: assume you won't get investment, and if someone offers some, assume you'll never get any more. One founder wished they'd assumed no outside money, which would have focused them on finding revenue early.
- Another founder's counterpoint, which Paul endorses: if someone offers you money, take it.
- Be optimistic about your ability to make something great, but not about things you can't control, like big companies or investors.
- Founders were surprised by investors' cluelessness. Angels were generally better than VCs because they usually have startup experience.
- Paul's explanation: VCs seem formidable because their profession is to. They win money from limited partners by seeming confident and seeming to understand technology.
- So you may have to play games. "The degree to which feigning certitude impressed investors" surprised one founder. At a YC alumni fundraising talk, nearly all the advice was about investor psychology, and the founders were more cynical than Paul.
- VCs often don't realize that the startups they like are the best at selling themselves to VCs. Paul's analogy: the dumber the customers, the more effort goes into selling rather than making.
- "VCs get money by seeming confident to LPs, and founders get money by seeming confident to VCs."

chunks.heading: Luck, community, respect, and how the job changes as you grow
chunks.text:
- Luck is a big factor, especially in deals, because there are "two such random linkages in the path between startups and money". His example: where would Microsoft be if IBM had insisted on an exclusive license for DOS?
- Paul's model is that the outcome is "the product of skill, determination, and luck", so zero luck means zero outcome.
- Founders who fail fast blame themselves, and those who succeed fast don't see their luck. It's the ones in the middle who see how important luck is.
- Community was a surprising value, both the YC peer group facing similar obstacles at similar times and the wider Silicon Valley scene, where you can't help hearing news and meeting useful people. Founders were surprised by how willing people were to help and how accessible important people are. Paul: creating wealth isn't zero-sum, so you don't have to stab people in the back to win.
- Outside the startup world, founders get no respect. Most good ideas seem bad, and about 95% of random people instinctively think your idea will flop.
- As you grow, the technical founder/CEO's job is rewritten every 6-12 months: less coding, more managing, planning, hiring and cleaning up messes. The employee equation differs from the founder equation.
- One founder said about 75% of the stress was gone after reaching cruising altitude, though Paul says 75% is probably on the high side.

chunks.heading: The super-pattern: everyone's model of work is a job
chunks.text:
- Paul notes that every surprise is something he already tells people. Starting a startup was "like I said, but way more so."
- His explanation: everyone's unconscious model of work is a job, so they expect a startup to resemble one. Jobs have far more damping, and no need to carefully choose and maintain relationships with coworkers.
- The same model explains why the good times are surprisingly good, since most people can't imagine such freedom.
- His fix is awareness. When you think "I can't believe it will be that bad", the next thought should be: "the reason I can't believe it will be that bad is that my model of work is a job."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Paul Graham lists the reasons people hesitate to start startups and says which are real and which are bogus. Most are bogus: youth, inexperience, intelligence, business knowledge and no idea matter little. The real ones are no cofounder and a family to support. The essay also argues for making something people love first and worrying about revenue later.

chunks.heading: Why startups beat jobs on risk: Y Combinator's early success data
chunks.text:
- Paul reports on the first YC batch (summer 2005, eight startups): at least four succeeded. Three were acquired (Reddit, a merger of Reddit and Infogami, plus one he can't name yet) and a fourth, Loopt, was doing well enough to be acquired "in about ten minutes."
- He won't predict that 50% rate will hold, since the first batch "could have been an anomaly." He would "feel safe aiming at 25%," versus the "oft-quoted (and probably made up) standard figure of 10%."
- Kiko was the closest to a traumatic failure: the founders worked on it for a year before being "squashed by Google Calendar." They sold the software on eBay for a quarter of a million dollars, repaid their angels, kept about a year's salary each, and started Justin.TV. Angels held convertible debt, so YC only got 38 cents on the dollar.
- Even failed founders did fine. Two others just moved on to other things after the summer.
- His key statistic: 0% of that batch had a terrible experience, and he expects the share who wish they'd taken a regular job to stay near 0%.
- The puzzle: YC gets only several hundred applications per cycle, not thousands, and most programmers still go "straight from college to cubicle."

chunks.heading: Handling uncertainty about founding: break it into components
chunks.text:
- Paul says YC, sitting at the very start of the funding process, is probably the leading expert on people unsure whether to start a company.
- Uncertainty is normal. Larry and Sergey hesitated before Google, as did Jerry and Filo before Yahoo. He guesses the most successful startups are started by "uncertain hackers rather than gung-ho business guys."
- Evidence: several of YC's most successful startups decided to apply at the last moment, some only hours before the deadline.
- Method: most reluctant people have about eight reasons tangled together. Analyze them into components, decide which are justified and which are bogus, and only then judge whether the overall doubt is mostly real.
- He says he is motivated to be honest, unlike confidence-building sellers who are paid when you buy. If he encourages the wrong people to apply, it only creates more applications for him to read.
- His approach is negative: go through the reasons you aren't doing it and show why most (not all) should be ignored.

chunks.heading: Too young, too inexperienced, not determined or smart enough
chunks.text:
- **Too young:** YC tried to find the lower bound on founder age and found it fuzzy. The limit may be as low as 16; YC doesn't look below 18 because minors can't legally sign contracts. Sam Altman, the most successful founder funded so far, was 19.
- Age matters less than whether you've crossed the "adult" threshold. Two tests: (1) the kid flake reflex, where a kid says "I can't do it" and gets let off while adults are "ruthlessly pruned" for flaking. (2) Reaction to challenge: told "that's a stupid idea," a kid submits or rebels (rebelling also presumes inferiority); an adult says "Really? Why do you think so?"
- **Too inexperienced:** he used to say founders should be 23 and work a few years first, and no longer believes it. He still thinks 23 beats 21, but "the best way to get experience if you're 21 is to start a startup." A normal job may turn you "into a tame animal who thinks he needs an office to work in and a product manager to tell him what software to write."
- Proof: the Kiko founders made many mistakes, but a year later were "extremely formidable." Working at Microsoft or Google they'd have stayed "diffident junior programmers." His advice is to start right out of college.
- **Not determined enough:** determination is "probably the single best predictor of success." Hackers usually underestimate theirs. Several founders who would first have been delighted with a $2 million acquisition became set on world domination. Test: are you driven to work on your own projects, as Larry and Sergey were?
- **Not smart enough:** if you worry about it, you probably are smart enough. Most companies do mundane work where "the decisive factor is effort, not brains." If you can't do technically hard work, write enterprise software: "Enterprise software companies aren't technology companies, they're sales companies, and sales depends mostly on effort."

chunks.heading: You don't need to know business; build what people want
chunks.text:
- Paul says the coefficient on business knowledge "should be zero." Focus on the product; making money is "so easy you can pick it up on the fly."
- Evidence: "pretty much 100% of startups that make something popular manage to make money from it." Acquirers tell him privately they buy for strategic value, meaning the product people want, not revenue. "If users love you, you can always make money from that somehow, and if they don't, the cleverest business model in the world won't save you."
- People argue with him partly because they hate the idea that twenty-year-olds could get rich building something cool that makes no money.
- Principle: "The most valuable truths are the ones most people don't believe. They're like undervalued stocks." When you find a good idea most people disagree with, push aggressively in that direction. Here: seek ideas that would be popular but seem hard to monetize.
- YC's stance: "We'll bet a seed round you can't make something popular that we can't figure out how to make money from."

chunks.heading: Cofounders and ideas
chunks.text:
- **No cofounder** is a real problem: "A startup is too much for one person to bear." All investors, without exception, are more likely to fund you with a cofounder.
- YC funded two single founders and told both to find a cofounder first; both did. YC would rather founders already have cofounders committed enough to sign up for something hard.
- Advice: get one, since it's more important than anything else. Move to where people want to start startups, or switch to an idea people want to work on.
- Best time to find one is school, with a big pool. Keep in touch with friends you schemed with. Conferences and user groups are unlikely to work, because you need to work with someone to know. An open source project may be the best way to test this.
- **No idea:** in the average YC startup, he guesses 70% of the idea is new after three months, sometimes 100%. YC was going to let applicants answer "We have no idea." It puts little weight on the idea and cares about "what cool things you've made." Lead developer of a popular open source project counts almost as much.
- Recipe for ideas: "Find something that's missing in your own life, and supply that need—no matter how specific to you it seems." Wozniak built himself a computer. "A need that's narrow but genuine is a better starting point than one that's broad but hypothetical."

chunks.heading: Fallacies and real reasons not to start: room, family, wealth, commitment, structure
chunks.text:
- **No room for more startups** is a fallacy. No one claims a limit on people working for salary at 1000-person companies, so why a limit on those working for equity at 5-person ones? Needs don't go away when companies shrink, wealth wants keep rising, and acquirers will "evolve to consume" any value founders will trade for upside.
- **Family to support** is real. He won't advise anyone with a family to start a startup, though he will tell 22-year-olds. Options: start a consulting business and gradually turn it into a product business (chances "very small," never Google, but you keep income), or join an early startup, where you are "roughly 1/n^2 founder" (n is employee number).
- **Independently wealthy:** his own excuse. Startups are stressful and "you can't do it half-heartedly." What makes a founder dangerous is "willingness to endure infinite schleps." Serial entrepreneurs are often driven by wanting to work with interesting people who aren't rich.
- **Not ready for commitment** is legitimate. A successful startup consumes at least three or four years. But a regular job often lasts as long and leaves less spare time than expected.
- **Need for structure:** if you need someone to tell you what to do, don't start or join one. Until about twelve people, no one should tell anyone what to do. He compares it to soccer: David Beckham said language was never a problem at Real Madrid because "everyone was so good they never had to talk." Test: if you'd bristle at being told you aren't independent-minded, you probably are.

chunks.heading: Risk, failure, and why a job isn't the safe default
chunks.text:
- **Fear of uncertainty:** his framing is "if you start a startup, it will probably fail... Hope for the best, but expect the worst. In the worst case, it will at least be interesting."
- Failure carries little stigma in the US. Managers at big companies told him they'd prefer to hire someone who tried a startup and failed over someone who spent the same time at a big company. Investors don't hold it against you unless you failed from laziness or "incurable stupidity."
- **Not realizing what you avoid:** summer tech internships aren't real jobs, since firms hire students to recruit them, not for labor. Real jobs mean boring work and the expectation of being present at set hours, including days "you have absolutely no desire to work on anything" and must "pretend to." In a startup, work and life mix and you never have to pretend.
- **Parents want you to be a doctor:** parents are more conservative for their kids because they share more of the bad luck than the good, but "reward is proportionate to risk," so protecting kids from risk also protects them from rewards. Parents also "fight the last war": doctor prestige is dated. Treat their opinions "like feature requests": work out what they need and see if there's a better way to deliver it.
- **A job is the default:** defaults are powerful because they need no conscious choice. The job-as-default is only about a hundred years old; before that it was farming. Paul thinks startups may signal a historic shift in how wealth is created, like the move from farming to manufacturing. He says that is why he works on YC: "It would be an amazing hack to make one happen faster."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Paul Graham names the "fatal pinch": a startup with about 6 months of runway, high burn and weak revenue growth that assumes it can raise more money. Founders overestimate investor interest, so he advises treating the odds of a raise as zero and then either cutting costs or making money in a different way, including consultingish work.

chunks.heading: When a startup is in the fatal pinch
chunks.text:
- Paul defines the "fatal pinch" as the point, a few months before many startups die, where the company has a significant amount of money in the bank but is losing a lot each month, and revenue growth is nonexistent or mediocre.
- Typical example: about 6 months of runway, or "6 months before they're out of business."
- The founders expect to escape by raising more from investors. Paul: "That last sentence is the fatal one."
- He admits he tries to resist coining phrases, but names this situation so founders may realize when they are in it.
- Exception: a handful of companies can't reasonably expect revenue for the first year or two because what they build takes so long. For them, substitute "progress" for "revenue growth."
  - A company is one of these only if its initial investors agreed in advance that it was.
  - Even these companies wish they weren't, because the illiquidity of "progress" puts them at investors' mercy.

chunks.heading: Why the second fundraise is much harder than the first
chunks.text:
- Paul says founders are prone to delude themselves about how interested investors will be in giving them additional funding. They expect the first raise to be hard but not the second.
- Three forces combine the second time:
  1. The company is spending more than it did when it first raised.
  2. Investors hold companies that have already raised to much higher standards.
  3. The company is starting to read as a failure. At the first raise it was too early to call it a success or failure. Now the question can be asked, and "the default answer is failure, because at this point that is the default outcome."

chunks.heading: Why the pinch is self-reinforcing, and how to avoid it
chunks.text:
- Founders overestimate their chances of raising more, so they are slack about reaching profitability, which further lowers their chances of raising.
- Y Combinator's advice: founders who raise money should act as if it's the last they'll ever get.
- The loop also works in reverse: "the less you need further investment, the easier it is to get."

chunks.heading: What to do if you're already in the pinch
chunks.text:
- Step one is to re-evaluate the probability of raising more money. Paul's estimate: "the probability is zero."
- Variant: existing investors seem to promise more money. Often the founder reads them as promising, while the investors think they are only mentioning the possibility.
  - Fix, if you have 8 months of runway or less: try to get the money right now.
  - Either you get it, which solves the immediate problem, or you stop investors from helping you stay in denial about your fundraising prospects.
- Three options remain: shut down, increase revenue, or decrease spending.
- Shut down only if you're certain the company will fail no matter what you do. Then you can return the remaining money and save the months you'd spend riding it down.
- Paul notes companies rarely have to fail, and that the shutdown option mostly gives founders a chance to admit they've already given up.

chunks.heading: Cutting costs: firing, salaries and overhiring
chunks.text:
- In most startups, expenses = people, so cutting expenses means firing people.
- Eliminate significant non-salary expenses first, if there are any.
- The easiest firing decision: people you already know you should fire but are in denial about. If that gets you to profitability, or lets you reach it on the money left, the immediate danger is avoided.
- Otherwise the options are firing good people, getting some or all employees to take less salary, or increasing revenue.
- Pay cuts are a weak solution.
  - They work only when the problem isn't too bad, for example when a small cut gets you over the profitability threshold and you can make that case to everyone.
  - Otherwise you're probably just postponing the problem, and the affected people will see that.
  - Exception: if the founders' own high salaries are the problem, cut them to the minimum you need. Paul says it's a bad sign if you needed this essay to realize that.
- Lean toward firing if the trouble comes from overhiring.
  - Example: hiring 15 people before you knew what you were building "created a broken company."
  - Figuring out the product is probably easier with a handful of people, and those 15 may not be the ones you need anyway.
  - The solution may be to shrink, then figure out what direction to grow in.
  - He argues you're not doing those people favors by flying the company into the ground with them aboard, since they eventually lose their jobs and the time spent on a doomed company.
- Keep the eventual goal in mind: to be a successful product company, "having a single thing lots of people use."

chunks.heading: Making money differently: everyone sells, and consultingish work
chunks.text:
- With only a handful of people, focus on making more money, not by trying harder but by making money in a different way.
- Example: if one person sells while the rest write code, have everyone work on selling. "What good will more code do you when you're out of business?"
  - Write code only if it's needed to close a specific deal. Work only on whatever gets the most revenue soonest.
- Sell different things, especially more "consultingish" work.
  - Between making products and pure consulting is a long slippery slope, and you don't have to go far down it before offering something attractive to customers.
  - Startup programmers are often far better than the ones customers have, or the startup may have expertise in a new field customers don't understand.
  - Shift the sales conversation from "do you want to buy our product?" to "what do you need that you'd pay a lot for?" and it may become much easier to extract money.
- Be "ruthlessly mercenary": make customers pay a lot, quickly.
- Avoid the worst pitfalls of consulting. The ideal setup is a precisely defined derivative version of your product built for the customer, otherwise a straight product sale: you keep the IP and there is no hourly billing.
- Best case, this work becomes the "thing-that-doesn't-scale" that defines the company. Don't expect it, but as you dive into individual users' needs, watch for "narrow openings that have wide vistas beyond."

chunks.heading: The slippery slope and surviving with least damage
chunks.text:
- Demand for custom work is so large that, unless you're really incompetent, there is some point down the consulting slope at which you can survive.
- Customers' insatiable demand for custom work will keep pushing you toward the bottom of the slope. The problem then becomes surviving with the least damage and distraction.
- Plenty of successful startups have passed through near-death experiences and gone on to flourish. The key is realizing in time that you're near death, "and if you're in the fatal pinch, you are."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Paul Graham argues that mean founders tend to fail because meanness makes you stupid, repels the best hires, and clashes with the benevolent drive that sustains great companies. As the games that matter shift from zero-sum control of scarce resources to building new things, the historical advantage of meanness is reversing.

chunks.heading: Why meanness correlates with failure in startups
chunks.text:
Paul noticed that almost none of the most successful people he knows are mean, and that Jessica Livingston (his wife and Y Combinator cofounder) sees the same pattern. She came from investment banking and is struck by "how consistently successful startup founders turn out to be good people, and how consistently bad people fail as startup founders."

- Meanness isn't rare. The internet exposed the "long tail of meanness" that used to be hidden.
- He admits selection bias: he only knows startup founders, programmers and professors. He allows that hedge fund managers or drug lords may be mean and successful.
- His claim is narrower: there are big chunks of the world that mean people don't rule, and that territory is growing.

chunks.heading: Being mean makes you stupid, and fights waste your brain
chunks.text:
Paul hates fights because "being mean makes you stupid."

- Winning a fight is a function of the specific situation and people involved. You win with tricks that work in one particular case, not with big ideas.
- Fighting takes as much effort as thinking about real problems, but it produces nothing general. His image: "your brain goes fast but you get nowhere, like a car spinning its wheels."
- He says you never do your best work in a fight.
- Startups "don't win by attacking. They win by transcending." Usually the way to win is to race ahead, not stop and fight.

chunks.heading: Mean founders can't hire the best people
chunks.text:
- A mean founder can hire people who tolerate him because they need a job.
- The best people have other options. A mean person can't persuade them to join unless he is "super convincing."
- Having the best people helps any organization, but Paul says it is critical for startups.

chunks.heading: Benevolence is an advantage in building great things
chunks.text:
- The richest founders are not the ones driven by money. Those driven by money take the big acquisition offer that nearly every successful startup gets along the way.
- The founders who keep going are driven by something else. They may not say so, but they are usually trying to improve the world, so people with that desire have a natural advantage.
- Caveats he adds: founders who don't take the offer aren't driven only by money, and money can have benevolent motives (supporting family, freedom to work on projects that improve the world).
- Not every successful startup improves the world, but founders, like parents, truly believe theirs does. Successful founders are in love with their companies, and that love is as blind as romantic love but genuine.

chunks.heading: The shift from zero-sum to non-zero-sum games
chunks.text:
Paul argues startups are the future of work, not a random niche.

- For most of history, success meant controlling scarce resources, won by fighting: literally (pastoral nomads driving hunter-gatherers into marginal lands) or metaphorically (Gilded Age financiers assembling railroad monopolies). In those zero-sum games meanness was probably an advantage.
- Increasingly the games that matter are not zero-sum. You win by "having new ideas and building new things" rather than seizing a scarce resource.
- Peter Thiel's counterpoint, which Paul accepts as largely true: successful founders still get rich from monopolies, but ones they create rather than capture. Paul says this still means a big change in who wins.

chunks.heading: Why this shift needs civil order
chunks.text:
- Ideas only win when people feel what they create can't be stolen. That requires more than absence of war: it also means preventing economic violence like that of nineteenth-century magnates or communist states against their citizens.
- Archimedes won by ideas, until an invading Roman army killed him (by accident; the Roman commander had ordered him spared).
- In sufficiently disordered times, "even thinking requires control of scarce resources, because living at all is a scarce resource."
- Thinkers were first to benefit: the non-ruthless successful figures of history are mathematicians, writers and artists. Paul says their way of operating is leaking into the real world, "reversing the historical polarity of the relationship between meanness and success."

chunks.heading: Paul's takeaway for parenting
chunks.text:
- He and Jessica teach their kids not to be mean. They tolerate noise, mess and junk food, but not meanness.
- The essay gave him an extra argument for cracking down: "being mean makes you fail."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Graham argues there is really one cause of startup death: not making something users want. He lists 18 controllable mistakes that feed into it, from single founders and derivative ideas to slow launches, bad fundraising and half-hearted effort. The deepest cause he names is not trying hard enough.

chunks.heading: Single founder, location, and co-founders
chunks.text:
- **One founder is a warning sign.** Paul notes that few successful startups had a single founder, and even "Oracle" usually turns out to have more. It reads as a vote of no confidence: the founder could not talk any friends into joining.
- **Brainstorming and morale.** Founders need colleagues to brainstorm with, to "talk you out of stupid decisions," and to cheer them up. The low points are "so low that few could bear them alone."
- **Esprit de corps.** With several founders, each thinks "I can't let my friends down." Paul calls this one of the most powerful forces in human nature, and a solo founder lacks it.
- **Location matters.** Startups prosper in Silicon Valley first, then Boston, Seattle, Austin, Denver and New York. Even New York has probably a 20th of Silicon Valley's startups per capita. Houston, Chicago and Detroit are too small to measure.
- **Why hubs win.** That is where the experts are. Standards are higher, people are more sympathetic, the right hires want to live there, supporting industries are there, and chance meetings are with people in the same business.

chunks.heading: Choosing the idea: avoid marginal niches and imitations
chunks.text:
- **Marginal niche (mistake 3).** Most Y Combinator applicants pick a small, obscure niche hoping to avoid competition. Paul compares it to a child afraid of the ball in outfield, who holds up the glove "for protection" rather than to catch. "You can only avoid competition by avoiding good ideas."
- **The fear is unconscious.** Founders do not consciously reject grand ideas; their unconscious will not let them think of them. His fix: imagine a great startup idea for *someone else* to do.
- **Derivative idea (mistake 4).** Many applications imitate an existing company. Few successful startups started as imitations. Most began with a specific unsolved problem the founders identified.
- **Examples of problem-first origins:**
  - His own startup made software for building online stores, when sites were hand-made by consultants at great expense. If online shopping took off, stores would have to be generated by software.
  - Apple: Wozniak wanted a computer.
  - Google: Larry and Sergey couldn't find stuff online.
  - Hotmail: Bhatia and Smith couldn't exchange email at work.
- **Method.** Don't start from companies and work back to problems. Start from problems and imagine the company that solves them. Ask what people complain about and what you wish existed.

chunks.heading: Know your user and stay flexible on the plan
chunks.text:
- **No specific user in mind (mistake 10).** Perhaps "you create wealth in proportion to how well you understand the problem you're solving, and the problems you understand best are your own." The converse is not a theory: "if you're trying to solve problems you don't understand, you're hosed."
- **Vague target markets are a red flag.** Teenagers, "people interested in local events" (a "perennial tarpit"), or "business" users. Which business users? Gas stations, movie studios, defense contractors?
- **If you build for others, fly on instruments.** Shift gears consciously and be empirical. You cannot guess what will work, so find users and measure their responses. If you cannot talk specific users into using it, "you're on the wrong track."
- **Obstinacy (mistake 5).** Sticking to a vision works for something well-defined like an Olympic gold medal. Startups are "more like science, where you need to follow the trail wherever it leads." The original plan is probably wrong, and most successful startups end up doing something so different it barely seems the same company.
- **Tune openness correctly.** Switching ideas weekly is equally fatal. Test: does each new idea reuse most of what you built before? Then the process converges. Restarting from scratch each time is a bad sign.
- **Ask your users.** If you consider a new direction and users seem excited, it is probably a good bet.

chunks.heading: Hiring and platform choices
chunks.text:
- **Bad programmers (mistake 6).** Most founders he knows are programmers, so this is rarely fatal for them; they can do the work themselves in a pinch. It killed many 1990s e-commerce startups run by business people who thought you "had some clever idea and then hired programmers to implement it."
- **Why it fails.** Business founders can't tell good programmers from bad (a resume line like "Microsoft Certified Developer"), and no one really good wants to implement a business person's vision. Such a startup "lumbers along like a World War II bomber while competitors scream past like jet fighters." He admits he has no answer for how a non-programmer picks good programmers.
- **Wrong platform (mistake 7).** Platform can mean an OS, language or framework; it both supports and limits, like a foundation.
- **Examples:**
  - Many Bubble-era startups built server apps on Windows.
  - Hotmail kept running on FreeBSD for years after Microsoft bought it, presumably because Windows couldn't handle the load.
  - PayPal's new CEO wanted to switch to Windows even after Max Levchin showed their software scaled only 1% as well on Windows as Unix. PayPal switched CEOs instead.
  - Java applets "killed just about 100% of the startups who believed" in them.
- **How to pick.** Hire good programmers and let them choose. If you aren't a programmer, visit a top computer science department and see what they use in research projects.

chunks.heading: Launching: not too slow, not too early
chunks.text:
- **Slowness (mistake 8).** Software is "always 85% done," and it takes an effort of will to release. Test of an excuse: if the software were 100% finished and launchable at the push of a button, would you still be waiting?
- **Two reasons to launch fast.**
  - It forces you to finish a quantum of work. Nothing is finished until released.
  - Only by bouncing the idea off users do you fully understand it.
- **Delays hide several problems:** working too slowly, not understanding the problem, fear of dealing with users, fear of being judged, working on too many things, and perfectionism. The cure is to force yourself to launch *something* fairly quickly.
- **Launching too early (mistake 9).** Slowness has killed "a hundred times more startups" than speed, but a weak launch can ruin your reputation because early adopters may never come back.
- **Minimum to launch.** Identify a core that is (a) useful on its own and (b) incrementally expandable into the whole project, and finish it ASAP. Early adopters are tolerant: the product has to do *something*, not everything.

chunks.heading: Money: raising, spending, and managing investors
chunks.text:
- **Funding is measured in time (mistake 11).** Runway: when it runs out you are "airborne or dead." Raise enough to reach the next visible step: prototype if you have an idea, launch if you have a prototype, significant growth if launched.
- **Take more than you think.** Note: 50% to 100% more, because software takes longer to write and deals longer to close. Advice: keep both spending and the first goal low, with the initial goal a solid prototype.
- **Spending too much (mistake 12).** Hard to separate from raising too little; "if you raised five million and ran out of money, you probably spent too much." Hiring is the classic burn, and it also slows you down (Brooks, *The Mythical Man-Month*).
- **Three hiring rules:**
  - Don't hire if you can avoid it.
  - Pay with equity rather than salary, to attract committed people.
  - Hire only people who will write code or get users.
- **Raising too much (mistake 13).** Quote from a VC: "Once you take several million dollars of my money, the clock is ticking." You move to proper offices and hire employees, who are less committed and bring politics. "When you raise a lot of money, your company moves to the suburbs and has kids."
- **Harder to pivot.** With a sales force built for companies, you won't notice you should sell to consumers. Large raises also take enormous time, and VCs "never quite say yes or no."
- **Take the first reasonable deal.** From a reputable firm, at a reasonable valuation, without onerous terms: "Who cares if you could get a 30% better deal elsewhere?" Startups are all-or-nothing, so bargain-hunting wastes time. (Caveat: some VCs lowball to test you, so push back a bit.)
- **Investor management (mistake 14).** Don't ignore investors, since they may have insights, but don't let them run the company. "If investors had sufficient vision to run the companies they fund, why didn't they start them?" Ignoring them is less dangerous than caving.
- **Control follows money.** At VC scale, a board majority makes them your bosses; with an even board, they only need to convince the outside directors. Apple's board fired Steve Jobs, and Google reportedly got grief from investors early on.

chunks.heading: Users before profit, and doing the dirty work
chunks.text:
- **Don't sacrifice users to profit (mistake 15).** The business model isn't unimportant; making something people want is simply much harder. Leave the model for later "just as you'd leave some trivial but messy feature for version 2."
- **Core problem.** Create wealth (= how much people want something x the number who want it), not convert wealth into money. Google made search work first, then worried about monetization.
- **Key line:** "It *is* irresponsible not to think about business models. It's just ten times more irresponsible not to think about the product."
- **Getting your hands dirty (mistake 16).** Most programmers prefer ideas to the messy business side. Larry and Sergey first tried to sell their algorithm to another company. But "there's not much of a market for ideas"; no one trusts one until you embody it in a product with users.
- **Users convince acquirers.** Acquirers can tell themselves they're buying users rather than cleverness. Example: Google paid $1.6 billion for YouTube 18 months after the founders could not have sold the same advice for $10 million.
- **Go find users.** In the summer 2005 YC batch, one startup's founder spent half his time pursuing deals with cell phone executives, and it was the most successful of the group "by an order of magnitude." At least one hacker must do business stuff.

chunks.heading: Founder fights and half-hearted effort
chunks.text:
- **Founder fights (mistake 17).** About 20% of YC-funded startups had a founder leave. YC now advises founders to vest, giving an orderly way to quit, though it doesn't require it.
- **Departures are survivable.** The least committed founder usually leaves. Blogger got down to one person and bounced back; Apple originally had three founders.
- **Choose co-founders carefully.** Most disputes come from the people, not the situation. Don't suppress misgivings; fix problems before the company starts. Don't add your housemate so he won't feel left out, and don't partner with someone you dislike for a skill you need: "The people are the most important ingredient in a startup."
- **Half-hearted effort (mistake 18).** The most common failure is a side project that is gradually abandoned. Most founders of failed startups kept their day jobs; most successful founders quit.
- **Interpretation.** Many would-be founders may lack the needed determination and know it. But he guesses the number who could have made it by quitting is perhaps an order of magnitude larger than the number who do.
- **Conclusion.** "Most startups fail because they don't make something people want, and the reason most don't is that they don't try hard enough." He admits he lacked the determination himself, bailing twice since Viaweb "without the spur of poverty."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Graham distills startup advice into 13 principles, from picking cofounders and launching fast to spending little and never giving up. If he had to keep one, it would be understanding your users, since it underlies launching early, evolving the idea, serving a few users deeply and good customer service.

chunks.heading: Cofounders and early launch as the foundation
chunks.text:
- Paul tells startups to pick good cofounders. His analogy: "Cofounders are for a startup what location is for real estate. You can change anything about a house except where it is."
- A startup's idea is easy to change; its cofounders are hard to change. He says "the success of a startup is almost always a function of its founders."
- He tells startups to launch fast. The reason is less about getting to market early and more that "you haven't really started working on it till you've launched."
- Launching teaches founders what they should have been building. Until they know that, they are wasting their time.
- He sees the main value of the initial launch as a pretext for engaging users.

chunks.heading: Let the idea evolve and understand users
chunks.text:
- Paul calls launching fast and letting the idea evolve two halves of one practice: launch fast and iterate.
- He calls it a big mistake to treat a startup as implementing some brilliant initial idea. "As in an essay, most of the ideas appear in the implementing."
- He pictures the wealth a startup creates as a rectangle: one side is the number of users, the other is how much the startup improves their lives. Founders have the most control over the second side, and growth in the first is driven by how well they do on the second.
- He says the hard part is asking questions, not answering them: seeing something new that users lack. The better founders understand users, the better the odds of seeing it.
- That is why many successful startups make something the founders themselves needed.
- If he could keep only one of the 13 principles, it would be "Understand your users." Once you know what to make, "it's mere effort to make it, and most decent hackers are capable of that."
- Understanding users sits behind half the list: launching early, evolving the idea, surprisingly good customer service, and morale ("having just ten users who love you will keep you going").

chunks.heading: Make a few users love you, and serve them surprisingly well
chunks.text:
- Paul learned from Paul Buchheit that it is better to make a few people really happy than a lot of people semi-happy.
- Early on, a startup must choose between satisfying all the needs of a subset of potential users or a subset of the needs of all potential users. His advice: take the first.
- Reason one: "It's easier to expand userwise than satisfactionwise."
- Reason two: it is harder to lie to yourself. If you think you are 85% of the way to a great product, you cannot tell whether it is 70% or 10%, but you can easily know how many users you have.
- He says to offer customer service that is not merely good but surprisingly good. Customers are used to being maltreated by quasi-monopolies, which unconsciously lowers founders' ideas of what is possible.
- Go out of your way to make people happy; "they'll be overwhelmed."
- In the earliest stages it pays to offer service that would not scale, because it is a way of learning about users.

chunks.heading: Measure what you want to improve
chunks.text:
- Paul learned "you make what you measure" from Joe Kraus. Merely measuring something tends to improve it.
- His tactic for growing users: put a big piece of paper on the wall and plot the number of users every day.
- Founders will be delighted when it goes up and disappointed when it goes down. Soon they notice what moves the number and do more of it.
- His corollary: be careful what you measure.

chunks.heading: Spend little and get ramen profitable
chunks.text:
- Paul stresses that a startup must be cheap. Most startups fail before they make something people want, and the most common form of failure is running out of money.
- He says being cheap is almost interchangeable with iterating rapidly. It is not exactly the same, because markets do not stand still: working twice as fast is better than having twice as much time.
- A culture of cheapness keeps companies young "in something like the way exercise keeps people young."
- "Ramen profitable" means the startup makes just enough to pay the founders' living expenses.
- He frames it as a way of hacking the investment process more than rapid prototyping of business models. Once crossed, it completely changes the relationship with investors, and it is great for morale.

chunks.heading: Avoid distractions, morale killers and falling-through deals
chunks.text:
- Paul says nothing kills startups like distractions. The worst are those that pay money: day jobs, consulting, profitable side projects. Founders keep interrupting the startup to answer calls from people paying them now.
- He calls fundraising this same kind of distraction, so founders should minimize it too.
- The immediate cause of death is usually running out of money, but the underlying cause is usually lack of focus. Either the people are stupid (which advice cannot fix) or smart people got demoralized.
- Starting a startup is a huge moral weight. He advises making a conscious effort not to be ground down, "just as you'd be careful to bend at the knees when picking up a heavy box."
- Even if demoralized, don't give up: "You can get surprisingly far by just not giving up." He notes this is not true in all fields (some people could never become good mathematicians however long they persisted), but in startups sheer effort is usually enough "so long as you keep morphing your idea."
- Deals fall through. At Viaweb, he says, they probably had 20 deals of various types fall through. After the first 10 or so they treated deals as background processes to ignore until they terminated.
- Depending on deals closing is dangerous for morale, because they often don't close, and depending on them makes them less likely to.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Paul Graham argues that wealth is what people want, not money, and that startups let small groups of ambitious people work as hard as possible on hard technical problems and get paid in proportion. The recipe is measurement (small teams) and leverage (new technology), with users as the test of whether you created wealth.

chunks.heading: How startups create wealth: compressing a working life
chunks.text:
- Paul treats a startup as a way to compress a whole working life into a few years: "Instead of working at a low intensity for forty years, you work as hard as you possibly can for four." This pays especially well in technology.
- He defines a startup as "a small company that takes on a hard technical problem."
- Back-of-envelope: a good hacker in their mid twenties earns about $80,000 a year, so must produce at least that much value to break even.
  - 2x from working twice the hours
  - 3x from more output per focused hour
  - 2x from removing the drag of a middle manager
  - 3x from being smarter than the job description expects
  - Combined: 36x, so about $3 million a year of work.
- He does not defend the exact numbers but stands by the structure: the multiplier is "certainly more than 10, and probably rarely as high as 100." $3 million is the limit case, working so hard you endanger your health.
- Startups are not magic. There is a conservation law: "if you want to make a million dollars, you have to endure a million dollars' worth of pain." A startup just compresses the pain into three or four years.

chunks.heading: Wealth versus money, and the Pie Fallacy
chunks.text:
- Wealth is "stuff we want": food, clothes, houses, gadgets, travel. Money is a medium of exchange, a side effect of specialization and a shorthand for moving wealth around.
- Most businesses do not really make money; they make wealth, meaning they do something people want.
- The Pie Fallacy is the belief that there is a fixed amount of wealth. There is a fixed amount of money in a family's account at a given moment, but not of wealth. Restoring a beat-up car creates wealth without making anyone poorer. "If you plan to start a startup... you're planning to disprove the Pie Fallacy."
- Programmers see this most clearly because they create wealth directly, one line at a time.
  - At Viaweb one programmer was "a sort of monster of productivity" who added several hundred thousand dollars to the company's market value in a long day.
  - A great programmer on a roll can create a million dollars of wealth in a couple of weeks. A mediocre one creates zero or negative wealth.
  - "The top 5% of programmers probably write 99% of the good software."
- Wealth can also be donated: penicillin, FreeBSD and open source software all make people richer without being sold.

chunks.heading: Skepticism about founder-centric ideas
chunks.text:
- Because wealth is whatever people want, and "what people will give you money for depends on them, not you," Paul says to be especially skeptical of plans centered on things you like doing.
- Example: a woman at the Internet Bubble who liked the outdoors wanted to start an "outdoor portal." His quip: if you like the outdoors, start a business recovering data from crashed hard disks.
- When starting a business it is easy to slide into thinking customers want what you do. Your idea of what is valuable is least likely to match other people's where your own enjoyment is involved.

chunks.heading: Measurement and leverage: why big companies cap what you can earn
chunks.text:
- To get rich you need two things: **measurement** (your performance can be measured, so doing more pays more) and **leverage** (your decisions have a big effect).
- Measurement without leverage is sweatshop piecework: you decide only how fast to work, which might raise earnings 2-3x.
- Both together: lead actor in a movie, CEO, hedge fund manager, professional athlete. A hint that leverage exists is the possibility of failure: "If you're in a job that feels safe, you are not going to get rich."
- Big companies cannot value individual work because contributions are tangled together (engineers, designers, marketers all feed one gadget's sales). So they punt and pay a predictable salary for fairly hard work. Exceptions are sales (revenue is measurable, paid as a percentage) and top management.
- A company that could pay everyone proportionally to the wealth they create would attract people who want to work especially hard and "crush its competitors." In a footnote: "A company will be maximally profitable when each employee is paid in proportion to the wealth they generate."
- You cannot tell your boss "I'd like to work ten times as hard, so pay me ten times as much." A startup is the closest equivalent, except you say it directly to customers, along with a small group of ambitious peers.

chunks.heading: Smallness, the all-star team and the galley
chunks.text:
- Revenue can be measured at the level of the whole company. A viable startup might have ten employees, which puts you within a factor of ten of measuring individual effort.
- Galley analogy: a big company is a galley of a thousand rowers. Individual rowers see no result from working harder, and the average rower is average. Ten rowers in their own boat get carrot and stick. Ten of the best rowers, each in the top 1%, get a far better deal averaging with peers than with everyone.
- "You don't want small in the sense of a village, but small in the sense of an all-star team." A startup is "not merely ten people, but ten people like you."
- He agrees with Steve Jobs that success depends on the first ten employees: "If anything, it's more like the first five." The people must be good because their work is what yours is averaged with.
- The larger a group, the closer its average member is to the population average, so a very able person who cares about money usually does better with a small group of peers.
- Startups also give "uninterruptability" (footnote): hacking has a long time quantum, perhaps an hour to load a problem into your head. Startups lack the personnel department and other interrupters.

chunks.heading: Technology as leverage, and running upstairs
chunks.text:
- Technology is technique. Solving a technical problem many people care about multiplies value by everyone who uses it, "the fishing rod rather than the fish." That is the difference between a startup and a restaurant or barber shop, which serve one customer at a time.
- Historical examples: Florence in 1200 (new techniques for fine woven cloth), the Dutch in 1600 (shipbuilding and navigation).
- Non-obvious technology: McDonald's franchise rules are "practically a piece of software. Write once, run everywhere." Sam Walton "got rich not by being a retailer, but by designing a new kind of store."
- Small companies suit fast-moving technology because they lack bureaucracy and are less bound by convention. Big companies develop technology mainly where capital requirements keep startups out (microprocessors, power plants, passenger aircraft).
- Viaweb's rule of thumb was **run upstairs**. A nimble guy chased by a big bully should go up the stairs, since climbing hurts the bully more.
  - If two features were equally valuable in proportion to their difficulty, they always took the harder one, "because it was harder."
  - Wrestling all day with a horrible technical problem was a good sign: "something that was hard for us would be impossible for our competitors."
- This is what VCs mean by barriers to entry: how hard would this be for someone else to develop? You need a convincing reason your technology is hard to duplicate, or a big company will copy it with its brand, capital and distribution.
- Patents offer weak protection: competitors work around them or violate them and invite a suit. Example: Philo Farnsworth invented television but RCA made the money. The best defense is "a good offense": pick a hard problem and take the harder choice at every decision point.
- He generalizes this to life: "If you have two choices, choose the harder." The only reason to consider the easier one is laziness.

chunks.heading: Risk, getting users, and getting bought
chunks.text:
- Catches: you cannot choose how hard to work, because competitors set it ("as hard as you possibly can"). And payoff is only proportionate on average: you may be 30x as productive and get paid between zero and a thousand times as much. "If the mean is 30x, the median is probably zero."
- A startup is like a mosquito: designed for one thing, to score, with no energy wasted on defense. It is all-or-nothing and you often don't know which until the last minute. Viaweb came close to tanking several times; its trajectory was like a sine wave, and it was bought at the top of the cycle. During the Yahoo sale talks they had to borrow a conference room to reassure an investor about to back out of a funding round.
- Viaweb's hackers were risk-averse and would have preferred a 100% chance of $1 million to a 20% chance of $10 million. The closest option is selling early for a smaller guaranteed payoff, but early-stage acquisitions are hard because acquirers are conservative and "would rather overpay for a safe choice." It is easier to sell an established startup, even at a large premium.
- He thinks getting bought is a good idea if you can: "Running a business is different from growing one," and selling lets you diversify.
- Acquirers are moved by fear of loss. The strongest motivator is the prospect that a competitor will buy you ("causes CEOs to take red-eyes"). Second is worry that you will keep growing and cost more later or become a competitor.
- Acquirers judge by **number of users**, not technology: "Users are the only real proof that you've created wealth."
- Paul's advice: make users the test and treat a startup as an optimization problem measured by number of users.
  - Guesses about what to optimize are almost always wrong; measurement is the key.
  - Number of users matters to acquirers, revenue, competitors, reporters and new users.
  - Avoid "techno-weenies" obsessed with interesting technical problems; solve problems users care about.
  - Avoid premature optimization: "Get a version 1.0 out there as soon as you can."
- In technology "you cook one thing and that's what everyone eats," so any gap between what people want and what you deliver is multiplied. Few companies pay attention to making customers happy.

chunks.heading: Why Bill Gates is a bad model, and wealth and power
chunks.text:
- Don't use famous billionaires as examples; press coverage favors outliers. Success has a large random factor: Gates was smart, dedicated and also lucky. Microsoft benefited from IBM's DOS licensing blunder; without it Gates would be "somewhere near the bottom of the Forbes 400."
- The essay is about getting rich by creating wealth, which is more legitimate and more straightforward than the alternatives: "You just have to do something people want."
- Wealth creation only became the main path once the rule of law let people keep what they made. In medieval Europe merchants in towns withstood feudal lords: "the bullies stopped stealing the nerds' lunch money."
- Paul argues that removing the incentive of wealth stalls technical innovation (the Soviet Union, Britain under 1960s-70s labor governments). Developing new technology is "one percent inspiration and ninety-nine percent perspiration," and mundane technologies like light bulbs and semiconductors get built by entrepreneurs.
- The recipe has been the same since Florence in 1200: measurement from a small group, leverage from new techniques. The same recipe that makes individuals rich makes countries powerful.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Graham argues the biggest startup ideas feel frightening, so most idea-hunters filter them out subconsciously. He sketches seven examples, then gives tactics: don't announce the giant goal, start with something deceptively small, and head "westward" like Columbus rather than plotting a precise future.

chunks.heading: Why the biggest startup ideas feel frightening
chunks.text:
- Paul says the most ambitious startup ideas are frightening, and that this is "one of the most important things you can understand about startups."
- The fear is not only about workload. The biggest ideas seem to threaten your identity, and you wonder whether you have the ambition to carry them through. He compares it to the line from *Being John Malkovich*: "If you ever got me, you wouldn't have a clue what to do with me."
- Big ideas tend to repel rather than attract. They are invisible to most people hunting for ideas because the subconscious filters them out.
- Even very ambitious founders are probably best off approaching these ideas obliquely.
- VCs miss this too. Most expect a founder to arrive with a clear plan for the future. Paul notes that in the biggest successes there is the least correlation between the initial plan and what the company becomes.

chunks.heading: Where to look: the "right side of impossible" and the future's view of us
chunks.text:
- Paul's rule of thumb is that the best ideas are "just on the right side of impossible."
- One of his idea-generating tricks is to imagine the ways we will seem backward to future generations, then build the fix. His example is that people 50 to 100 years from now will find it barbaric that we wait for symptoms before diagnosing heart disease or cancer.
- Another source is a dominant player that has lost its way. Microsoft lost the plot when it entered search out of fear of Google. That made Google set Microsoft's agenda, and the agenda was stuff Microsoft was not good at. He frames it as Microsoft : Google :: Google : Facebook.
- A good sign is when an idea is wrong in many ways at once. He likes the sufficiently smart compiler idea because the forum troll he has internalized "doesn't even know where to begin in raising objections."

chunks.heading: Search engine: win the top 10,000 hackers first
chunks.text:
- Paul sees cracks in Google's fortress. Its results used to be fast, uncluttered and right, "like the output of a Unix utility," and now feel cluttered and personalized. For the first time in over a decade, switching seems thinkable to him.
- The route is to build the search engine all the hackers use. A product whose users were only the top 10,000 hackers would be in a very powerful position, as Google was when it had that audience.
- Since anyone able to start this company is one of those 10,000 hackers, the instruction is to build the search engine you yourself want. Be excessively hackerish, for example by making code search excellent, or even making queries Turing complete.
- Constraints you create for the long term do not matter: "if you don't get that initial core of users, there won't be a long term."
- If you build something you and your friends genuinely prefer to Google, you are "about 10% of the way to an IPO, just as Facebook was" when it had the Harvard undergrads.

chunks.heading: Replacing email with a todo list protocol
chunks.text:
- Paul's framing is that email is not a messaging protocol. His inbox is a todo list and email is how things get onto it, and it is a disastrously bad todo list.
- He suspects tweaking the inbox is not enough and that a new protocol is needed.
- The new protocol should give the recipient more power:
  - Restrict what others can put on the todo list.
  - Require senders to say what they want from you, how important it is, and when it is due.
  - Include some mechanism to stop everyone from marking everything important.
  - Treat "read the following text" as a degenerate case.
- On adoption, he calls this an irresistible force meeting an immovable object. Entrenched protocols are hard to replace, but it is unlikely people in 100 years will still live in email hell, so why not now?
- He suggests the chicken-and-egg problem may be avoidable because some of the most powerful people in the world would switch first, since they are also at the mercy of email.
- Speed is a wedge. GMail has become painfully slow because Google cannot afford to spend much on it. Something no better than GMail but fast could pull users away.
- On pricing, he says people will pay for this. He would have no problem paying $50 a month. Given the hours he spends in email daily, he thinks he would be justified paying "at least $1000 a month."

chunks.heading: Replacing universities, and internet drama
chunks.text:
**Universities**
- He thinks universities will not disappear wholesale. They will lose their de facto monopoly on certain types of learning, and many new ways to learn will exist, some looking quite different. He cites Y Combinator as arguably one of them.
- If learning breaks into small pieces, credentialling may separate from it, and campus social life may need replacements.
- High schools could be replaced too, but bureaucratic obstacles would slow a startup, so universities are the place to start.

**Internet drama**
- He says the race between delivery mechanisms now has a winner: the Internet, not cable. He and his family replaced their TV with an iMac bolted to the wall because they hated the TV interface.
- Attention can be taken by unrelated things (social apps), closer things (games), but residual demand for passive conventional drama will remain.
- Whatever is made must be bigger than YouTube clips. Viewers want either a series with familiar characters or a longer "movie" with a known premise.
- Two ways delivery and payment could play out: a Netflix or Apple becomes the app store for entertainment, or those players overreach or are technically inflexible, and companies arise to supply payment and streaming a la carte to producers. In the second case there is also a need for infrastructure companies.

chunks.heading: The next Steve Jobs and bringing back Moore's Law
chunks.text:
**Next Steve Jobs**
- Paul asked someone who knew Apple well whether the current team could keep creating new things as under Jobs. The answer was a flat "no," with no qualification. Revenue may keep rising, but he notes "revenue is a lagging indicator in the technology business."
- No existing player is run by a product visionary, and "empirically you can't seem to get those by hiring them." The way you get one as CEO is for him to found the company and not get fired. So the next hardware wave likely comes from a startup.
- Aiming to be as big as Apple is no more ambitious than Apple becoming Apple, and a new startup has Apple as an example. He compares this to Roger Bannister (showing what is possible) and Augustus (making people believe one person could unroll the future).
- The "next Steve Jobs" only has to do a better job than Samsung, HP and Nokia, which he calls pretty doable.
- Tactical note: you may not want to start with consumer electronics. Start with something hackers use, or something popular but apparently unimportant like a headset or router. "All you need is a bridgehead."
