**Moore's Law**
- Moore's Law actually promises circuit densities doubling every 18 months, not clock speeds. Until about 2002 the misreading was harmless. Now Intel can give more CPUs, not faster ones, so slow software must be rewritten for parallelism.
- The idea: software that makes many CPUs look like one very fast CPU. The most ambitious version is a compiler that parallelizes code automatically, "the sufficiently smart compiler," a byword for impossibility. He argues that if you think it impossible you should try to prove it, and if it is merely hard, "the expected value would be high even if the chance of succeeding was low."
- Expected value is high because of web services: offering it as a service could capture practically all users, and since nobody sees server processors, it would be indistinguishable from being a processor maker that still turned density into clock speed.
- Approaches by ambition:
  - Least ambitious: offer parallelizable building blocks like Hadoop and MapReduce, with the programmer still optimizing.
  - Middle ground: a "semi-automatic weapon" with humans in the loop. It looks like the smart compiler to users but inside has people (employees, or a marketplace for optimization) using tools to find bottlenecks.
  - An optimization marketplace would build the compiler piecemeal as participants write bots, possibly with no one holding a complete copy.

chunks.heading: Ongoing automatic medical diagnosis
chunks.text:
- Paul expects this to face even greater resistance. His example: in 2004 Bill Clinton, presumably with the best care available, still had to wait until his arteries were over 90% blocked and he felt short of breath, then had a quadruple bypass 3 days later. He expects future people to know such numbers the way we know our weight, and cancer to show up on a radar screen immediately.
- Radar may reveal tens or hundreds of microcancers at any time, most amounting to nothing.
- Obstacles: it goes against the grain of medicine, which starts from patients presenting problems. Doctors dislike "fishing expeditions" and call findings "incidentalomas."
- The false alarm worry: a friend's research brain scan showed an apparent large tumor that was a harmless cyst, costing days of terror. He argues this is an artifact of current limitations. With constant scanning and better judgment she would have known about the cyst her whole life, like a birthmark.
- He says there is room for many startups, facing technical obstacles, medical-bureaucratic obstacles, and thousands of years of tradition, but "it will happen."

chunks.heading: Tactics: start deceptively small and head west
chunks.text:
- Do not attack a giant problem head-on. Don't announce you will replace email, because it raises expectations, employees and investors keep asking "are we there yet?", and haters wait for failure. Say you are building todo-list software, and people notice you replaced email when it's a fait accompli.
- "Empirically, the way to do really big things seems to be to start with deceptively small things." Examples: a Basic interpreter for a machine with a few thousand users (microcomputer software), and a site for Harvard undergrads to stalk one another (the universal web site).
- Start small for your own sake too. Neither Bill Gates nor Mark Zuckerberg knew at first how big their companies would get. Big initial ambitions take longer and project further into the future, making errors more likely.
- Operate like Columbus and head in a general westerly direction rather than constructing the future like a building from a blueprint that is probably wrong. Start with something you know works, and expand westward.
- "The popular image of the visionary is someone with a clear view of the future, but empirically it may be better to have a blurry one."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Paul Graham distills what makes a good startup founder into two words: relentlessly resourceful. Relentlessness alone fails because startup difficulties are novel and of unknown hardness, so founders must keep trying new approaches. The quality can often be taught, and works as a self-test and a cofounder-selection test.

chunks.heading: What makes a good founder, in two words
chunks.text:
- Paul says he finally got being a good startup founder down to two words: "relentlessly resourceful." Before that, the best he had was the opposite quality in one word: "hapless."
- "Don't be hapless" is not much of a rallying cry, because there is no antonym of hapless. That made it hard to tell founders what to aim for.
- He treats the phrase as the answer to "what should founders aim for?" He found it while writing a talk for investors about what to look for in founders.
- He says "Make something people want" is the destination, but "Be relentlessly resourceful" is how you get there. If he were running a startup, this is the phrase he would "tape to the mirror."
- He doubts the description "could be made more precise."

chunks.heading: What "hapless" means and why it is the opposite
chunks.text:
- Paul says dictionaries wrongly define hapless as unlucky. A team that outplays its opponents but loses to a bad referee decision is unlucky, not hapless.
- Hapless implies passivity. To be hapless is "to be battered by circumstances," to let the world have its way with you instead of having your way with the world.
- He thinks the dictionaries are wrong because the word's meaning has shifted. A couple hundred years ago, people were more at the mercy of circumstances, so many words for good and bad outcomes come from words about luck.
- The good founder is the reverse: active, and shaping outcomes instead of absorbing them.

chunks.heading: Why relentless alone is not enough
chunks.text:
- He says "Not merely relentless." Pure persistence only makes things go your way "in a few mostly uninteresting domains."
- In any interesting domain, the difficulties will be novel. You can't plow through them, because you don't know up front how hard they are: "a block of foam or granite."
- So you have to be resourceful. You have to keep trying new things.
- His metaphor is a running back: not merely determined but flexible. They want to get downfield, but adapt their plans on the fly.
- He admits the metaphor is weak, since it means little to most people outside the US. "Be like a running back" is no better than "Don't be hapless."

chunks.heading: Where the recipe applies and where it does not
chunks.text:
- Paul says the recipe is not just a description of success in general. In writing or painting, the recipe is more to be "actively curious."
- The difference is where the obstacles are. "Resourceful implies the obstacles are external, which they generally are in startups." In writing and painting they are mostly internal: "the obstacle is your own obtuseness."
- Some parts of startups call for active curiosity, when the work is almost pure discovery. He says these are a small proportion of the whole, as they are in research.
- He allows that other fields may share the recipe. He thinks it is the best short description of a good startup founder.
- In big companies and most schools, being relentlessly resourceful is not the recipe. He says the recipe there is "longer and messier," combining resourcefulness, obedience and building alliances.

chunks.heading: Can it be taught?
chunks.text:
- After four years of trying to teach it at Y Combinator, Paul says that yes, "surprisingly often it can." Not to everyone, but to many people.
- Some people are "constitutionally passive." Others have a latent ability that only needs to be brought out.
- It is especially true of young people who have so far always been under the thumb of some kind of authority.
- He adds a hedge. He would almost say "most people," but he has no idea what most people are like, and he is "pathologically optimistic about people's ability to change."

chunks.heading: Using the test: founders, cofounders and how many startups there can be
chunks.text:
- **For yourself:** to know whether you are the right sort of person to start a startup, ask whether you are relentlessly resourceful.
- **For cofounders:** to decide whether to recruit someone as a cofounder, ask whether they are relentlessly resourceful.
- **For investors:** it is the quality to look for in founders.
- **Limit on startups:** Paul says there is no economic upper bound on the number of startups. There is no reason to think consumers can only absorb so much newly created wealth, "any more than there is a limit on the number of theorems that can be proven."
- So the limiting factor is the pool of potential founders. Now that the quality is named, it is possible to put an upper bound on the pool.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Graham argues founders should stop relying on pitch skills and instead make a startup worth investing in, understand why, and explain it plainly. Investors want formidable founders and a plausible path to owning a big piece of a big market. Seeming formidable comes from truth and domain expertise, not swagger.

chunks.heading: Investors judge founders first, ideas second
chunks.text:
- Paul says most investors decide within the first few minutes whether a founder seems like a winner or a loser, and that opinion is hard to change. Every startup has reasons both to invest and not to invest. If investors like the founders they focus on the former, and if not on the latter.
- Example: a rich market with a slow sales cycle. Impressed investors say they want to invest because of the rich market. Unimpressed ones say they can't invest because of the slow sales cycle.
- Investors are usually unclear in their own minds why they like or dislike a startup. Paul notes founders have the same weakness.
- Ideas are "fuel for the fire that starts with liking the founders." When investors like you they say "yes, and you could also do x." When they don't, they say "but what about y?"
- Investors decide whether you're a loser or possibly a winner. If you seem like a loser they are done, at least for roughly the next year, and usually decide in far less than the 50 minutes they may have allotted. Paul says this explains stories of VCs checking messages during pitches: they have already decided.

chunks.heading: Why investors want power-law winners
chunks.text:
- Startup outcomes follow a very steep power law. The big successes "dwarf the rest," and conventional wisdom says there are only about 15 a year.
- Investors therefore treat "big success" as nearly binary. Most are interested if you have even a small chance of being one of those 15, and otherwise not.
- A handful of angels would back a company with a high chance of moderate success, but angels like big successes too.
- Paul says there is no reason to think 15 is a constant. Increasing it by encouraging more people to start startups is an explicit goal at Y Combinator.
- Three things make you seem like one of the big successes: formidable founders, a promising market, and (usually) some evidence of success so far.

chunks.heading: Seeming formidable: stick to the truth
chunks.text:
- "Formidable" means seeming like you'll get what you want regardless of obstacles. It is close to confident, except confident people can be mistaken. Formidable is roughly "justifiably confident."
- A few people are very good at seeming formidable, either because they really are or because they are more or less con artists. Most founders, including many who later build very successful companies, are not good at it the first time they fundraise.
- Paul says not to imitate the swagger of experienced founders. Investors are not always good at judging technology but they are good at judging confidence, and acting like something you're not lands you in an uncanny valley: "You'll depart from sincere, but never arrive at convincing."
- How formidable you seem varies with what you're saying. Anyone sounds confident saying "one plus one is two." Skilled people can do the same with "we're going to make a billion dollars a year." You can do it with fairly impressive sentences too, as long as you convince yourself first.
- Paul's reason early founders don't seem formidable: family, school and jobs reward cooperation, not conquest, so people emerge "compressed into the shape of the tube." Some find they have wings, but it takes a few years.

chunks.heading: Convince yourself first, then convince investors
chunks.text:
- "Convince yourself that your startup is worth investing in, and then when you explain this to investors they'll believe you." This does not mean mind games to boost confidence. It means truly evaluating whether the startup is worth investing in.
- If it isn't, Paul says don't raise money. In fact, change what you're doing, since you're investing your own time. If you're not convinced it's a sufficiently good bet, why work on it?
- If it is worth investing in, you'll be telling the truth, investors will sense it, and you don't need to be a smooth presenter.
- Doing this evaluation requires being a domain expert. Otherwise your conviction looks like Dunning-Kruger to investors, and it usually is. They find out quickly from how well you answer questions. "Know everything about your market."
- When asked something you don't know, don't bluff or give up. Explain how you'd figure out the answer, and if you can work out a preliminary answer on the spot, do so and say that's what you're doing.
- Founders try to convince investors of things they don't believe because school trains us to talk when we have nothing to say (a ten page paper due means ten pages, even with one page of ideas). The quoted professor question: "Which one of these conclusions do you actually believe?"
- Unless you're a good con artist, you can't convince investors if you aren't convinced. "They're far better at detecting bullshit than you are at producing it." Pausing to convince yourself also forces you to organize your thoughts and gives you a provisional roadmap to success.

chunks.heading: When to raise money
chunks.text:
- "The time to raise money is not when you need it, or when you reach some artificial deadline like a Demo Day. It's when you can convince investors, and not before."
- At YC, Paul says startups are encouraged to ignore investors and focus on their company until about a week before Demo Day, so most reach a convincing stage well before it. Any startup that isn't ready can defer to a later Demo Day.
- Raising too early wastes both sides' time.

chunks.heading: Market: a good bet, not a sure thing
chunks.text:
- You don't have to prove you'll succeed, only that you are a sufficiently good bet. No one knows whether a startup will succeed, and if they did the stock price would already equal the future price and investors couldn't make money.
- Beyond formidable founders you need a plausible path to owning a big piece of a big market. "Founders think of startups as ideas, but investors think of them as markets."
- TAM: if x customers would pay an average of $y per year for what you make, the total addressable market is $xy. Investors don't expect you to capture it all, but it is an upper bound.
- The market must be big and capturable by you, but need not be big yet, and you need not be in it yet. It is often better to start in a small market that turns into a big one, or from which you can move into one. You need a plausible sequence of hops to dominating a big market a few years out.
- Plausibility standards depend on age. A three-month-old company at Demo Day only needs to be a promising experiment worth funding. A two-year-old company raising a Series A must show the experiment worked.
- Paul says the next round is much harder: investors' attitude shifts "like the difference between being judged as a kid and as an adult." Growth graphs work at both stages, but at three months they mostly show the founders are effective, while at two years they must show a promising market and a company tuned to exploit it.
- Every huge company is "lucky" in that its growth comes mostly from an external wave. To make the case for becoming huge, identify a specific trend you'll benefit from, usually by asking "why now?" Ideally something recently changed and no one else has noticed.
- Microsoft example: it wasn't going to grow huge selling Basic interpreters, but starting there it was poised to expand up the stack of microcomputer software as microcomputers became powerful enough. Paul says Microsoft probably looked only "good, but not great" a few months in, and no company ever looks more than a pretty good bet that early.
- Paul says at least half of the startups YC funds could make as good a case as Microsoft could have, and asks who can reasonably expect more.

chunks.heading: Handling rejection and "who else is investing?"
chunks.text:
- Even a Microsoft-quality case won't always convince. Many VCs would have rejected Microsoft and some rejected Google. The most common investor question is "who else is investing?"
- Skilled formidable-seeming founders imply that several investors are about to commit. Paul calls this arguably permissible ("scamming a scammer"), since it is slightly dickish of investors to care so much about it, but he doesn't recommend it. It is the single most common lie told to investors, so you'd have to be very good at lying to pull it off.
- His recommended approach is to tackle it head-on: explain why investors turned you down and why they're mistaken. Experienced investors know the best ideas are also the scariest and know about the VCs who rejected Google.
- Talking candidly about what scared investors makes you seem more confident, probably improves how you present that weakness, and puts the worry in the open instead of leaving it as a gotcha for the current investors to "discover" and become attached to.
- To use this, find out why previous investors rejected you, even if it requires asking. Make clear you're not disputing the decision, just that you need to know about any weakness in your plans. You won't always get a real reason, but try.
- The strategy works best with the best investors, who are hard to bluff. Paul says the best investors rarely care who else is investing, while mediocre ones almost all do, so the question is a test of investor quality.
- Rejection isn't like college admissions, where getting into MIT implies getting into Foobar State. The best startup ideas initially look like bad ideas, so startups are often rejected by every VC except the best.
- Dropbox example: it was in a Boston YC batch, and the Boston investors all passed ("yet another backup and syncing thing"). A couple of weeks later Dropbox raised a Series A from Sequoia. Paul adds that one East Coast firm wanted to invest but tried to lowball them.

chunks.heading: Explaining it: concise, plain language, and a three-step recipe
chunks.text:
- When you convince investors, use the same matter-of-fact language you used to convince yourself. Vague, grandiose marketing-speak doesn't work on investors and "seems a mark of incompetence."
- Be concise. Many investors explicitly test for it, reasoning correctly that if you can't explain your plans concisely you don't understand them. Even those without the rule get bored and frustrated by unclear explanations.
- Alfred Lin's point, which Paul endorses: clarity matters doubly because the pitch must convince at one remove, since the partner you talk to re-tells it to colleagues. At YC, the last step of building a Demo Day pitch is imagining how an investor would sell it to colleagues.
- Raising money asks you to convince investors of something much less speculative than "this will be huge." The question is only whether the company has all the elements of a good bet, so you can convince yourself, then convince them.
- Paul's recipe for founders who aren't naturally formidable:
  1. Make something worth investing in.
  2. Understand why it's worth investing in.
  3. Explain that clearly to investors.
- "As long as you stay on the territory of truth, you're strong. Make the truth good, then just tell it." His opening analogy: lift with your legs (the startup), not your back (the pitch).

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Graham argues persistence and obstinacy are different behaviors, not labels applied after the fact. The persistent are attached to the goal and open to disagreement; the obstinate cling to their first ideas. Persistence is built from five qualities: energy, imagination, resilience, good judgement, and a focus on a goal.

chunks.heading: Persistence versus obstinacy are different behaviors, not just outcomes
chunks.text:
- Paul argues the two are genuinely different kinds of behavior, not labels applied after the fact based on who turned out right. If it were only hindsight, "be persistent rather than obstinate" would just mean "be right rather than wrong," which is useless advice.
- Both are "hard to stop," but in different senses: "The persistent are like boats whose engines can't be throttled back. The obstinate are like boats whose rudders can't be turned."
- They look identical only when a problem has a single solution path, where the only choice is whether to give up. As problems get more complex, the difference shows.
- Terminology: Paul uses "persistent" for the good kind of stubborn and "obstinate" for the bad kind, and admits this stretches normal usage.

chunks.heading: Where each one is attached: goals versus ideas
chunks.text:
- "The persistent are attached to the goal. The obstinate are attached to their ideas about how to reach it."
- The persistent are attached to points high in the decision tree, not minor ones lower down. The obstinate "spray 'don't give up' indiscriminately over the whole tree."
- Obstinate people tend to cling to their first ideas, which are the least informed by experience working on the problem. So they are disproportionately attached to wrong details.
- The persistent will give way on any low-level point if its expected value drops enough, while energy and resilience keep them pushing toward whatever they chose higher up.

chunks.heading: How to tell them apart in conversation
chunks.text:
- The obstinate won't listen. When you point out problems, "their eyes glaze over, and their replies sound like ideologues talking about matters of doctrine."
- Successful people are "never more engaged than when you disagree with them."
- Example: the Collison brothers are the most determined people he can think of, yet when you point out a problem they listen "with an almost predatory intensity." If there is a hole in the bottom of their boat, they want to know.
- Paul says the difference he senses in conversations ("Wow, that guy is determined" versus "Damn, that guy is stubborn") is not only about whether the person seemed right.
- Obstinacy can win in some domains, such as politics, but not where you must pass external tests. Obstinate political leaders are famous for getting power, not for using it well.

chunks.heading: Why people are obstinate: it is personality, not circumstance
chunks.text:
- His first theory was that the obstinate are overwhelmed and grab onto ideas like handholds on a rolling ship. He rejected it.
- Evidence against: handing the Collisons a much harder problem would make them less obstinate, since they would know they must be open to anything. And the obstinate stay obstinate on easy problems.
- Conclusion: obstinacy comes from within. It is "a reflexive resistance to changing one's ideas," closely related to stupidity and a form of not giving up that is easy for the stupid to practice. You skip the tradeoffs and dig in your heels.
- It even works on simple problems, "up to a point."
- The two are not opposites. Paul compares them to aerobic and anaerobic respiration: obstinacy is the more primitive process, but it has uses, like leaping away from a threat.
- The optimal amount of obstinacy is not zero. An unthinking "I won't give up" as a first reaction to a setback helps prevent panic. But the further toward obstinate someone is, the less likely they are to solve hard problems.
- Obstinate people do sometimes succeed: by luck (a stopped clock right twice a day), or when obstinacy cancels another error. Example: a leader with overcautious subordinates whose estimates are always biased one way, so a mindless "push ahead regardless" is usually right.

chunks.heading: The five qualities that make up real persistence
chunks.text:
Obstinacy is simple, and animals have it. Persistence has a complex internal structure of five qualities:
- **Energy:** the persistent "persist rather than merely resisting." They keep trying things.
- **Imagination:** to keep trying things you must keep thinking of things to try. Energy creates demand for ideas, and imagination gives energy somewhere to go. Energy plus imagination alone gives the caricature of an artist or poet.
- **Resilience:** not having morale destroyed by setbacks. Without it you can only do good work on a small scale. It differs from obstinacy: "setbacks can't change your morale, not that they can't change your mind."
- **Good judgement:** persistence often requires changing your mind. The persistent are rational and focus on expected value, which lets them work on unlikely-to-succeed things without being reckless.
- **A goal:** see below.

Anyone can do obstinacy ("kids and drunks and fools are best at it"). Very few people have enough of all five, but when they do "the results are magical."

chunks.heading: Choosing problems: be irrational at the top, pick a specific goal
chunks.text:
- The persistent are often irrational at the very top of the decision tree. Between two problems of roughly equal expected value, the choice comes down to personal preference. They often classify projects into deliberately wide bands of expected value so the one they want still qualifies.
- Paul says this is fine empirically, for two reasons: people work harder on problems they love, and preferences among problems aren't random. Loving a problem others don't often means you've unconsciously noticed it is more important than they realize.
- A vague aim like "do something great" is the most inclusive motivator but useless in practice, because it doesn't tell you what to do at this moment.
- The goal must be fairly specific, but "not too specific, or you might miss a great discovery adjacent to what you're searching for, but not too general, or it won't work to motivate you."
- Tactic: start by erring on the small side. A too-broad goal gets you nowhere, while a too-small one at least keeps you moving. Once moving, expand the goal.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Paul Graham argues the best startup ideas grow organically from your own life rather than being decided from afar. Focus on fixing things that seem broken, don't worry about whether it's a company, and don't be put off if others call it a toy.

chunks.heading: Organic ideas beat made-up ideas
chunks.text:
Paul splits startup ideas into two types: those that grow organically out of your own life, and those you decide from afar some other class of users will need. Apple was the first type: Steve Wozniak wanted a computer and, unlike most people who wanted one, could design it. Viaweb (online store software, founded when Paul was 30 and Robert Morris 29) was the second type.

- Core question: "what do you wish someone would make for you?"
- There is no sharp line between the types, but "the most successful startups seem to be closer to the Apple type than the Viaweb type."
- Examples of organic origins: Bill Gates writing a Basic interpreter for the Altair, Larry and Sergey writing the first Google.
- Apple still works this way: the iPhone is the phone Steve Jobs wants. Paul infers Apple will be weak where Jobs isn't a user (e.g. gaming).

chunks.heading: Why young founders should stick to organic ideas
chunks.text:
- It takes experience to predict what other people will want. Paul and Robert only managed Viaweb because they were old enough to have "seen enough to know users would need this type of software."
- "The worst ideas we see at Y Combinator are from young founders making things they think other people will want."
- Young founders are the best source of organic ideas, though. They use the latest technology, so they discover valuable types of fixable brokenness first.
- Advice for anyone without an idea: focus initially on organic ideas.

chunks.heading: How to spot what's broken
chunks.text:
- Ask: what's missing or broken in your daily life? Sometimes the answers are immediate. It was obviously broken that the Altair could only be programmed in machine language.
- You may need to "stand outside yourself a bit," because people get used to brokenness and take it for granted.
- Example: in 2004 it was ridiculous that Harvard undergrads still used a Facebook printed on paper.
- "There are always great ideas sitting right under our noses." Obvious ones exist today, and are overlooked for the same reason Facebook would have been overlooked in 2004.

chunks.heading: Focus on the idea, not the startup
chunks.text:
- Organic ideas usually don't look like startup ideas at first. Putting undergraduates' profiles online wouldn't have seemed like much of a startup.
- Mark Zuckerberg told a YC dinner he wasn't trying to start a company when he wrote the first Facebook; it was just a project. Woz didn't think he was starting a company with the Apple I.
- If they had thought they were starting companies, they might have been tempted to do something more "serious," "and that would have been a mistake."
- Advice: fix things that seem broken, regardless of whether the problem seems important enough to build a company on. Keep pulling such threads and you'll likely make something valuable to many people, and "surprise, you've got a company."

chunks.heading: Toys are a good sign
chunks.text:
- Don't be discouraged if people dismiss your first version as a toy. That's probably why everyone else overlooked the idea.
- Precedents: the first microcomputers, planes and cars were all dismissed as toys.
- At YC, when users like something that forum trolls could dismiss as a toy, that makes Paul's group "especially likely to invest."

chunks.heading: Unmet needs that are just becoming fixable
chunks.text:
- "There's nothing more valuable than an unmet need that is just becoming fixable."
- If you find something broken that you can fix for a lot of people, "you've found a gold mine." You still have to work hard to extract the gold, but you know where the seam is, "and that's the hard part."

chunks.heading: Become your own user
chunks.text:
- In hindsight, Paul says Viaweb should have *become* direct marketers. Done again, he'd open his own online store, which would have given them a much better understanding of users.
- Advice: "become one of its users, however unnatural it seems."
- Caveat: it's hard to compete directly with open source software. You can build things for programmers, but there has to be some part you can charge for.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Graham reflects on what YC learned from advising many startups: most share the same problems, founders misjudge which matter most, and they resist advice because startups are counterintuitive. Speed defines startups, focus enables speed, and YC's value is improving focus and providing colleagues.

chunks.heading: Why "explain what you've learned from users" is the best advice per word
chunks.text:
- Paul told Y Combinator applicants that the best advice for getting in, per word, was: "Explain what you've learned from users."
- He says the question tests three things at once: whether founders are paying attention to users, how well they understand them, and how much users need what the founders are making.
- He then asked himself the same question about YC's own users, the startups it funds. The lessons below are his answers.

chunks.heading: Most startups share the same problems, which is why funding many early companies works
chunks.text:
- No two startups have exactly the same problems, but the problems stay surprisingly similar regardless of what the company makes.
- After advising 100 startups that all do different things, Paul says you rarely meet a problem you haven't seen before.
- He did not know this when YC started. He only had his own startup and friends' startups as data points.
- A YC partner gets this experience in the first year or two. Later-stage investors may not advise 100 startups in a whole career, so many never see the pattern.
- Funding large numbers of early-stage companies gives more data, "not just because you're looking at more companies, but also because more goes wrong."
- Knowing nearly all the problems does not mean advising can be automated or reduced to a formula. Each startup is unique and needs a specific partner who knows it well.
- He dislikes calling YC a "bootcamp." It is intense like one, but opposite in structure: instead of everyone doing the same thing, each startup talks to partners to find out what it specifically needs.

chunks.heading: The batch that broke YC: advising doesn't scale as a pool
chunks.text:
- Until the summer 2012 batch, partners were treated as a pool. A startup requesting office hours got the next slot posted by any partner, so every partner had to know every startup.
- This worked up to 60 startups. At 80 it broke: halfway through the batch the partners still didn't know all the companies and were confused and unhappy.
- Paul's diagnosis: "We were using an O(n2) algorithm. So of course it blew up." A third more startups broke it because pairwise knowledge grows quadratically.
- The fix was the classic one: shard the batch into smaller groups, each overseen by a dedicated group of partners. It has worked ever since.
- Founders probably didn't notice a problem, and that batch did unusually well. "Broken" meant it felt wrong to the partners.
- Lesson: advising startups has to be individualized.

chunks.heading: Founders misjudge their problems, and the biggest one is often hidden
chunks.text:
- Founders often come in to discuss one problem, and a much bigger one turns up during the conversation.
- Common example: founders say they struggle to raise money. Digging in shows the company is doing badly and investors can tell.
- Another example: founders worried they haven't cracked user acquisition. The real cause is that the product isn't good enough.
- Paul has asked "Would you use this yourself, if you hadn't built it?" and had founders answer "No" after thinking. "Well, there's the reason you're having trouble getting users."
- Even when founders know their problems, they often don't know their relative importance. A typical visit has three worries: one moderate, one irrelevant, one that will kill the company if not fixed immediately.
- His analogy is a horror movie heroine upset about her cheating boyfriend and only mildly curious about the door that's mysteriously ajar: "never mind about your boyfriend, think about that door!"
- Office hours let partners say that. Startups still die, but "it's rarely because they wandered into a room containing a murderer."
- He links this to research showing people are much better at answering questions than at judging how accurate their answers are.

chunks.heading: Why founders don't listen, and why that is useful
chunks.text:
- Founders often don't take YC partners' advice. A partner told Paul: "They come back a year later and say 'We wish we'd listened to you.'"
- Stubbornness is part of it, but the more important reason is that so much about startups is counterintuitive. When you tell someone something counterintuitive, "what it sounds to them is wrong." Founders don't listen because they don't believe, until experience teaches them.
- Startups are counterintuitive because they differ from most people's other experiences. Nobody knows what it's like except people who've done it, which is why YC partners should usually have been founders.
- The counterintuitiveness is also part of why YC works: if startups weren't counterintuitive, founders wouldn't need the advice.
- Exception: the Airbnb founders were particularly good at listening, partly because they were flexible and disciplined, and partly because they'd had such a rough time the year before. "They were ready to listen."

chunks.heading: Focus enables speed: weekly cycles of action and measurement
chunks.text:
- Early-stage startups have a hundred problems and only the founders to work on them. If founders focus on things that don't matter, nobody is focusing on the things that do.
- The essence of YC, in his words: figure out which problems matter most, cook up ideas for solving them "ideally at a resolution of a week or less," try them, and measure how well they worked. The focus is on action with measurable, near-term results.
- This does not mean rushing regardless of consequences. If you correct course often enough, you can be "simultaneously decisive at a micro scale and tentative at a macro scale." The path winds but is executed very fast, like a running back's path downfield.
- In practice there is less backtracking than expected. Founders usually guess the right direction, especially with an experienced partner to test hypotheses against, and when they guess wrong they notice fast because they report results at office hours the next week.
- Better navigation has a double effect: the path is shorter, and you travel faster along it when more certain it's right.
- His summary: "Speed defines startups. Focus enables speed. YC improves focus."
- The right unit of decisiveness depends on how long results take. Negotiating with investors might take a couple of days; building hardware might take months.

chunks.heading: Why founders are uncertain, and the habit of hacking the test
chunks.text:
- Founders are uncertain partly because startups do something new, so nobody knows how to do it or even what "it" is, partly because startups are counterintuitive, and partly because ambitious young founders were trained to win the wrong way.
- The education system in most countries trains people to win by hacking the test instead of doing what the test is supposed to measure. That stops working in a startup.
- Part of what YC does is retrain founders to stop hacking the test. It takes a surprisingly long time: a year in, founders still revert to old habits.
- YC is not simply experienced founders passing on knowledge. It is "more like specialization than apprenticeship": partners have encyclopedic knowledge of startup problems, founders have deep domain knowledge, and neither would find it worthwhile to acquire the other's.
- That is why even an experienced founder can benefit from YC, like an experienced athlete benefiting from a coach.

chunks.heading: Colleagues matter as much as advice, and founders help each other
chunks.text:
- Paul thinks colleagues may matter even more than partners' advice. Great work clusters in places and institutions: Florence in the late 15th century, Göttingen in the late 19th, The New Yorker under Ross, Bell Labs, Xerox PARC. "However good you are, good colleagues make you better."
- Very ambitious people probably need colleagues most, because they are so starved for them in everyday life.
- YC was deliberately designed to be such a cluster, and Paul says it is now the biggest cluster of great startup founders.
- Before YC, most people assumed colleagues and independence couldn't be combined: loneliness was the price of independence. That was how it felt when he started his own startup in Boston in the 1990s: a few older advisers of varying quality, but no peers to commiserate with about investors or speculate with about technology.
- YC was designed to be what he wanted as a founder, in line with his advice to make something you yourself want.
- Seed funding without "making the rounds of random rich people" has become a commodity, at least in the US. Great colleagues can't become a commodity, because they cluster in some places and are proportionally absent elsewhere.
- Of the energy in the room at a YC dinner: "like nothing else I've experienced."
- The happiest thing he has learned about founders is how generous they are in helping each other. YC noticed it in the first batch and designed the program to magnify it, so founders are surrounded by partners, alumni and batchmates who want to help and can.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Paul Graham argues startup founders can afford to be nice because great products spread by word of mouth and compound, while rapacity doesn't. Being bad at extracting money only scales the growth curve by a constant factor, whereas improving growth rate changes its shape. The math: a founder extracting half as much is only 15 weeks behind, and a faster growth rate overtakes quickly.

chunks.heading: Why nice founders lose little: the growth-curve math
chunks.text:
Paul argues that startup founders can safely be nice, because making great things compounds and rapacity (squeezing every penny from customers) does not. His reasoning came from a founder's email. The founder worried he was "fundamentally soft-hearted," gave away too much for free, and thought he might need "a little dose of sociopath-ness."

- Paul told him not to worry. If he built something good enough to spread by word of mouth, he would have a superlinear growth curve.
- Being bad at extracting money only shrinks that curve by a constant multiple below 1.
- A constant multiple of any curve has the same shape. The Y-axis numbers are smaller, but the curve is just as steep, "and when anything grows at the rate of a successful startup, the Y axis will take care of itself."
- Paul's one-line summary: "The reason startup founders can safely be nice is that making great things is compounded, and rapacity isn't."

chunks.heading: Worked example: extracting half the money costs 15 weeks
chunks.text:
Paul's numbers assume a company making $1000 a month and growing 5% a week.

- After two years it makes about $160k a month.
- A founder who extracts only half as much from users makes $80k a month at that point instead.
- The un-rapacious founder catches up to where the rapacious one would have been in "a mere 15 weeks." After two years, he is only 3.5 months behind.
- Paul's footnote gives the reason: since 2 ≈ 1.05^15, a founder extracting half as much is always 15 weeks behind the one extracting everything.

chunks.heading: Optimize growth rate, not extraction
chunks.text:
Paul says that if you are going to optimize one number, it should be your growth rate. He extends the same example:

- The nice founder still extracts only half as much from users, but grows 6% a week instead of 5%.
- After two years he is already ahead: $214k a month versus $160k for the rapacious founder.
- A year later he makes $4.4 million a month, against the rapacious founder's $2 million.
- Small differences in weekly growth outweigh large differences in how much money is taken per customer.

chunks.heading: When rapacity might help (and why it usually doesn't)
chunks.text:
Paul concedes rapacity helps where growth depends on it. His claim is that for startups it usually doesn't.

- Startups usually win by making something so great that people recommend it to their friends.
- Being rapacious "not only doesn't help you do that, but probably hurts."
- Second possible benefit: startups usually lose money at first, so higher revenue per customer makes it easier to reach profitability before the initial funding runs out.
- Paul notes it is very common for startups to die from running through their funding and being unable to raise more. But he says the underlying cause is usually slow growth or excessive spending, "rather than insufficient effort to extract money from existing customers."

chunks.heading: The deal founders can make with themselves
chunks.text:
Paul's practical advice is a conscious tradeoff:

- Tell yourself you can be as nice as you want, so long as you work hard on your growth rate to compensate.
- He says this deal "will both make you happy and make your company successful."
- Most successful startups make this tradeoff unconsciously. Paul suggests that making it consciously may let founders do it even better.

chunks.heading: What drives the most successful founders
chunks.text:
Paul contrasts his childhood "cartoon" of a successful businessman with what he has seen in startups.

- The cartoon was a rapacious, cigar-smoking, table-thumping man in his fifties who wins by exercising power and "isn't too fussy about how."
- He says few of the most successful startup founders are like that. He is unsure about other industries, but not startups.
- Many assume founders are driven by money. Paul says the secret weapon of the most successful founders is that they aren't. If they were, they would have taken one of the acquisition offers that every fast-growing startup gets on the way up.
- What drives them is what drives most people who make things: the company is their project.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Paul Graham lists the five qualities Y Combinator looks for in founders. Determination matters most, balanced by flexibility. The other three are imagination, a naughty streak of beating the system, and a strong bond between cofounders. Each is illustrated with YC founders such as WePay, Greplin, Airbnb and Justin.tv.

chunks.heading: Determination as the top founder quality
chunks.text:
- Paul says that when YC started, the team expected intelligence to be the most important quality in founders. That's "the myth in the Valley."
- His view after funding many startups: as long as a founder is over a certain intelligence threshold, "what matters most is determination."
- Founders hit many obstacles, so they can't be the sort of person who gets demoralized easily.
- Example: Bill Clerico and Rich Aberman of WePay run a finance startup, which means endless negotiations with big, bureaucratic companies. When a startup depends on deals with big companies, it often feels like they're trying to ignore you out of existence. Paul's point is that when Clerico starts calling you, "you may as well do what he asks, because he is not going away."

chunks.heading: Flexibility: determination without stubbornness
chunks.text:
- Paul does not want the kind of determination in phrases like "don't give up on your dreams."
- Startups are so unpredictable that founders must be able to modify their dreams on the fly.
- His best metaphor is a running back. He is determined to get downfield, but at any moment may need to go sideways or even backwards to get there.
- Example: Daniel Gross of Greplin applied to YC with a bad ecommerce idea. YC said it would fund him if he did something else. He thought for a second and said ok. He then went through two more ideas before settling on Greplin.
- He had worked on Greplin only a couple of days when he presented to investors at Demo Day, and he still got a lot of interest. Paul says he "always seems to land on his feet."

chunks.heading: Imagination: the kind of intelligence that matters
chunks.text:
- Intelligence matters a lot, and the type that matters most is imagination.
- What counts is not solving predefined problems quickly, but coming up with surprising new ideas.
- In startups, "most good ideas seem bad initially." If they were obviously good, someone would already be doing them.
- Founders therefore need the kind of intelligence that produces ideas with "just the right level of craziness."
- Example: Airbnb. YC thought the idea was too crazy and couldn't believe large numbers of people would want to stay in other people's places. YC funded it because it liked the founders so much. They were in as soon as YC heard the founders had been supporting themselves by selling Obama and McCain branded breakfast cereal. The idea turned out to be on the right side of crazy.

chunks.heading: Naughtiness: the piratical gleam
chunks.text:
- The most successful founders are usually good people, but they tend to have "a piratical gleam in their eye." They're not "Goody Two-Shoes type good."
- Morally, they care about getting the big questions right, not about observing proprieties.
- Paul prefers "naughty" to "evil." They delight in breaking rules, but not rules that matter.
- He notes this quality may be redundant, since it may be implied by imagination.
- Application question: Sam Altman of Loopt, one of YC's most successful alumni, was asked what question to put on the YC application to find more people like him. He suggested asking about a time they had hacked something to their advantage, meaning beating the system, not breaking into computers.
- That question became one of the ones YC pays most attention to when judging applications.

chunks.heading: Friendship: founder relationships
chunks.text:
- Empirically it is hard to start a startup with just one founder. Most of the big successes have two or three.
- The relationship between founders has to be strong. They must genuinely like one another and work well together.
- His line: "Startups do to the relationship between the founders what a dog does to a sock: if it can be pulled apart, it will be."
- Example: Emmett Shear and Justin Kan of Justin.tv have known each other since second grade and "can practically read one another's minds." Paul says he has never sensed any unresolved tension between them, though he assumes they argue like all founders.

chunks.heading: Summary of the five qualities
chunks.text:
- Determination, flexibility, imagination, naughtiness and friendship are what YC looks for in founders.
- Determination is the most important, and it must be paired with flexibility.
- Imagination is the form of intelligence that matters most.
- Naughtiness may be implied by imagination.
- Founder friendship matters because startups strain the relationship.
- Paul wrote this essay in October 2010 for Forbes. The print version cut the last item (friendship) for lack of room.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Paul Graham argues that people have one "top idea" their mind drifts to (e.g. in the shower), and it gets all the benefit of ambient thought. Letting money or disputes become that idea kills progress on everything else, so you must shape your situations to control it indirectly.

chunks.heading: Ambient thought and the top idea in your mind
chunks.text:
- Paul says what he thinks about in the shower in the morning matters more than he used to believe. He already knew it was a good time to have ideas. Now he says "it's hard to do a really good job on anything you don't think about in the shower."
- He calls the effect "ambient thought": thinking you do without trying to. A typical case is working hard on a problem, failing, then seeing the answer later while doing something else.
- He is "increasingly convinced" this kind of thinking is necessary for hard problems, not just helpful. You can only control it indirectly.
- Most people have one top idea in mind at any time. It is the idea your thoughts drift toward when they drift freely. That idea gets all the benefit of ambient thought, and every other idea is starved of it.
- So "it's a disaster to let the wrong idea become the top one in your mind."

chunks.heading: Why startups stall when they raise money
chunks.text:
- Paul had noticed that startups got far less done once they started raising money. He only understood why when his own team raised money for Y Combinator.
- The cost is not the hours spent meeting investors. Raising money becomes the top idea in your mind, so it is what you think about in the morning shower. Other questions stop getting that thinking.
- He had hated raising money at Viaweb and had forgotten why until the YC raise.
- Money matters are especially likely to become the top idea because they have to. Money doesn't arrive by default. It only happens if you let it occupy your shower thoughts, and then you make little progress on what you'd rather work on.
- The pattern is not unique to him. He says "just about every startup I've seen grinds to a halt when they start raising money," or when they start talking to acquirers.
- Neither fund he raised for YC was difficult, yet each process dragged on for months. Moving large sums is never treated casually. The attention required rises with the amount: "maybe not linearly, but definitely monotonically."
- He sees the same thing in professors, who have become "professional fundraisers who do a little research on the side."

chunks.heading: Controlling your top idea indirectly
chunks.text:
- You can't directly steer where your thoughts drift: "If you're controlling them, they're not drifting."
- You can steer them indirectly by choosing which situations you get into. His lesson is "be careful what you let become critical to you."
- Aim for situations where the most urgent problems are ones you want to think about.
- Control is incomplete. An emergency can push everything else out. Barring emergencies, you have a good deal of indirect influence.

chunks.heading: The two thoughts to avoid: money and disputes
chunks.text:
- Paul names two types of thought that push out more interesting ones, "like the Nile Perch."
- Money: getting it is "almost by definition an attention sink."
- Disputes: they are engaging in the wrong way. They have the same velcro-like shape as interesting ideas but no substance. His advice is to avoid disputes if you want to get real work done.
- Corollary: avoid becoming an administrator, or your job will consist of dealing with money and disputes.

chunks.heading: Newton and the cost of disputes
chunks.text:
- After publishing his theory of colors in 1672, Newton was distracted by disputes for years. He concluded that the only fix was to stop publishing.
- Newton wrote that "a man must either resolve to put out nothing new or become a slave to defend it."
- His critics included Linus and his students at Liege. Biographer Westfall thought Newton overreacted, since the "slavery" was five replies totalling fourteen printed pages over a year.
- Paul sympathizes with Newton. The cost was not the 14 pages. It was the pain of having a stupid controversy repeatedly reintroduced as the top idea in a mind that wanted to think about other things.

chunks.heading: Forgiveness as a selfish habit
chunks.text:
- Someone who injures you hurts you twice: by the injury, then by the time you spend thinking about it afterward. Ignoring injuries avoids the second half.
- His method is to tell himself, "this doesn't deserve space in my head."
- He is delighted to find he has forgotten the details of a dispute, because that means he wasn't thinking about it.
- His wife thinks he is more forgiving than she is, but he says his motives are "purely selfish."

chunks.heading: Diagnosing what your top idea actually is
chunks.text:
- Many people aren't sure what their top idea is. Paul is often wrong about his own, because he tends to name the idea he'd want to be on top rather than the one that is.
- The test is to take a shower and notice which topic your thoughts keep returning to.
- If it isn't what you want to be thinking about, change something about your situation.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Paul Graham argues fundraising is the second hardest part of a startup because investors are few, random and herd-like. He gives survival techniques: expect deals to fail, keep building, take reasonable offers, stay flexible on amount, get ramen profitable, treat rejection analytically, and know where you stand.

chunks.heading: Why fundraising is brutal and why morale is the real risk
chunks.text:
- Paul calls fundraising "the second hardest part of starting a startup." The hardest is making something people want, which is why most startups die.
- Investors judge startups the way customers judge products, not the way bosses judge employees. A valiant effort that fails earns no credit for this startup. It might help with the next one.
- Raising money is harder than selling to customers because there are so few investors. A startup rarely has more than 10 interested, so one investor's randomness can swing the outcome.
- Paul says all investors, YC included, are "by ordinary standards incompetent." They make big decisions about things they don't understand, so they get skittish. One day they seem ready to write a check, and the next they don't return calls. He says this is indecision, not game-playing.
- Investors' strongest influence on each other is each other's opinion, so there is no damping. Nobody wants a "bargain" startup that everyone else hates.
- His advice: "The most important thing is not to let fundraising get you down." Startups live or die on morale, and lost morale becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy.
- The biggest danger is surprise, that founders cruise through the early steps and then give up when fundraising turns out to be hard. His fix is to warn them in advance.

chunks.heading: Bootstrapping is really consulting, and the trade-off
chunks.text:
- Paul says raising money is usually the lesser evil, but it still has to be treated as a threat to survival. The process itself can kill a startup.
- Founders need money to live on, and "you can't create instant customers." Viaweb charged about $140 per user per month, yet it would have taken at least a year for revenue to cover even its "paltry" costs. The founders didn't have a year of savings, so they could not have bootstrapped it.
- Once you exclude founders who funded themselves with savings or a day job, "bootstrapped" companies either (a) got really lucky or (b) began as consulting companies and gradually became product companies.
- Consulting is "the only option you can count on," but the pain is spread over years. That delay can be fatal if the idea is obvious. Delicious could be built on the side only because no one else saw the idea.
- Famous bootstrapped companies are famous because they are rare. "If it worked so well, it would be the norm."
- He expects bootstrapping to get easier as startups get cheaper, but "technology tends to get dramatically cheaper, but living expenses don't."
- His framing: "choose your pain," either the short, sharp pain of raising money or the chronic ache of consulting. For the same total pain, raising money is the better choice because new technology is usually more valuable now than later.
- A VC who read the essay told Paul they avoid companies bootstrapped with consulting because it "creates very bad behaviors/instincts that are hard to erase from a company's culture."

chunks.heading: Expectations, focus and conservatism
chunks.text:
**Have low expectations**
- Fundraising kills morale because it is much harder than founders expected. Lower expectations mean less disappointment.
- Assume investors will let you down, and acquirers too. A YC mantra: "Deals fall through." Paul says "the predictive power of this simple rule is amazing."
- Deals don't progress linearly like other human interactions, and they often fall through at the last moment. The other party often doesn't decide what it wants until then. Founders should "tie yourself to the mast" and become "pathologically cynical."
- It is flattering when eminent investors show interest, which makes it easy to believe the raise will be quick. It hardly ever is.

**Keep working on the startup**
- Fundraising sucks up attention. One investor meeting a day burns the whole day, counting travel, prep and afterthought.
- Best option: one founder handles investors while the others keep building. This works better with 3 founders than 2, and when the CEO isn't also the lead developer. Even then the company moves at about half speed.
- Usually the company stalls. A "2 week interruption" turns into a 4-month one, and a company that hasn't done anything new in 4 months stops looking dynamic. Investors lose interest partly because of "the damage done by their own indecision."
- Put the startup first: fit investor meetings into spare moments in the development schedule, not the reverse. Keep releasing features, growing traffic, doing deals and getting written about. That makes meetings more productive and keeps your own morale up, which investors use to judge you.

**Be conservative**
- As conditions worsen, the best strategy gets more conservative. Paul advises approaching fundraising "as if it were always going badly."
- What he tells most funded startups: if someone reputable offers funding on reasonable terms, take it. Some startups held out for a better offer and got it, but he'd give the same advice again: "Who knows how many bullets were in the gun they were playing Russian roulette with?"
- If an investor seems interested, don't let them sit. Interest isn't real until you try to convert it into money. A hot prospect should be closed now or written off, and unless you already have enough funding, that means close now.
- "Startups don't win by getting great funding rounds, but by making great products."

chunks.heading: Flexible round sizing and how to answer VC questions
chunks.text:
- Two VC questions not to answer: "Who else are you talking to?" and "How much are you trying to raise?"
- Paul says VCs don't expect an answer to the first. They ask it just in case. The optimal answer is to say naming names would be improper while implying you're talking to many VCs about to give you term sheets. Only try this if you understand how, because "nothing annoys VCs more than clumsy efforts to manipulate them."
- On the second question, he says you shouldn't have a fixed amount you need to raise. The fixed-amount custom is left over from when startups needed factories or 50 hires.
- Instead, tell investors there are several routes depending on the amount:
  - As little as $50k pays for founders' food and rent for a year.
  - A couple hundred thousand gets office space and a few smart hires from school.
  - A couple million lets them "really blow this thing out."
- The message, and the fact behind it, should be: "we're going to succeed no matter what. Raising more money just lets us do it faster."
- For angel rounds, the size can change on the fly. Start small and expand, rather than aiming big and risking the investors you already have.
- A "rolling close" has no predetermined size: you sell stock to investors one at a time as they say yes. This breaks deadlocks, since you can start when the first investor is ready.
- The downside of expanding on the fly is that the valuation is fixed at the start. A sudden rush of interest forces a choice between turning investors away and selling more of the company than intended.

chunks.heading: Independence and ramen profitability
chunks.text:
- A startup with a couple of founders in their early twenties can have expenses low enough to be profitable on as little as $2000 per month. That revenue is negligible, but the effect on morale and bargaining position is large.
- YC calls this being "ramen profitable": making just enough to pay living expenses. After that, "you may still need investment to make it big, but you don't need it this month."
- If a little more effort on sales would carry you over that threshold, do it.
- Investors like it because it shows you've thought about making money, have the discipline to keep expenses low, and "above all, it means you don't need them."
- "There is nothing investors like more than a startup that seems like it's going to succeed even without them."
- Paul says that when YC predicts which funded startups will do well, it says things like "Oh, those guys can take care of themselves. They'll be fine." It doesn't say "those guys are really smart" or "working on a great idea."
- The qualities cited in those predictions are toughness, adaptability and determination. To the extent YC is right, those are what founders need to win. He notes this comparison is among YC startups, who have already cleared a certain intelligence threshold.
- Sam Altman conveys this without profit: "You could parachute him into an island full of cannibals and come back in 5 years and he'd be the king." Paul says he himself lacks that deal-making ability. Founders without it can "let the numbers speak for you."

chunks.heading: Handling rejection precisely
chunks.text:
- Rejection is common. David Hornik of August described his own funnel for a year:
  - 500 to 800 plans received and read
  - 50 to 100 initial one-hour meetings
  - about 20 companies he got interested in
  - about 5 he got serious about
  - 1 to 2 deals done
- Paul says a VC partner does at most 2 new investments a year however many good startups approach. "The average VC is a rejection machine." Angels reject less.
- Investors are also poor judges because great startup ideas tend to seem wrong. An idea must be both good and novel, so it probably seems bad to most people or someone would already be doing it. Good startup investors need to be intellectual contrarians.
- Most VCs are "money guys, not people who make things." Angels appreciate novel ideas better because most were founders. The best VCs tend to be the least VC-like.
- How to read rejection:
  - Don't ignore it, since it might mean something, and don't get automatically demoralized.
  - If an investor gives specific reasons, check whether they are right and fix real problems. "You're supposed to be the domain expert; you have to decide."
  - A rejection doesn't necessarily say anything about the startup, but it suggests the pitch could improve. Don't just think "investors are stupid." Work out precisely where you lose them.
  - Sort and analyze rejections rather than letting them pile up as "a depressing, undifferentiated heap." Then "no one likes us" becomes a known size of problem with a known fix.
- "You're too early for us" really means "we can't figure out yet whether you'll succeed." An hour old is not too early if it's the right startup.

chunks.heading: Downshifting into consulting and avoiding novice investors
chunks.text:
**Downshift into consulting (if appropriate)**
- Consulting is a dangerous way to finance a startup but better than dying. Paul compares it to anaerobic respiration: not optimal long term, but it can save you from an immediate threat.
- It fits some startups better. It wouldn't have suited Google, but a company making software for building websites could degrade gracefully by building sites for clients with it.
- Be careful not to get sucked in permanently. Upsides: you understand users well, and you may land big-name users you wouldn't get as a product company.
- At Viaweb the founders initially operated like a consulting company because they were desperate for users, and offered to build merchants' sites if they signed up. They never charged for it, so merchants wouldn't treat them as consultants and call whenever they wanted a change. They knew they had to stay a product company "because only that scales."

**Avoid inexperienced investors**
- Novice investors seem unthreatening but are the most dangerous because they are nervous, especially relative to the amount they invest. "Raising $20,000 from a first-time angel investor can be as much work as raising $2 million from a VC fund."
- Their lawyers are inexperienced too. One YC startup negotiated a tiny round with an angel and got a 70-page agreement from his lawyer. The lawyer couldn't admit the mistake in front of his client, insisted on the draconian terms, and the deal fell through.
- If you take novice money, either (a) drive the process yourself, including supplying the paperwork (YC publishes Series AA paperwork), or (b) use them only to fill out a larger round led by someone else.

chunks.heading: Knowing where you stand and prioritizing investors
chunks.text:
- Paul says the most dangerous thing about investors is indecisiveness. The worst case is "the long no," the no that arrives after months of meetings. Rejections are like design flaws: inevitable, but much cheaper to find early.
- While talking to investors, constantly collect data on where you stand:
  - How likely are they to offer a term sheet?
  - What do they have to be convinced of first?
  - You needn't always ask outright, since that can get annoying, but always be gathering data.
- Investors resist committing except to the extent you push them. They want maximum information with minimum decisions.
- Best way to force action: competing investors. You can also focus the discussion by asking what specific questions they need answered, then answering them. If you clear several obstacles and they keep raising new ones, "assume that ultimately they're going to flake."
- Be disciplined, or investors' wish to lead you on will combine with your wish to be led on and produce "completely inaccurate impressions."
- Weight your strategy by investor value, which is how good a yes would be times how likely they are to say it. Put the most weight on likelihood, because "the most important quality in an investor is simply investing."
- Focusing on hot investors doesn't sacrifice lukewarm ones. One investor over the threshold makes the others much more interested, since the biggest factor in investor opinion is other investors' opinion.
- Investor opinions also spread indirectly through founders. Many interested investors raise your confidence, which makes you more attractive. No VC admits to being swayed by buzz, but few can say they aren't swayed by confidence.

chunks.heading: The fundraising opportunity and where the market is heading
chunks.text:
- Paul says YC is working to fix the inefficient market by growing the number of investors as the number of startups grows. "As t approaches infinity, Demo Day approaches an auction," but t is still far from infinity.
- Most investors don't realize that dealing with them is a threat to a startup's survival. They don't see that 10 other investors also want a little more information, and that talking to all of them can stall a startup for months.
- Because investors don't understand this cost, he sees room for a competitor to undercut them by deciding faster. YC cut its own decision time to 20 minutes: 5 minutes reading an application, a 10-minute interview and 5 minutes of discussion. Bigger checks would justify longer, but "should it take anyone longer than a couple days?"
- He predicts that either existing investors will decide faster or new investors who do will emerge.
- He expects startups getting cheaper and investors multiplying to make raising money "if not easy, at least straightforward."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Paul Graham argues that returns to performance are superlinear, driven by two causes: exponential growth and thresholds. He draws practical rules for founders and ambitious people: seek work that compounds, keep learning, focus on growth rate, do things that don't scale early, and follow curiosity into new fields.

chunks.heading: Returns for performance are superlinear, not linear
chunks.text:
- Paul says one of the most important things he didn't understand as a child was that returns for performance are superlinear. Teachers and coaches implicitly said they were linear: "You get out what you put in."
- His business example: "If your product is only half as good as your competitor's, you don't get half as many customers. You get no customers, and you go out of business."
- He argues this is a feature of the world, not an artifact of capitalism's rules. The same pattern shows up in fame, power, military victories, knowledge and benefit to humanity. "The rich get richer."
- He says you can't understand the world without it, and that for the ambitious "this will be the wave you surf on."
- All superlinear returns reduce to two fundamental causes: exponential growth and thresholds.

chunks.heading: Exponential growth: why growth rate matters for startups
chunks.text:
- Startups can grow exponentially. Some achieve high growth rates and most don't, so outcomes differ qualitatively. High-growth companies tend to become immensely valuable, while lower-growth ones may not survive.
- Y Combinator tells founders to focus on growth rate rather than absolute numbers. Paul gives three reasons:
  - It keeps founders from being discouraged early, when absolute numbers are low.
  - It works as a compass for deciding how to evolve the company.
  - The main one: focusing on growth rate tends to produce something that actually grows exponentially.
- If growth rate is proportional to performance *p*, the reward over time *t* is proportional to *pt*. Paul still finds that "startling" after decades of thinking about it.
- Whenever how well you do depends on how well you've done, you get exponential growth. Humans don't find this natural (the rice-on-a-chessboard story surprises every child).
- He notes sufficiently fast exponential growth guarantees both the shape and the magnitude of the return curve, because something that grows fast enough gets big even if it starts trivially small. Thresholds only guarantee the shape.
- Historical examples of exponential growth: conquest (territory makes your army stronger, which wins more territory) and scholarship (the more you know, the easier it is to learn more).

chunks.heading: Thresholds and winner-take-all dynamics
chunks.text:
- A sports match is a step function: the winner gets one win whether they win by a lot or a little. The source is thresholds in the outcome, not competition itself. Thresholds exist even when you're alone, like proving a theorem or hitting a target.
- The two sources often coexist and feed each other:
  - Crossing thresholds leads to exponential growth (the winning side in a battle usually suffers less damage, so it is likelier to win again).
  - Exponential growth helps you cross thresholds: "in a market with network effects, a company that grows fast enough can shut out potential competitors."
- Fame combines both. It grows exponentially because fans bring new fans, and it is concentrated because "there's only so much room on the A-list in the average person's head."
- Thresholds alone don't make a game worth playing (Russian roulette has a threshold). "Seek competition" is also useless if the prize isn't worth it, and a clamoring crowd chasing one problem is often trumped by someone quietly working on another.
- His test for whether a threshold game is worth playing: if something is mediocre yet still popular, it could be a good idea to replace it. If people dislike a product yet still buy it, they'd presumably buy a better alternative.
- Caveat: be careful with this rule. Popular mediocrity often has a hidden reason, such as monopoly or regulation making competition hard, customers with bad taste, or broken buying procedures.

chunks.heading: How to find work with superlinear returns
chunks.text:
- **Seek work that compounds.** It can compound directly (doing well in one cycle helps the next, as with building infrastructure, an audience or a brand), or by teaching you, since learning compounds.
- Learning-based compounding can feel like failure. You may miss your immediate goal but still be growing exponentially. This is why Silicon Valley tolerates failure, but only if you're learning from it.
- Heuristic: always be learning. If you're not learning, you're probably not on a path to superlinear returns. Don't over-optimize what you learn or limit it to things already known to be valuable, or "you'll lop off the outliers."
- **Look for fields where a few big winners outperform everyone else.** Superlinear returns imply inequality, so work where everyone does about the same is unlikely to have them. His examples: sports, politics, art, music, acting, directing, writing, math, science, starting companies and investing.
- Excluding sports, politics and fame effects, the remaining fields are exactly those where you must be independent-minded and your ideas must be novel, not just correct. In investing, believing a company will do well only pays if most other investors don't.
- For intellectual thresholds, he suggests being driven by curiosity rather than careerism. Problems that lead to new fields tend to seem mystifying but perhaps unimportant, while ones that seem legit but boring rarely lead to discoveries.

chunks.heading: Do things that don't scale: paying the initial cost
chunks.text:
- Superlinear returns seem small at first ("At this rate, I'll never get anywhere"), but because the curve rises steeply at the far end, "it's worth taking extraordinary measures to get there."
- In startups this is "do things that don't scale." If you pay "a ridiculous amount of attention to your tiny initial set of customers, ideally you'll kick off exponential growth by word of mouth."
- The same applies to learning: make the initial effort to get a toehold, because it gets easier the more you learn.
- At the far end of the curve incremental effort is a bargain, and there is less competition there because people find the prospect intimidating and few even try. It's a bargain even to try.

chunks.heading: Why this territory is expanding, and who should pursue it
chunks.text:
- The territory is growing in both directions: more types of work offer superlinear returns, and the returns themselves are larger. Two causes: progress in technology and the decreasing importance of organizations.
- Fifty years ago you needed an organization for resources, colleagues and distribution, so your prestige was the organization's. Organizations damped variation in returns. Now many ambitious projects need little initial funding, and there are new ways to learn, earn, find colleagues and reach audiences.
- Without that damping, outcomes vary more: people who do well do even better, and those who do badly do worse. "Exposing oneself to superlinear returns is not for everyone. Most people will be better off as part of the pool."
- Who should shoot for it: people who know they're so good they'll come out net ahead in a higher-variation world, and those, particularly the young, who can afford to risk trying to find out.
- He expects many new winners to be people institutions would never have let in, making the democratization of opportunity greater and more authentic than what institutions would offer themselves.
- Wealth now comes more from discovering or building something uniquely valuable than from capturing resources like an emperor, and the ratio has shifted dramatically toward discovery in the last half century.
- Work is not the same as a job. Your work is whatever you're studying or creating, a portfolio you carry between jobs.

chunks.heading: Paul's recipe for doing exceptional work
chunks.text:
- To be an outlier you need to get nearly all the variables right. You must be interested in the work, since "mere diligence is not enough." Knowing what you're interested in matters even more in a superlinear world. Choose work that suits your circumstances (for example, energy-intensive work while young and without children).
- His one-paragraph recipe:
  - Choose work you have natural aptitude for and deep interest in.
  - Develop a habit of working on your own projects, however excitingly ambitious.
  - Work as hard as you can without burning out. This eventually brings you to a frontier of knowledge, which looks smooth from afar but is full of gaps. Explore the gaps, and one may expand into a whole new field.
  - Take as much risk as you can afford. "If you're not failing occasionally you're probably being too conservative."
  - Seek out the best colleagues, develop good taste, learn from the best examples, and be honest, especially with yourself.
  - Exercise, eat and sleep well. "When in doubt, follow your curiosity. It never lies."
