- Luck matters, more so when working on your own than in an organization. The answer is to take multiple shots, which is another reason to start taking risks early.
- Ambition makes you climb existing peaks, but curiosity may be more powerful: "if you stick close enough to an interesting enough question, it may grow into a mountain beneath you."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Paul Graham argues a startup needs three things: good people, a product customers actually want, and minimal spending. Ideas matter little; founders who watch users, ship early, grow slowly, stay cheap and avoid unnecessary hiring are most likely to win.

chunks.heading: The three requirements and why ideas matter little
chunks.text:
- Paul says a startup needs three things: "good people, to make something customers actually want, and to spend as little money as possible." Most failures come from missing one of these.
- A startup that does all three "will probably succeed." None needs brilliance; each is "hard, but doable."
- An idea is only a starting point. VCs will tell you to get lost if you demand an NDA, so "the market price is less than the inconvenience of signing an NDA."
- Plans change en route. Microsoft started by selling programming languages and found its real model only when IBM "dropped it in their lap five years later."
- "Good people can fix bad ideas, but good ideas can't save bad people."

chunks.heading: Finding ideas: do it in a way that doesn't suck
chunks.text:
- Google's plan was "simply to create a search site that didn't suck." Its three ideas were indexing more of the Web, ranking by links, and clean pages with unintrusive keyword ads. The result brought in about a billion dollars a year (Paul's note: roughly $2B in revenue, half from ads on other sites).
- His main heuristic: look at something people are trying to do and figure out how to do it better. Dating sites in 2005 were worse than pre-Google search because they modelled "database matches" instead of how dating works.
- Look for people unlike you. The only software you can build without studying users is software for which you are the typical user, which is mostly open source. So ask what people who are not like you want from technology.
- Niche markets give the best odds. For every Apple or Google there are twenty startups in niches or infrastructure. Corporate IT departments are a prime target: companies spend huge sums on software and get "crap in return."
- Tactic: spend a couple of weeks watching a middle-sized non-technology company use its computers.

chunks.heading: Hiring and founders: the "animal" test
chunks.text:
- Paul's best hiring rule: "Could you describe the person as an animal?" It means someone who takes their work a little too seriously: a salesperson who won't take no, a hacker who stays up till 4 AM rather than leave a bug, a PR person who cold-calls New York Times reporters.
- To apply it, imagine the sentence "so-and-so is an animal." If you laugh, they aren't one.
- Programmers also had to pass three tests: genuinely smart, able to get things done, and bearable to have around.
- A sign of real smarts is the ability to say "I don't know," "Maybe you're right," and "I don't understand x well enough." Robert Morris was the model.
- Hire through friends. Being friends with someone for a couple of days tells you more than interviews can.
- Aim for two to four founders. One is too heavy a moral burden, and more than that breeds factions. "You don't want mere voting; you need unanimity."
- Founders must include technical people. Business people can't tell which hackers are good ("for business people it's roulette") or which problems are hard.
- Business is no great mystery: "You just try to get people to pay you for stuff." Few Forbes 400 members have MBAs, so learning to hack beats an MBA.
- On hiring generally: "hiring people is the worst thing a company can do." Staff are a recurring expense, they slow decisions into meetings, and they push you out of your space. "The only reason to hire someone is to do something you'd like to do but can't." Fewer employees at the same revenue is more impressive.

chunks.heading: Making what customers want
chunks.text:
- Failed businesses almost always failed because customers didn't want the product. Restaurants with great food prosper despite crowding, noise or bad service; Paul says he can't name a startup with a massively popular product that failed.
- "Ran out of funding" is only the proximate cause. The deeper cause is usually that the product was "a dog."
- Release version 1 as soon as possible and refine it from user reactions. He rejects the "Hail Mary" approach of planning elaborately, hiring engineers, and spending two million dollars on something nobody wants.
- Viaweb changed plan repeatedly. Web consultants disliked it because the easy, hosted software made them easy to fire. Catalog-company middle managers saw the Web as extra work in 1996. Most users ended up being small individual merchants, so the team focused on ease of use.
- Ease of use compounds: "A 10% improvement in ease of use doesn't just increase your sales 10%. It's more likely to double your sales."
- Method for learning what users want: watch them. Viaweb used trade shows as market research rather than lead generation, showing people how to build real stores and watching them use the software.
- Put users before advertisers: "get all the users, and the advertisers will follow." Design to please users first, then work out how to make money.
- Understanding your business is the key. Google understood search; Yahoo treated it as a shrinking share of page views, though search is where sessions start.

chunks.heading: Selling to small customers and owning the low end
chunks.text:
- Start by selling to smaller companies. Big-company sellers spend heavily on sales: "you can outhack Oracle with one frontal lobe tied behind your back, you can't outsell an Oracle salesman."
- Smaller customers are also strategically more valuable because "the low end always eats the high end." It is easier to make a cheap product more powerful than a powerful product cheaper.
- Examples: Sun over mainframes, Intel over Sun, Microsoft Word over Interleaf and Framemaker, Avid over specialized video editing, Henry Ford over earlier car makers.
- "It's very dangerous to let anyone fly under you." Own the cheapest, easiest product or you're in the crosshairs of whoever does.
- Avoid selling to the government (note 4).

chunks.heading: Raising money and setting up the company
chunks.text:
- Paul advises taking investor money: self-funding means starting as a consulting company, which is hard to turn into a product company. "Financially, a startup is like a pass/fail course", so maximize the chance of success, not the stock you keep.
- Seed capital is a few tens of thousands of dollars from angels, often tech-rich people. Checks can arrive within a week on a half-page agreement. Viaweb began with $10,000 from Julian, who also gave legal and business help, and in return took 10%. The company was valued at $1 million because Julian said no one would invest at a lower valuation.
- The business plan at this stage is a brief description of what you'll do, how you'll make money, and founders' resumes. It takes a couple of hours to write.
- Valuation has "no rational way" of being set at this stage. A 5% stake for $100,000 implies a $2 million pre-money valuation.
- Stock split rule of thumb: "When everyone feels they're getting a slightly bad deal... the stock is optimally apportioned."
- Have all founders sign that their ideas belong to the company and that it is their only job. Ask everyone about prior IP agreements. At Viaweb, an early employee's grad-school sponsor agreement threatened the acquisition; it nearly killed the company, then Yahoo bought it six months later for more than the first acquirer had offered.
- Start talking to VCs before cash runs low, since they take months to decide. VCs may want to install a mature "newscaster" CEO; Viaweb avoided this by funding entirely with angels.
- Your leverage is higher than you think because it is a seller's market. Treat a VC mainly as a source of money and favor "whoever offered the most money the soonest with the least strings attached."
- Don't be overtly secretive with VCs, but keep a few critical technical details back. Talk to many VCs even if you don't want their money: they may sit on the board of a future acquirer, and impressing them discourages them from funding competitors.

chunks.heading: Not spending money and growing slowly
chunks.text:
- Almost every failed startup's proximate cause is running out of money. Despite millions in the bank, "you're still poor": a rich company is one with large revenues, and investor money isn't revenue.
- Brand advertising is a "sign of breakage" unless products are undifferentiated, like cigarettes or vodka. Google never advertised and still overtook Yahoo, Lycos, Excite and Altavista.
- "Get big slow." Viaweb launched in early 1996 and had about 70 users by year-end. That year was a lab for improving the software, so competitors never caught up. The founders learned every job, including sales and customer support (Paul fixed bugs while customers were on the phone).
- Smart early users are the most valuable asset: they tell you how to make a winning product, and they pay you.
- Culture of cheapness: Yahoo's David Filo called himself "Cheap Yahoo." Model the company on a grad student, not a law firm. Viaweb had office chairs whose arms fell off.
- Office tactics: rent an apartment instead of corporate space. People work better there, and locations with restaurants nearby let teams eat dinner together and return to work. "The key to productivity is for people to come back to work after dinner."

chunks.heading: Who should start a startup
chunks.text:
- Paul's profile: a good hacker aged roughly 23 to 38 who wants to "solve the money problem in one shot."
- The lower bound of 23 exists so you've seen an existing business first (negative lessons count) and so VCs, customers and employees take you seriously. The upper bound reflects stamina and financial risk.
- A startup "compresses your working life into the smallest possible space": work like hell for four years instead of 40. Paul worked nearly constantly for three years, and only about 10% of the work was fun.
- "So mainly what a startup buys you is time."
- Grad students can stay in school at first; two of Viaweb's three original hackers kept their degrees.
- His closing summary: "Build something users love, and spend less than you make."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Paul Graham argues that falling startup costs shift power from employers and investors to young hackers. Rather than being undervalued as employees, talented people can be valued directly by users and acquirers by building something people want. Big companies will increasingly buy early startups, fusing recruiting and product development.

chunks.heading: Why founders can now start companies young
chunks.text:
- Paul notes that the founders of Yahoo, Google and Microsoft averaged 24 years old, so "grad students can start successful companies." He asks, "if grad students can do it, why not undergrads?"
- Starting a Web startup now costs so little that "it has disappeared into the noise." The main cost is "food and rent," so "you can probably start a startup on ten thousand dollars of seed funding, if you're prepared to live on ramen."
- The cheaper it is, the less founders need investors' permission. The group freed up most are people with "everything investors want except experience."
- He thinks undergraduates are undervalued. There is a huge spread in the value of 20-year-olds, and some are "more capable than all but a handful of 30 year olds."
- Young people are hard to judge because they change fast, vary a lot and are individually inconsistent. Filtering out anyone who says stupid things produces many false positives.
- Large organizations will always undervalue the most productive young people. The young have no performance to measure yet, and guesses about them regress to the mean.

chunks.heading: Starting a startup as a way to be paid market rate
chunks.text:
- Any employer is economically a proxy for the customer, and its salary offer is a guess at your value to users.
- A productive young person can skip that guess by starting a company, so users value them directly.
- The market is "a lot more discerning than any employer" and "completely non-discriminatory." Users don't know or care if you are 22.
- Paul asks: "Why go work as an ordinary employee for a big company, when you could start a startup and make them buy it to get you?"
- Most successful startups succeed by getting bought, and acquirers usually want the people as well as the technology.
- Big companies often buy before profitability. "When a startup gets bought for 2 or 3 million six months in, it's really more of a hiring bonus than an acquisition."
- This helps founders, who get money up front. It helps acquirers too, because valuing each person's work is the central problem of big companies. Buying "larval startups" means they "don't pay till the developers have proven themselves," so they are protected on the downside and keep most of the upside.

chunks.heading: Why big companies are bad at product development
chunks.text:
Paul says this is "the raison d'etre of startups." Big companies are good at extracting value from existing products and bad at creating new ones. His reasons:

- **Turf:** They protect existing businesses. Microsoft must be ambivalent about Web-based software because it threatens the desktop, so a product like Hotmail ends up coming from outside.
- **Power:** "Disruptive technologies are developed by disruptive people," who have little influence in big companies or don't work there.
- **One of each thing:** With one Web browser you can't take risks. Ten startups building ten browsers, with the best taken, gives something better. There may be 500 startups Microsoft might buy, more than it could run in-house.
- **Pay:** Big-company staff get paid about the same whether the product succeeds or fails. Startup staff get rich or get nothing, so they work harder.
- **Bigness:** Startup developers must talk to users because nobody else does sales and support. "It's painful doing sales, but you learn much more from trying to sell people something than reading what they said in focus groups."
- **Speed:** Product development needs many fast iterations, and everything is slower in big companies.

chunks.heading: What acquirers should do
chunks.text:
- Pride is a main obstacle. Buying startups feels like an admission of failure, so companies delay and pay more.
- Paul says acquirers should find startups young, before VCs have "puffed them up into something that costs hundreds of millions." Much of what VCs add, the acquirer doesn't need.
- Grabbing a likely winner for a tenth or a twentieth of the later price means predicting only a twentieth as well.
- He expects a hybrid of investment and acquisition, such as buying a chunk with an option to buy the rest later.
- Buying a startup fuses recruiting and product development. The team is committed to what it works on and its conflicts have been "ironed out under the very hot iron of running a startup." That matters in software because many bugs occur at the boundaries between different people's code.

chunks.heading: Founders' growing power over investors
chunks.text:
- Investors' power comes from money, so cheaper startups mean less investor power.
- Conventional VC wisdom has hackers accept MBAs as bosses, taking a title like CTO. Paul expects founders to push back on control.
- Fairchild Semiconductor, the first VC-backed startup, started in 1959 and needed factories. Today, more money "can't get software written faster," and facilities are cheap.
- Money mainly buys sales and marketing, and "marketing is increasingly irrelevant. On the Internet, anything genuinely good will spread by word of mouth."
- Google is his example. Investors required an older, experienced CEO, but the founders delayed a full year and chose someone with a computer science PhD. He suspects Google did better than if they had let an MBA take over after the first round.
- Paul grants that VC-installed business people have value but says they don't need to be bosses. He predicts they will increasingly be COOs rather than CEOs, with founders running engineering directly and the rest of the company through the COO.

chunks.heading: Taking risk early, and the "open cage"
chunks.text:
- Risk and reward are proportionate because "people will pay extra for stability." Choosing stability, such as a job at a big company, costs you.
- Young people have time to invest, and "your early twenties are exactly the time to take insane career risks."
- Extreme choices like startups scare most people off, so there is less competition than the prizes suggest.
- The math is "brutal": perhaps 9 in 10 startups fail, but the one that succeeds pays founders "more than 10 times what they would have made in an ordinary job." In a note he says the 1-in-10 success rate is "a bit of an urban legend" and the odds are probably slightly worse.
- Failing at 22 means being "broke and a lot smarter" at 23, which is roughly what a graduate program gives.
- A failed startup doesn't hurt job prospects. Paul asked managers at Yahoo, Google, Amazon, Cisco and Microsoft about two 24-year-olds of equal ability. One had a failed startup and the other had worked at a big company, and all preferred the startup founder. Zod Nazem, head of engineering at Yahoo, said: "I actually put more value on the guy with the failed startup. And you can quote me!"
- He compares this to animals not noticing the cage is open, and to blogging, which only took off about eight years after people could have published online. He thinks most undergrads haven't realized "the economic cage is open."

chunks.heading: Think about users, not employers
chunks.text:
- Undergrads spend their lives thinking about what employers want, but "what really matters is what customers want," because customers fund the employer.
- Big companies like "docile conformists," but that is "an artifact of their bigness, not something customers need."
- Paul says the end of school is "the fulcrum of your life," where you go from net consumer to net producer.
- Inexperience usually means not realizing you must make something people want. Technical skill and spending discipline are rarely the problem.
- His fix is to "smack hackers on the side of the head": "Don't sit here making up a priori theories about what users need. Go find some users and see what they need."
- Most successful startups do something very specific and solve a problem people already know they have.
- Real use differs from stated purpose. The stated purpose of PowerPoint is to present ideas, but its real role is to overcome fear of public speaking.
- "The goal in a startup is not to write a cool piece of software. It's to make something people want." Little school software has users, so this takes a mental adjustment.
- Employers are "proxies for users in which risk is pooled." A young, smart person can figure out what users want and doesn't want to pool risk.

chunks.heading: Grad school, dropping out, and caveats
chunks.text:
- Grad school is a good launch pad: smart people around you and large blocks of free time. With a tolerant advisor you can develop an idea first.
- David Filo and Jerry Yang started the Yahoo directory in February 1994 and had a million hits a day by fall, but left grad school and started the company only in March 1995.
- Another route is to try the startup first and go to grad school if it fails. Startups that tank usually do so quickly, so "within a year you'll know if you're wasting your time."
- His official advice is "Don't drop out of college to start a startup." He says it may be fine to work for a company for a couple of years first to learn how companies work.
- He concedes he couldn't have told 19-year-old Bill Gates to wait. Gates was at "ground zero of the microcomputer revolution," and waiting four years would have meant missing the Altair Basic interpreter. The Apple II launched two years later.
- Paul admits this is advice "the old tell the young, but don't expect them to listen to."
